president-in-office of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished members of the european commission, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour to appear before you for the first time as president of the government of spain, which holds the presidency of the council of the european union, to set out the priorities of the spanish presidency. the spanish presidency coincides with the change of president of this parliament. yesterday we saw the appointment of a new president of the house and the departure of a president who has carried out her work very effectively. mr cox's political and institutional figure and career guarantee that this house and the presidency will develop fruitful political and institutional relations aimed at strengthening the european union and increasing the role of the european parliament. the european parliament has made a considerable contribution to the european union through its work and its proposals, which are a constant and innovative pursuit of greater efficiency in the functioning of the union. the house has also been able to adapt the various european parliamentary traditions and to try out new forms of relationship between civil society and its political representatives, strengthening democratic control and increasing the legitimacy of the european project. nothing illustrates this better than the codecision procedure, which, however, needs to be improved in the interests of transparency and effectiveness. the spanish presidency will therefore work to ensure that the eight conciliations planned for this semester are concluded quickly. spain wishes to deepen institutional cooperation and democratic control of the union, and i therefore want to ensure the presence of the presidency in plenary sessions, as has been the practice since the previous presidency. i am committed to reporting to the house after the barcelona european council and to taking a final account of the work of this half-year after the seville european council. (applause) ladies and gentlemen, the political horizon today requires the union to be ambitious in three directions. the first is to devise a response to terrorism, from the perspective of building an area of freedom, security and justice. the second is to create an area of greater economic prosperity that safeguards the european social model. and the third is to conclude the historic opportunity of enlargement and lay the foundations for the future enlarged union. to achieve these goals successfully we need to work towards a deeper europe. with 'more europe' we will strengthen the fight against terrorism and ensure the successful introduction of the euro and, only if we are ambitious, we will complete enlargement, make progress in creating a zone of greater prosperity, strengthen the union's external role and conclude the next intergovernmental conference in a positive way. ladies and gentlemen, i want to acknowledge and thank the responsibility that this house and the european commission have shown in the fight against terrorism. the european parliament adopted a resolution calling on the european commission to present a number of initiatives to make the fight against terrorism in the european union more effective. we must continue to work on the path you and the european commission set out at that time. the european union's counter-terrorism action plan must be further developed in the rule of law to prevent any sanctuary for terrorism within our borders. in december 2001, last december, great progress was made in this area. all the union's institutions, and especially the presidency and parliament, must now work to ensure that the instruments adopted then become effective as quickly as possible. these instruments will not be effective unless, at the same time, greater cooperation is achieved between the security services and forces of the states of the union. the presidency therefore considers it a priority to set up joint investigation teams quickly, to increase the efficiency of europol's work and to prevent the financing of terrorists and those who shelter or support them. (applause) as you are well aware, terrorist organizations establish cooperation links with each other in such a way as to enable them to achieve an operational capability that goes beyond the limits set by our borders. spain wants the union to play a more active role in the fight against terrorism at international level. and a first step in this direction is the development of close cooperation in criminal law with the united states, in accordance with the principles which inform the legal order of the european union, as this house has stressed. the fight against terrorism is part of the construction of the area of freedom, security and justice. the presidency therefore considers it a priority to make progress towards a common asylum and immigration policy, improve the management of the union's external borders, strengthen the fight against drug trafficking and achieve mutual recognition of judicial decisions both in civil matters, through the european enforcement order, and in criminal matters. these initiatives require close institutional cooperation if we are to meet the deadlines for building the area of freedom, security and justice. ladies and gentlemen, the introduction of the euro is developing - i can use this expression - more than brilliantly. by the end of this month, few euro-zone citizens will be using national currencies. this is a good sign of the acceptance of the union's policies when they are implemented seriously and effectively. the strength of our currency also requires closer coordination of economic policies. this will result in a boost to the role of the eurogroup, in the strengthening of the broad economic policy guidelines and in strict compliance with the stability and growth pact. the euro will also increase the visibility of the euro area, which will oblige the presidency to ensure that the views of the union are taken into account in international forums. in the last decade, it should be remembered that europe has suffered a six-point decline in its per capita income relative to the united states of america. we must therefore push forward the modernisation of our economies to achieve greater growth. the creation of an area of greater economic and social prosperity will therefore be another focus of the presidency's work. spain intends that the european council in barcelona should address five specific areas in order to achieve 'more europe' as well. first, we will promote the interconnection and openness of european transport and communications systems. the presidency will devote its efforts to the revision of the transeuropean transport networks, the realisation of the single european sky and the further liberalisation of rail transport. the second area of barcelona's work will be the design of a european energy market based on openness, liberalisation, competition, transparency and interconnection. guided by these criteria, the presidency will examine the opening of gas and electricity markets to businesses and consumers, the rules for third party access to networks and the creation of infrastructures and interconnections between national energy markets. the integration of financial markets is also an essential condition for the proper functioning of the single currency and a basic requirement for european growth. spain will work towards meeting the timetables of the financial services action plan and to implement as soon as possible the new approach introduced by the lamfalussy report, based on the necessary respect for institutional balance. we are all aware that employment is the best way of social integration. fourthly, the barcelona european council will therefore seek, on the basis of the luxembourg process and its current framework, to place greater emphasis on the employment strategy in the analysis of the structural rigidities of labour markets, tax and social protection systems and also labour market institutions. the possibility of obtaining a good job is, of course, dependent on the possibility of obtaining a solid training which will encourage student mobility. the fifth item at the barcelona council will therefore be the work programme on education systems for 2010. we must achieve an increase in the quality and openness of european education systems to the rest of the world. ladies and gentlemen, in barcelona the candidate countries will take part for the first time in a working session of the european council. the integration of the candidates into the work on economic and social modernisation is, in my view, the best political signal of support for the enlargement which the union is seeking to achieve. enlargement will undoubtedly put an end to a bitter chapter in the past of our continent and bring countries that belong to the european family, with which we share the same values and which have suffered greatly at the hands of history, into the european family. the spanish presidency has the political will to help all the states which are ready to conclude their negotiations by the end of 2002. based on the current community acquis and the financial perspective, chapters on agriculture, regional and social cohesion policy, financial and budgetary provisions and institutional matters will be negotiated during the spanish presidency. spain will also endeavour to close all chapters which have not been concluded so far. the final conclusion of the negotiations depends on all the members of the union showing their capacity for compromise, on the commission presenting its proposals in time and, above all, on the efforts of each of the candidate countries. the european council in seville in june will assess progress. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we also know - and we want to - that the european union is called upon to play an important and growing political role in international life. the success of european integration and its economic and commercial weight require an increasingly important external profile of the union. the international situation calls for a stronger union presence in areas where peace and security are directly threatened. the spanish presidency therefore hopes to contribute to the development of an ambitious global regional strategy in central asia and afghanistan which will prevent the emergence of new foci of conflict. but it will be useless to ensure a european presence if we do not have the possibility of managing the crisis effectively and, in particular, of having military forces for operations of a limited nature requiring a rapid response. this objective will have to be completed in the near future by the effective implementation of the european security and defence policy and the definitive design of the relations of consultation and cooperation with the atlantic alliance. spain also intends to initiate a debate on this matter so that the fight against terrorism can also become an objective of the european security and defence policy. the credibility of the union's foreign policy must be based not only on its international presence but also on effective instruments for its development and, above all, on a privileged level of dialogue. in this last area, spain considers it a priority to deepen relations between the european union and north america on the one hand and the european union and russia on the other. with the former we must strengthen the transatlantic dialogue to give it greater strategic content. and with russia, spain believes that the european union should support the strategy that this country is developing at the moment. the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. ladies and gentlemen, next may the second summit between the european union, latin america and the caribbean will take place in madrid, renewing and promoting the strategic partnership between these two regions. one of the objectives of the summit will be to work with chile to advance the association and free trade agreement, and to push forward the european union's negotiations with mercosur. specific meetings between the union and the andean community and central america will also be held. i cannot but mention here our interest and concern at the development of the situation in argentina. the european union will cooperate with the argentine authorities to find realistic solutions, based on dialogue, which will restore confidence and the potential for growth and competitiveness of the argentine economy. ladies and gentlemen, the european union will also play an important role in the stability of the middle east. to do this, we must step up coordination with the united states and the other sponsors of the peace process. i hope that the recent declaration by the european union and the contacts which have been established in the last few days on the initiative of the spanish presidency will help to unblock a situation of instability which affects the countries of the region and the mediterranean. the middle east conflict has a powerful influence on the barcelona process, the only forum for dialogue bringing together all those involved in the peace process and which will meet at the ministerial summit in valencia. spain will also promote the conclusion of the outstanding association agreements between the european union and the riparian countries, and will work towards the creation of a euro-mediterranean internal market and the development of regional infrastructure strategies. to facilitate this objective, the laeken european council, at the initiative of spain, adopted the project for the creation of a bank specialising in operations in the mediterranean countries, which we will be working on in the coming months in collaboration with the european investment bank and the monetary authorities. we are convinced that only by encouraging balanced development can we effectively combat illegal immigration. conscious of the importance of this phenomenon, spain, together with the sponsorship of china and viet nam, has been working for some time to make the ministerial meeting on immigration between the european union and asem a success. we know that poverty and lack of development cause illegal immigration. that is why the presidency attaches particular importance to the monterrey summit on financing for development, which we are preparing in close cooperation with the united states and mexico. i think i can say that few people could have imagined that, 45 years after the signing of the treaties of rome, 300 million europeans would be using the same currency. we must continue this trajectory of success in a transcendent era for the union. this requires greater participation by our citizens in shaping the future of the union. the laeken european council decided to convene a convention on the future of europe. the inaugural session will be held on 28 february at the european parliament in brussels. there is no better place to reflect both the importance of the new stage of the european union and the recognition that the presidency wishes to give to the work of the european parliament on the future of europe. the spanish presidency will be determined to contribute to the success of this convention. it is up to us to consolidate the process of gradual constitutionalisation of the treaties in which we are engaged and to ensure that the convention will serve as a good method of preparing intergovernmental conferences in the future. i hope that the president of the convention - and it has been agreed - will be able to present a first report of his work at the european council in seville next june. ladies and gentlemen, i have come here today to set out the priorities of the spanish presidency. these priorities must be translated into greater de facto solidarity in order to continue to consolidate, on the basis of balance and mutual respect for the various interests, the greatest period of peace, prosperity and freedom that europe has known. we know that the task is complex and arduous, both because of the number of issues that require our dedication and because of the ambition of our goals. only with this ambition and only through close cooperation between the institutions will we be able - i am convinced of this - to make a reality of this project which has as its ultimate aim the improvement of the lives of all our citizens. thank you very much, your honours, for your attention. president of the commission. - mr president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, on new year's eve we celebrated the launch of the euro with great joy throughout europe. it has been only fifteen days since then, but that was enough to complete the transition to the new currency almost completely. in the 12 euro area countries, 90% of payments are now made in the single currency: the changeover to the euro was a huge operation and a huge success. we can all be proud of it because we all contributed to it: the european parliament and national parliaments, governments, the european central bank, national central banks, the commission, commercial banks, post offices, the trade sector, business, the media and all citizens, one by one, who have facilitated this historic change. for millions of europeans, the banknotes and coins they carry in their pockets are the tangible sign of the great political project of a united europe. it is symbolically more than the emotional impact of the abolition of identity checks at intra-community borders. the euro thus becomes a key element in their sense of european identity and common destiny, as well as a tangible sign of the irreversible nature of european integration. the changeover to the euro shows that europeans are ready to embrace change with enthusiasm and determination when it is needed to prepare for a better future and when the issues on the table are discussed in a broad and transparent way. the changeover to the euro shows that europe is capable of great things when there is the political will to do so. we must draw on this lesson to prepare all the steps we are about to take in the process of integration. mr president, mr prime minister, 'more europe' is the motto spain has chosen for its six-month presidency of the union. in the aftermath of the launch of the euro, we can safely say that no choice could have been happier. at the same time, mr prime minister, your government has drawn up a broad, but balanced and ambitious work programme, and i am pleased to note that the priorities set out in this programme are in line with those which the commission has set for 2002. i can assure you, therefore, that you can count on the commission's full cooperation. mr president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, the same ambition that enabled us to launch the new european currency successfully must now be demonstrated and put to use in order to achieve the union's economic and social agenda. we have achieved monetary union: the time has come to focus on economic union and make it a reality. we need growth, which means jobs and a better quality of life. two years ago, the lisbon european council set the objective of making the union the most dynamic and competitive economic area in the world by the end of the decade, an area based on knowledge: a europe capable of enjoying full employment and renewed social and economic cohesion at the same time. since then, the spring meetings of the european council have become the meeting place for economic, social and environmental issues within the framework of an overall sustainable development strategy. the barcelona council will therefore be called upon to take stock of the progress made so far and to define priorities for the coming years. in preparation for the council, the commission adopted yesterday its spring report, which will serve as a basis for the council's work: this year's report is entitled 'the lisbon strategy: making change happen'. the communication adopted by the commission yesterday has a central message: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. we have no choice. the strategy agreed in lisbon is the key to developing and consolidating the european economic and social model. the reforms affect a society which already has its own dynamic values, shared and distinctive from the rest of the world, and which thus contribute to the foundation of the european union. when we speak of the european social model, we have these values in mind. from this point of view, we must continue to update the model of society that is possible and desirable in europe: a free, democratic and just society that is at the heart of our citizens. it is not a question of selling off the social heritage, however, but of adapting it, modernising it and also making it permanent. we are forced by history, we are forced by the protection of future generations, we are forced by the challenge of globalisation. finally, we must do so in the present uncertain and risky environment, where the values of genuine solidarity - and not just formal and partial solidarity - are of practical significance for our citizens, especially the most vulnerable. the commission's report examines the progress made so far in implementing the lisbon strategy and concludes that all the conditions for success are in place. on the macroeconomic front, the efforts made over the last decade to introduce the euro have enabled the union to achieve economic stability and protected it at a time when international economic and financial crises were becoming more acute. even in this phase of slowdown, the underlying conditions of the economy remain good in europe. the implementation of the lisbon strategy is also progressing encouragingly. significant achievements have already been made in a number of areas, such as the environment, telecommunications, education, pension reform and research. in other areas, however, progress has been less satisfactory. the commission's proposals are blocked and the deadlines set by the european council itself are in danger of not being met. these areas include some important aspects of the integration of financial services, transport and energy, the community patent and the galileo project. i am pleased, mr president, that you have listed these areas as a priority for your action over the coming months. this delay must be made good, and it must be made good as soon as possible. it is about our credibility and, even more, about our ability to make real progress. without change, we will have less growth and less employment. the commission's report identifies three priorities for 2002: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. firstly, there is employment. europe needs an active employment policy. more needs to be done to remove the obstacles that citizens still have to overcome to find and keep a job. member states must reduce labour costs by lowering contributions to wages and salaries, especially the lowest, and must review those aspects of unemployment benefits which discourage re-entry into the labour market and the excessive ease with which early retirement is accessed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of women in the labour market. the employment rate is also supported by improving skills, education and mobility of citizens within europe and between productive sectors. this means that we must take an active rather than a passive approach to change. secondly, reforms and the completion of the internal market. we need to connect europe and its markets. efforts must be stepped up to complete the interconnection of national markets and to accelerate the integration of financial markets by completing the reforms already initiated. we need to open up and connect energy and transport markets and develop broadband networks in europe. these sectors are the backbone of our economy. we need more competition to reduce prices and increase growth, while maintaining an adequate level of basic services for all. thirdly, education, training and research. education, training and research are certainly the key components of economic renewal, sustainable growth and job creation. the 'knowledge society' is not possible without knowledge. we must therefore increase investment in these areas substantially. an integrated strategy for education and research at community level is needed. this strategy must be based on the concept of networking and mobility and must give priority to technologies of the future such as biotechnologies and clean technologies. finally, as regards the post-barcelona period, our report points to the need to take measures to strengthen the coordination of the overall economic strategy. the aim is to build consensus on economic policy principles and rules that take account of economic interdependencies within the euro area. the three processes involved must be synchronised: the main guidelines for economic policies, the employment guidelines and the process of economic reform launched in cardiff. in this way, the spring council will be able to assess economic and social policy as a whole each year and thus ensure its sustainability. only a more coherent approach will enable us to make more full and effective use of the various instruments at our disposal. we must therefore abandon the methods of the past which were fragmented by sector. mr president, the president of the commission has a role which can sometimes be uncomfortable: the european council is the body responsible for calling on its members to respect the commitments they have collectively made. however, i am sure that you will offer your support when i call on the member states in barcelona to pursue with determination the reform agenda agreed together in lisbon, following the recommendations of the report. we have a duty to ensure that the barcelona council is a complete success. if the process were to come to a halt, the cost of 'non-reform' would become unsustainable in economic terms and also in terms of the union's political credibility. ladies and gentlemen, 2002 will be a crucial year for the enlargement process and we know that the spanish presidency will spare no effort - as we have heard - to maintain the momentum so that it can conclude negotiations this year with those countries which have shown that they meet the criteria for accession. while crucial for its future, enlargement to the east is not the only external dimension in which the union is called upon to engage. relations with the mediterranean countries are a necessary priority of our external action. the spanish presidency expects the euro-mediterranean dialogue to proceed swiftly during the six-month period. it was in barcelona, moreover, that this dialogue was launched. to this end, we must adopt a more flexible approach, by initiating new forms of subregional cooperation with certain groups of countries on the southern shore. secondly, we must put into practice the common idea of the spanish presidency and the commission of a mediterranean bank. whether it is an autonomous bank or a branch of the european investment bank, it must be a place of development where european and southern mediterranean actors work side by side. it is also essential to foster and promote mutual understanding and knowledge between peoples and cultures through specific actions of different kinds. i believe that it is by exporting our experience as peacemakers and our commitment to democracy that we will bring more europe to the world. mr president, you reminded us that latin america is a region of the world geographically distant but very close to european culture and roots, a region which has shared a long historical journey with many european countries. this is the moment when the union must show strong solidarity with argentina, and mercosur in general, in a period of dramatic crisis. argentina must find the path of economic growth again, which is the only way to improve the difficult social situation it is going through. to achieve this goal, there is only one recipe, and that is to regain trust: the european union has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to fulfil its obligations under the treaty. our experience of financial recovery and economic development promoted by trade and integration can be a valuable contribution to latin america's recovery with benefits for all parties involved. mr president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to conclude by saying a few words about the convention which will be taking up its work during the spanish presidency. the convention will have the importance and the opportunity to write an exciting page in the history of europe. it is up to all of us to do everything possible to make this happen. i have already assured president giscard d'estaing of the full support of the commission and its representatives at the convention. the commission expects to work equally closely with the european parliament, the legitimate representative of the aspirations of its people. we must ensure that the debate is intense and fruitful and, above all, that it gives rise to a vision for the future in which the majority of our citizens can identify. the convention and the intergovernmental conference which will follow it must complete the construction of an open, responsible, democratic and just europe. i would like to mention three conditions: the first is a consistent implementation of the stability and growth pact. it is almost ironic that we now realise that it was my country, germany, which fought the hardest for this stability and growth pact and its strict criteria, and that in the present situation it can or must almost be assumed that germany will be the first country to be affected by the sanctions of this treaty. but i believe we must be consistent here if we want the euro to become and remain a stable currency in the long term and if we want to keep interest rates in the european union low for our companies in the long term as a prerequisite for investment and growth. the second condition is that we must pursue economic policy in the member states and the european union on the basis of common principles. these principles should be the principles of the social market economy, as the european parliament, which voted in favour by a large majority, wanted. thirdly, we must move towards political union. we said before maastricht that we wanted both monetary union and political union. we said at the time that without political union, monetary union would not be viable in the long term. we must be consistent here. we must take these steps towards political union now. the european union has a common foreign and defence policy at its core. i would like to conclude by quoting jacques delors. jacques delors has rightly pointed out in these endless debates we have had on the european single market that you cannot fall in love with a single market. so there's very little emotion involved. i would say the same thing about a currency, although there are some of us who have a very emotional, almost erotic relationship with currency. but what we need and what we must uncover is the awareness of the common european identity, of europe. i believe that this is certainly the most important task facing us as a european parliament. proposals for an environmentally friendly product. the commission must ensure that the statements are made more clearly in its future work. the important thing for my group is that the total environmental costs are included in the price of the product. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster. the european product standardisation needs to be more closely involved, but services should also be provided from an environmental perspective. another option for creating a market for environmentally friendly products is, for example, the use of economic steering instruments. we should examine their use and impact and, most importantly, we should ensure that eu environmental legislation is not relaxed. the rapporteur has done a good job in the face of the unsatisfactory commission proposal. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. we urgently need concrete proposals for the promotion of environmentally friendly products. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank parliament for its resolution on the commission's green paper and just remind you that it is a green paper, the start of the debate on integrated product policy. in particular i would like to thank mrs garcía-orcoyen tormo being such a committed rapporteur on this challenging and difficult issue. i would also like to thank you for your speeches. i would agree with a lot of what has been said during this short debate. in reducing the environmental impact of products throughout their life cycle, the objective of ipp is fundamental to addressing our environmental problems. for this reason ipp is a key measure within the sixth environment action programme and the sustainable development strategy also underlines its importance. the difficulty we face is that there are so many products on the market today, products that often have long supply chains involving many different actors. because of this it is impossible to develop a "one size fits all" instrument. instead we need a variety of instruments and exactly which ones depends on what is most effective at each point in the supply chain. they can be both voluntary and mandatory. i agree that voluntary measures should be complementary and we should make sure that they are not the only instrument used. when thinking about ipp at european level, we should also recognise the experience gained in several member states – denmark, germany, sweden and italy, to name but a few- over the last few years. there is, therefore, widespread acceptance of the concept and interest in it. in 1999 the informal environment council asked the commission to come forward with a green paper on the issue. i therefore delivered this paper to start the debate on what form the european ipp should take. the reactions to it from the 130 stakeholders who submitted comments were generally positive, but what came back was what has been reflected here, namely that it is sometimes seen as being too fluffy and not really an understandable concept. but it sounds nice, as they say, and in general the opinions of the council, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions were favourable as well. the green paper suggested a strategy and tools for making a european ipp a reality. many such tools already exist – public procurement legislation, european eco-labels and emas, to name but a few. in other areas we will have to be innovative and think of new instruments. the green paper sought to canvas the views of stakeholders on the way forward. the commission did this not just because it wanted to develop the best possible policy, but also because ipp needs the active involvement of all stakeholders to succeed. your resolution concludes this stakeholder consultation process and will enable us to develop the white paper. from your resolution and the comments from stakeholders it is clear that the white paper needs to start with concrete environmental problems. this is what we have learnt from this discussion. issues such as climate change, hazardous chemicals and biodiversity affect us all. if we take environmental problems rather than instruments as our point of departure, we can better convey the idea that ipp is more than just a collection of tools, something that we perhaps did not do sufficiently in the green paper. we have to link it to concrete environmental problems to describe how to use these instruments. this is also what mrs paulsen referred to. these tools will still be important. we need to continue developing them because we cannot address millions of products individually. however, i too am coming to the conclusion that we need to focus our actions on particular products and sectors. you rightly make this suggestion in paragraphs 24 and 25 of your resolution. we will also need to set out the strategy for implementing ipp and its advantages and the commission will need to consider carefully the measures within ipp's scope as well as how it relates to other policies. it is my intention to ask the commission to adopt this paper during the second quarter of this year.

- the next item is the recommendation (a5-0412/2001) by mr rod, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the proposal for a council decision on the conclusion of the partnership agreement between the african, caribbean and pacific states, of the one part, and the european community and its member states, of the other part [2117/2000 - com (2000) 324 - c5-0417/2000 - 2000/0124 (avc) ].
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is not left in the lurch. the limited speaking time does not allow for a full assessment of the agreement, and i must therefore confine myself to a few aspects. the cotonou agreement represents the continuation of european cooperation with the developing countries of africa, the caribbean and the pacific. it began with the yaoundé agreement and has been extended since 1975 by a total of four lomé conventions. the first lomé convention was signed by 46 acp countries and nine member states of what was then the european community. the cotonou agreement now links 77 acp countries and 15 eu countries. the broadest content base is more important than the geographical extension. the breakdown of the blocs and the political upheavals which followed throughout the world, including the acp states, gave greater importance to the political and commercial dimensions. respect for human rights and the application of democratic principles, the rule of law, good governance and the strengthening of civil society are important treaty provisions, the violation of which may be subject to sanctions. the political dialogue enshrined in the cotonou agreement and the commitment to peacebuilding, conflict prevention and resolution, and the fight against poverty as a stated objective, are important instruments of acp cooperation, but unfortunately they are no guarantee of success. the keywords may suffice: sudan, the horn of africa, the congo, zimbabwe, islamism and hiv/aids. parliamentary monitoring of acp cooperation is a world model. it has been upgraded by the cotonou agreement. this strengthens its role as an open forum for discussion and control, in addition to its parliamentary character. this is also part of the new quality of the cotonou agreement, and this also makes it easy for us as a group to agree to this agreement. commission. – mr president, allow me first to congratulate members of parliament on having taken this important step in the process of approval of the cotonou agreement. you all know how important it is to complete the ratification process in order to be able to implement the agreement fully, including its financial component. you also know how important the acp-ec relationship is in the framework of the community’s development policy. one very important aspect is that the text of the cotonou agreement is a negotiated text. this is also indirectly reflected in the comments from many in this debate about the fact that having the agreement is quite an achievement. the way we obtained it was through real negotiations. this is what mr howitt pointed out in presenting this as a model for a more global relationship between north and south. there are many deficiencies in it and much of the criticism comes from the fact that it is still very ambitious and it is difficult to implement. this has to do with the expectations we have as to what our partner countries actually put into the programming process. this is not for us alone to decide, which is partly my response to mr howitt's comments. i shall now make some brief comments on the report as such. i find the report’s approach towards the trade dimension of cotonou interesting, although i cannot agree with all of it. certainly, the report’s evaluation of the economic and trade regime under cotonou is based on a political view of development and north-south relations. for example, we do not agree with the report that the cotonou agreement is in favour of "development only through market laws". in our view, the cotonou agreement provides a comprehensive framework, integrating trade as one instrument among others to promote sustainable development. the core element of future trade relations will be the economic partnership agreements which aim to create favourable conditions to enhance both the volume and the benefits of trade. it is true, negotiations of regional economic partnership agreements will aim at the progressive and flexible liberalisation of trade flows and at the integration of acp countries into the world economy. but this will be in line with their level of development and will take into account the socio-economic impact of trade measures. repas will be based on regional integration, strengthening and deepening the existing regional integration initiatives. this is also why i do not share the view expressed by mr belder that these initiatives could be some sort of risk, in relation to conflict prevention. we clearly have the expectation that this regional cooperation will be part of conflict prevention and strengthen it. this is what experience tells us. repas will also be linked to comprehensive economic and social measures which can be financed through the edf. this is not sufficiently reflected in the report. some statements in the report could, in our view, be more precise. for example, the reference to eu beef exports to western africa is highly critical of substituting local beef by subsidised eu beef. however, this argument is based on eu exports from 1981 to 1991. we are now in 2002 and the community’s export policy to developing countries has changed in recent years. in particular, since the early 1990s we have considerably reduced the export refunds for beef exports to western africa, precisely to avoid any substitution of local beef by subsidised eu beef. as a consequence, there has been a progressive decrease of eu beef exports to ecowas countries from a level of 54 000 tonnes in 1991 to only 1600 tonnes in 2000. this is a classical case. we have had a number of them in the debate about coherence. most of these cases are historical cases and they have all been solved. but there are other very real, meaningful important problems to discuss within the framework of the debate on coherence, so i would strongly advise everybody in this debate to put the finger on the real problems instead of providing only archaeological material. there is also a certain confusion in the report when it comes to trade relations with ldcs. it is stated that ldcs would automatically opt for the everything but arms regime, whereas non-ldcs had the choice between economic partnership agreements and the normal gsp regime. this is not the case. on the contrary, it is important to stress that ldcs will be part of the regional economic partnership agreements process. repas will tackle all barriers to trade, including issues such as sanitary and phytosanitary measures or technical barriers to trade and will build on the existing regional integration initiatives. both are highly relevant for ldcs. finally, let me emphasise that repas need to be integrated into the development strategies of the acp and the ec. it will therefore be essential that negotiations on the repas and implementation on the one hand, development policies on the other, are mutually supportive and that appropriate eu support measures are included in regular edf financing. repas will set a trade policy framework which will need to be fully coherent with development policies. it is true that the objectives of the cotonou trade agenda are ambitious but doing nothing and continuing with our past approach would incur major risks and would probably not reverse the economic marginalisation of acp countries. when we look at what has happened so far on the basis of the instruments of the past, this is quite obvious. the cotonou agreement provides the instruments to help acp countries to integrate in the world economy and to reduce poverty. we have to use them in the best possible way. it would be a misunderstanding to think that our agreement here and our instruments can do the trick. there are very good basic reasons why these poor countries are not well integrated into the world economy. there are real problems there. the report is written as if it were a realistic assumption that as part of the engineering and the negotiations underlying the cotonou agreement we could easily have confronted and changed many of the underlying global issues. i hope i am not shocking anyone by saying that it is not as easy as that. it never was an option to offer the acp countries a framework of economic development that was not based on the fact that the market economy is here to stay. but this is not the same as saying that the market is the only method. the commission disagrees with that statement. in fact the whole endeavour of our acp-eu cooperation, as well as the rest of our global development cooperation effort, is proof of the fact that we are trying to do something that could never have been done if development was left to the market as such. this is why we do it. let me end on a more conciliatory note by quoting from the conclusion of the report, which i strongly support. the commission is aware of the seriousness of the situation in the member states, and it is aware of the seriousness of the problems facing the community. this proposal is not the whole of the european drug policy: this proposal concerns only a specific component which has to do with the fight against drug trafficking. but the approach to drugs in the european union is set out in the action plan for 2000-04, which will be evaluated midway through this year. in laaken, the heads of state and government asked us to adopt by the end of may this year the framework decision on the harmonization of criminal sanctions at european level for drug trafficking. and that is the sole purpose of this proposal. the commission believes that in the fight against drug trafficking, close cooperation between the different judicial, police and customs authorities of the member states is necessary to respond to the challenge of transnational drug trafficking. such cooperation, if it is to be effective, needs to be based on a common approach at union level, in particular the approximation of the definitions of criminal offences and penalties applicable to trafficking, which must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. we welcome the objectives of mr oostlander's report. it is clear that the repressive measures against traffickers must be supplemented and completed by a policy of prevention and social reintegration of drug addicts. the nature of the instrument envisaged is that it is aimed solely at the repressive aspects of the drug phenomenon. the commission has worked to prepare this criminal initiative with full knowledge of the facts, thanks to the considerable preparatory work we have carried out, in particular by studying the definitions in each of the member states, the sanctions applicable in law and - not least - the concrete conditions for applying criminal sanctions for drug trafficking in each of the 15 member states. this study, which has been made public, has thus made it possible to compare the drug trafficking legislation of all the member states. the first important point to be made is that the aim is to harmonize criminal sanctions for drug trafficking. this proposal cannot be considered as restricted to transnational or cross-border trafficking. because one of two things: either in most cases the drug trafficking originates outside europe and is always transnational, or i do not see how it is possible to want to punish more severely a cross-border trafficking than serious trafficking that occurs within each member state. states cannot have two criminal codes, one to apply to drug trafficking exclusively within their borders and another to apply to drug trafficking when it involves a cross-border dimension. we now come to the second question: the definition of drug trafficking. the commission has already been criticised for being too unambitious in this respect. what did we do? we have simply taken the key elements of the 1988 united nations convention against illicit traffic in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances and integrated this definition with national provisions on the definition of drug trafficking offences. it is, in that sense, an attempt to find a synthesis of drug trafficking definition. but here - third important point - we have respected the principle of subsidiarity. and so this definition does not include individual drug use, nor does it include non-profit transactions for personal use. these matters are left to the exclusive jurisdiction of each member state because, as this debate has shown, the solutions of the 15 member states differ substantially in this area. the commission proposal does not therefore alter these differences in national legislation in those areas where drug trafficking for personal consumption is considered to be outside the scope of criminal sanctions. but when trafficking is of such a scale and gravity that it should be subject to criminal sanctions, the commission proposes that they be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. the minimum sentence of a maximum sentence of five years is a penalty which not only gives the judges a wide margin of manoeuvre in applying the law according to the circumstances of each trafficking case, but is also a proposal which is intended to give an idea of the severity with which the drug trafficking cases to which this penalty applies are intended to be punished. i know that in some countries - mr carlos coelho referred to the portuguese case - the minimum penalty of the maximum penalty is heavier. i should like to say that in others it is lighter, and that this figure of five years seems to us to correspond to a minimum level of harmonization, naturally leaving it to the legislation of each member state to establish other, more severe levels of minimum sanction for the maximum penalty applied. but this is a matter for discussion at council level. i therefore believe that this proposal, which i hope parliament will adopt, is a first step in a fight in which all member states are involved against drug trafficking which threatens the health, safety and quality of life of citizens and which, as mr oostlander has pointed out, is one of the sources of funding for many other criminal activities, including terrorism itself. in this context, i hope that parliament will support the report and create the conditions for the council to adopt this framework decision by the end of may this year.
- doc. a5-0436/2001 by mrs ludford, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on the status of third-country nationals who are longterm residents (com (2001) 127 - c5-0250/2001 - 2001/0074 (cns)); - a5-0455/2001 by mrs kessler, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on the conditions under which third-country nationals may move freely within the territory of the member states for a period not exceeding three months, introducing a specific travel authorisation and laying down the conditions of entry for a stay not exceeding six months.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i have to go. the common rules governing the conditions under which third-country nationals may move freely within the territory of the member states are very welcome. the committee's work has repeatedly criticised the fragmented attempts to regulate the situation, following a french and a portuguese initiative. a more global approach to free movement in the schengen area was called for. this requirement is met by the present commission proposal for a directive. the first is to regulate and harmonise the conditions under which third-country nationals may enjoy freedom of movement for a maximum of three months. this is in accordance with the treaty of amsterdam, which requires the council to define the conditions within five years of its entry into force. the second is the introduction of a completely new instrument - the special travel authorization. this allows for a travel exemption extended to six months under special conditions. first of all, i do not understand why the legal instrument of the directive was chosen and not that of the regulation. the text is sufficiently specific. since a directive requires national transposition, the application of the act is delayed indefinitely. in addition, this act replaces, inter alia, regulation 1091/2001, which has already entered into force. it is for this reason that the legal instrument of the regulation is the most appropriate instrument. the content of the freedom of movement for third-country nationals who are not subject to the visa requirement and for holders of long-term residence permits has not changed. however, a new regulation will apply to holders of national long-stay visas issued by the member states who do not yet have a residence permit. contrary to the commission's proposal, i believe that such thirdcountry nationals should continue to be able to travel within the territory of the member states even before an application for the issue of such a residence permit has been made. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the schengen agreement is respected. this would be incomprehensible to all concerned. moreover, there is no reason why this category should be treated differently and worse than the other third-country nationals covered by the directive as regards the beginning of the freedom to travel. however, third-country nationals travelling on a national visa must then also meet the same criteria as third-country nationals travelling on a schengen uniform visa. this is the result of the equalization of visas for the area of freedom of movement. this means that the consultation procedures between member states on the confidential lists 5a and 5b of the consular instructions must also apply to national visas. the member states which have reservations about third country nationals from certain countries would otherwise have no means of knowing and controlling the issuing of national visas by other member states. this would create a security gap which is unacceptable after the events of 9/11. the committee held a lively discussion on this point. nevertheless, the committee supported my proposal by a large majority. this result confirms the strength of the committee to take a new decision on a matter which has already been voted on, in the light of changed circumstances.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i now turn to the ludford report, which is primarily concerned with ensuring better conditions through more rights for people who have been living here legally for a long time. that's a good approach. the problem is that third country nationals are a kind of third class of citizens within the eu, after the nationals of a particular country and then, secondly, the nationals of the other eu countries. the report continues this distinction, and thus also justifies the fact that there will never be a definitive non-discrimination. because if you really want to ensure that there are equal rights for all, you must also level these differences. the second point is even more important to me. once again, it is about improving the rights of long-term residents in the eu. but this is only a very specific group, those with legal status. that's gonna get rid of all the people who live here illegally. now, one might say, okay, the illegal immigrants are not part of the report and that is why we do not want to talk about them today, but that is precisely the problem: it is always only about people with legal residence status and almost all other legislative projects - the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, and that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. in our view, the status of third-country nationals who are long-term residents in the territory of a member state is a fundamental element in the development of a common immigration policy. the long-term resident status puts admission policies in a long-term perspective, offering third-country nationals who so wish the guarantee of being able to reside permanently in their host state. this status, as proposed by the commission, gives them the legal certainty they need to be able to integrate successfully into european societies. the objective stated in tampere and reiterated in laaken is to ensure fair treatment for legal immigrants and to offer them rights and obligations comparable to those of citizens of the european union. the commission proposal aims to bring the rights of longterm residents closer to those of union citizens. we have defined the precise and objective conditions to which third-country nationals must be subject to obtain long-term resident status. these conditions were formulated essentially to assess whether the third-country national has in fact permanently established his residence in the member state in question and whether he intends to integrate there. you must have lived in that member state for a sufficiently long period (five years) and have proven your economic integration through income and sickness insurance. furthermore, the person concerned must not constitute a threat to public policy. the report on which the honourable members are debating also indicates an additional condition for the status: the knowledge of the language of the country of residence. the commission considers that language is a criterion of integration and therefore language learning must be at the heart of the new integration policies on which the commission is currently working in the spirit of its november 2000 communication and on which we intend to present an initiative to the parliament and the council in 2003. that is why i am willing to take account of the language question, which is proposed in an amendment signed by mrs eva klamt, especially in its objective dimension and, in particular, when the host state provides immigrants with effective conditions for their learning. as regards the addition of a new requirement on old age insurance or retirement insurance, i do not think it is useful to multiply the conditions for obtaining long-term resident status. the legislation of most member states now grants this status automatically without checking whether or not such a condition for old-age insurance is fulfilled. this question must be integrated into a wider and more complex issue which has to do with the relationship between migrant workers and social benefit schemes in general. the commission is therefore working to extend to thirdcountry nationals the benefit of regulation no 1408/71 on the coordination of social security schemes. and we think that's the context in which this issue should be addressed. with regard to some of the proposed amendments, the commission believes that only when longterm resident status is granted will the beneficiary be able to enjoy equal treatment with nationals of the member states in virtually all areas of socioeconomic life. however, we are sensitive to the amendments which are being tabled to enshrine, even before the granting of status, equal treatment in legal proceedings and in appeals as contained in the amendments tabled by mrs ludford, and we will incorporate them into the text. the commission does not comment on participation in political life, as it considers that there is no legal basis in the treaties for dealing with this matter. some of the proposed amendments reflect a particular concern for public order, which is fully understandable after the events of 11 september. i share the view expressed here in the course of the debate that we must avoid making the mistake of making a dangerous conflation between immigration and terrorism, which would lead to a kind of general suspicion of all third-country nationals. the commission has drawn up a working document on the relationship between safeguarding internal security and respect for international protection obligations and instruments. in the light of this document we have checked all the public policy clauses in our proposals. this work aimed to ensure that member states were able to effectively protect their public order in the face of the terrorist threat. this examination has led the commission to revise some of its proposals, including the present proposal, in particular with regard to two points: abolish the requirement that the threat be effective before the granting of status, thus addressing cases of potential risk as they can already be interpreted in the light of the current wording of the 1951 geneva convention; we also lifted the ban on emergency expulsion measures, provided certain assumptions are verified. i believe that these two amendments are in response to the concerns of ensuring internal security and the fight against terrorism and that in this sense the proposed amendments should not be considered. finally, the innovation and the important added value of this proposal is the right granted to longterm residents to move to another member state. in this case, integration is no longer only at national level, but also at european level. and people who have lived for a certain time in one member state will be in a better position than those who come directly from their country of origin whenever they want to move to another member state. i think this is a very important aspect which should not be neglected. as regards the proposal on the free movement of thirdcountry nationals, which is the subject of a report by mrs kessler, i would first like to stress that the proposal contains important elements in terms of creating an area of freedom, security and justice. the schengen acquis already includes certain rules on the movement of thirdcountry nationals. however, the conditions attached to the exercise of this freedom to travel are not always transparent and are spread over several instruments. the commission shares the view of the european parliament that it is necessary to bring together in a single legal instrument all the fragmented elements which define this freedom to travel. the proposal thus lays down the conditions under which third-country nationals may move freely, whether or not they are subject to the visa requirement, whether they have a residence document or a long-stay visa, while awaiting the issuance of a residence document. the proposal also aims to regulate the movement of various categories of persons who have a legitimate interest in staying for a period of between three and six months in the borderless area without their situation being equivalent to immigration in the strict sense. for example, tourists, researchers, touring musicians, people visiting family, hospitalization and convalescence cases. for these people, a specific travel authorisation is to be introduced allowing them to travel for a maximum of six months without staying for more than three months in the same member state, which is fully in line with the letter of the treaty. the majority of the amendments in mrs kessler's report are intended to clarify and clarify the content of the proposal. as regards the question of the legal instrument, it is proposed that a regulation be chosen rather than a directive. the commission supports any solution which, in the council, takes up its suggestions. the only point of disagreement we have with mrs kessler's proposal concerns amendment no 5 on movement in a borderless area with a long-stay visa, which, as mr deprez has already pointed out, must be examined with caution. we ask parliament not to approve it. a long-stay visa is a national visa, which will be issued according to national rules and not according to the rules of chapter 3 - section i of the convention implementing the schengen agreement. in this context, i think it is difficult to impose on long-stay visas the rules laid down for short-stay visas, i.e. prior consultation. during the debate on the french initiative on long-stay visas, this type of proposal was already rejected by parliament, which questioned in particular the legal basis and, above all, the fragmented approach. in the same spirit as parliament had already approved it, the commission also questioned the legal basis and stated that it would in any case submit a proposal which would also include long-stay visa holders and thus take up the objective of the french initiative and place it in a more global framework. i share the concern underlying amendment no 5, namely that a third country national should be able to move about immediately in the borderless area. but this possibility already exists today because a third country national can always apply for a uniform visa, the so-called 'c' visa, and move freely on the basis of it. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs and hope that the proposals put forward by the commission will find support across the border in this parliament.

european council. the aim is, of course, to achieve a strong and solid capital market throughout the union, and for its citizens and businesses a market which will produce better prospects for employment and growth throughout europe. we have reached a fair and honourable compromise and together we must seize this moment. i am confident that this day will produce a positive result, a strong it clear, in order to avoid any possible misunderstanding, that together with this declaration the commission will also implement the resolution of the stockholm european council and the elements points of major importance: firstly, the commission will respect the co-decision rights of this parliament and the rights of information and transparency which are the basis of our democratic process. in full respect of the present institutional balances, the commission will deal with this parliament and the council on an equal footing; secondly, the commission will take into account fully and without exception the position of the european parliament, as set out in the stockholm european council resolution, and will do everything in its power to find appropriate solutions within the framework of the current institutional balances; thirdly, in the future, in the context of the revision of the treaties, the commission would like to see article 202 amended and more clarity on the future executive tasks and the equal role of the two co-legislators. i now read the formal statement on behalf of the european commission. 'the integration of financial services markets is fundamental to the consolidation of the european economy, as established by the lisbon and stockholm european councils. in order to achieve this objective, it is crucial that the financial services action plan is implemented within the time limits set by the european council conclusions: 2005 for the action plan as a whole and 2003 for the securities market measures. in the context of the barcelona european council, which will examine the state of progress of the union's economic reform defined in lisbon, the commission welcomes the close cooperation between the community institutions. it also expresses its confidence in its harmonious development in order to implement its proposals, drawn up on the basis of the recommendations of the committee of wise men, chaired by baron lamfalussy. in general, the commission stated in the white paper on european governance that its executive responsibilities should be better defined and that the council and parliament should have the same role in monitoring how the commission exercises this mandate. in the white paper the commission also indicated its intention to initiate a discussion on this subject at the next intergovernmental conference and expressed its support for an amendment to article 202 of the treaty establishing the european community. pending the next revision of the treaties, flexible regulatory mechanisms are needed in the field of financial services, without setting a precedent and in full respect of the institutional balance. in this connection, the commissioner responsible sent a letter to the chairman of parliament's committee on economic and monetary affairs on 2 october 2001. in this context, the commission is therefore able to: - take note of parliament's intention to limit the duration of the delegation of executive powers to the commission to four years. the period shall be calculated from the entry into force of the corresponding directive and may be extended by an extension proposed by the commission and accepted by the parliament and the council. the commission could accept amendments adopted by parliament to this effect; - to allow parliament a period of three months, starting from the first transmission of the draft implementing measure, to examine it and to give its opinion. however, in cases of duly justified urgency, this period may be shortened; - ensure full transparency towards parliament throughout the procedure for adopting implementing measures, including broad public consultation on the preparation of draft implementing measures; - to share parliament's wish that a group of market operators should take part in the committee of european securities regulators and to strongly support its establishment as soon as possible; - to recall its political will that parliament should be treated equally, reaffirming its commitment to ensuring effective cooperation between the institutions, to taking utmost account of parliament's position and of any resolutions it may adopt if it considers that implementing measures exceed the powers laid down in the basic acts, and, finally, to reaffirming its desire to reach a balanced solution in such cases. we all know that sort of destruction of infrastructure, health and education services, people's livelihood and jobs destroys hope and any prospect of political stability and security. the high representative referred to what we are doing in afghanistan and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. why is europe spending eur 600m this year in afghanistan – eur 200m from the community budget? we are doing that not just out of humanitarian motives, but also to try to ensure a more stable and secure future for the people of afghanistan. we know that economic development and social progress help contribute to political stability and to greater security. that is why we are making that investment in afghanistan and why, so far, the european union, the member states and the commission have pledged about 45% of what the world bank and the undp say is going to be needed in afghanistan over the next five years. i hope some others – the united states, japan, saudi arabia – will be as generous as we have been in the next few years. why are we spending what we spent in the balkans, in fyrom, for example? in the last few months, with the reconstruction agency starting to do as good a job in fyrom as elsewhere in the region, we have already repaired 400 houses, there will be 300 more repaired by april; electricity has been restored in aracinovo; water and electricity are restored in kumanovo. we have made a considerable contribution to restoring normality to macedonia and will keep on doing that. again, why? not only because of a humanitarian impulse but also because we know from our experience in europe that there is a relationship between economic stability and political stability and security. i do not labour this point as a sort of demented chartered accountant. i make these arguments because they are so obviously true. we know they are true from our experience. if you make people unemployed, if you destroy any infrastructure for people's social well being, then what you are doing is not only making their lives miserable but also, almost certainly, making sure that everyone's lives become more violent. i hope that even now in the palestinian territories and in israel more people will be prepared to listen to the moderates, to those who made their views about the future so bravely known at kalandria checkpoint before christmas. i hope that the voice of peace movement will be listened to because the people who argue in that brave way for peace are the only ones who really chart a way forward for the middle east, for the palestinian state in the future, and for israel. anybody who does not believe that should ask members of this parliament; should ask somebody like mr hume what helped to produce peace in northern ireland. it was moderates being prepared to stand up for their beliefs, it was moderates having the courage and decency to go out there and argue for what we all know is the only way in which you turn off the violence and turn on the peace and security. look at what has happened in south africa, which the voice of peace movement from the middle east has recently been visiting – exactly the same process occurred there. so in endorsing everything which the high representative has said, i just wanted to ask this question: how many more people have to die before the voices of the moderates who are left in the palestinian territories and israel are actually listened to by the citizens of those communities?
