the commission - mr president, i have the pleasure of presenting, albeit briefly, the draft vehicle block exemption regulation which the commission adopted this afternoon. this parliament is aware of the rather serious limitations on the practical operation of the current block exemption regulation, which is due to expire next september. consumers are not getting enough benefits, particularly when they want to exercise their right to a single market. the existing rules also hinder the development of new methods, including distribution via the internet; finally, access to technical information by independent repairers must also be improved. we have therefore drawn up, and the commission has adopted today, this draft block exemption regulation, the main elements of which i would like to briefly describe. the underlying motivation is that the new system must be stricter than the existing regulation and must allow for more competition in the sales and after-sales markets. what are its main features? first, as regards the sale of new cars, flexibility and choice are the key terms of the project. when designating their own distributors, car manufacturers will be able to choose between a selective distribution system or a system based on territorial exclusivity and will no longer be able to combine the two systems. both systems will enable the car manufacturer to ensure that the members of its distribution system are qualified and that its distribution network covers all areas of europe, thus ensuring full coverage of the territory. in both cases the rights connected with the single market will be much, much better protected than they are today. with exclusive distribution, distributors will be assigned to a specific geographical area, such as a city, in which no other distributor will be allowed to open a showroom or to make active sales. the exclusive dealer may, however, sell to any potential buyer who comes to his shop. this also applies to independent retailers, so-called grey retailers. such retailers could be, for example, supermarkets and would take advantage of price differences to buy cars in countries where prices are lower and then resell them in member states where prices are higher, thus helping to create a true single market. if, on the other hand, the houses opt for selective distribution, the distributors will be able to advertise, send personalised letters and e-mails to consumers throughout europe, or even go to them. however, consumers may still encounter difficulties in their dealings with a dealer in another member state, in particular with regard to direct and simple contact with the dealer abroad, payment of invoices and arrangements for the delivery of the vehicle. we therefore felt that a more radical approach was needed to achieve greater integration of the markets, giving consumers a real possibility to buy cars abroad. a car dealer must be able to open sales or delivery points closer to the place of residence of consumers, including those in other member states. in practice, this means that, for example, a volkswagen dealer in amsterdam could open a showroom in the uk and sell the volkswagen golf there at the dutch retail price, which is 23% lower than the uk retail price. this measure will clearly create the market conditions to reduce the considerable price differences that exist for passenger cars in the european union. there is also a consumer demand for multi-brand retailers. the draft regulation makes multi-brand sales much easier. the only acceptable condition is that models of different brands are displayed in different areas of the same showroom, in order to avoid confusion between brands. this type of display is already used in car shows with general satisfaction. the draft regulation also aims to reorganise the existing link between sales and after-sales services by allowing specialisation. distributors will be able to choose to provide after-sales services themselves, as retailers currently do, or they may subcontract to one or more authorized repairers. these repairers must meet all the quality criteria set by the vehicle manufacturer. the block exemption also makes the work of intermediaries much easier: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information it receives from consumers. all these factors give distributors greater flexibility to organise their activities in line with market conditions, exploiting new commercial opportunities and thus strengthening their independence from producers. a further way of making dealers less dependent on producers is to require the latter, i.e. the producers, to give adequate reasons for decisions to terminate distribution contracts. if the distributor does not agree with the reasons given, he may have recourse to arbitration or to a court of law. in addition, the commission decided in this draft regulation that a reasonable period of notice should be given for termination of the contract. this period is normally two years. all these measures ensure that distributors can take full advantage of the new opportunities offered by this proposal for a regulation. i should like to say a word now on the question of after-sales services, which is also very important. the new proposal for a regulation aims to ensure that consumers have a real choice and can turn to both authorised repairers and independent operators. in the interests of the safety and reliability of all motor vehicles - and we have stressed this very strongly - we must ensure that all operators can compete with each other in all sectors, without this being to the detriment of the quality of the service offered, which must remain at the highest level. the new regulation allows all car manufacturers to establish the quality criteria which must be met by all repairers wishing to be authorized repairers. producers can therefore ensure that the members of their network meet high quality standards. this will prevent new entrants from being excluded from this market, and they could now be appointed as authorized repairers, provided they are prepared to comply with the criteria set by the vehicle manufacturers. the proposal also provides for the benefit of dealers whose contracts have expired, who can continue to operate as official repairers of their brands as long as they meet the quality criteria. the overall level of technical competence in the market is therefore increased and a dense network of official repairers is maintained throughout europe, which will contribute to high quality of service and road safety. it is also possible to foresee that the proposal will have positive effects on employment and on small and mediumsized enterprises. the proposal aims to increase the competitive position of independent operators in the after-sales services market. given the increasing complexity of motor vehicles, it is important that independent repairers have better access to all necessary technical information, including diagnostic equipment, equipment and training. any discrimination between official repairers who are part of the network and independent repairers is therefore unacceptable. the proposed changes will also encourage the use of cheaper spare parts of equivalent quality, and thus repair work will be less costly. i would like to conclude, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with a word on procedure. the next procedural step is the consultation of the european parliament and the member states and the publication of the draft regulation in the official journal. this will allow the commission to receive comments from all interested parties before adopting the definitive regulation. the whole procedure should be completed before next summer. i shall also be particularly pleased to present the draft regulation in greater detail to parliament's committee on economic and monetary affairs on 19 february and to continue the fruitful dialogue already begun with members of parliament, in particular with mr konrad, who is your rapporteur on the subject, and with the president, mrs randzio-plath. i think, mr president, that we have dealt with a complex subject: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. if we want the citizens of europe to really see themselves in the construction of europe, we cannot allow such a fundamental part of the single market as the single market for motor vehicles to continue to be non-unique, and this is to the detriment of consumers.

in the european union's education and training systems. this objective includes the establishment of indicators to measure over a period of 10 years the extent to which member states ensure the president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have the pleasure today of informing you of three important subjects dealt with by the commission. this speech needs to be clear but also needs to be a little analytical. so i apologize if this is going to be a little boring! the first item is the commission's political priorities for 2003. secondly, the commission's human and financial resources; thirdly, a reference to the convention which will be opening its work tomorrow. i shall start with the commission's political priorities for 2003, one of the most important steps in the organisation of our political life. this year, for the first time, the three main institutions will engage in an in-depth dialogue on the political priorities and the legislative and work programme for the coming year. the dialogue will be conducted on the basis of the new agreement presented to the conference of presidents on 31 january. we have set out three priorities for the coming year: the enlargement; stability and safety; a sustainable and inclusive economy. since its inception, this commission has focused on the full success of the enlargement process, and so enlargement remains a key priority throughout the second part of my mandate. in this respect, 2003 will be a very important year, as we must all be prepared to assume our responsibilities towards the new member states. we must be ready to welcome colleagues from the new member states to the commission and we must meet the new requirements. for the record: if we are to complete the negotiations in 2002, 2003 must be the turning point, in which we will prepare to ensure that enlargement is as good as possible on 1 january 2004. the commission therefore intends to take a number of measures in 2003: first, we must help the future member states to prepare themselves to assume fully all the responsibilities that come with membership. secondly, we must ensure that the commission fully complies with its obligations from the first day of accession. thirdly, we must rethink the community's policies. in the face of the most important enlargement in the history of european integration, it is imperative to ask ourselves what common policies the enlarged union will need. but to make enlargement a complete success, we must also give a very high profile to the other two priorities i mentioned above. the three subjects of today are in fact profoundly interrelated. first of all: stability and security. within the union our main objective is to accelerate the creation of a european area of justice, security and freedom. the fight against crime in all its forms - including terrorism, indeed, starting with terrorism - is and remains the first item on our agenda. i also believe that special attention should be paid to immigration in all its complex effects. on the external front, the extension of stability and security to the whole of the european continent and to the regions adjacent to the enlarged union is another of our priorities. for this, we must strengthen our partnership with our neighbours. the relaunch of the euro-mediterranean partnership must not only aim at the creation of a new market but also at the creation of a genuine community of good neighbours. to this end, we will continue to pursue our strategy of strengthening the barcelona process. in particular, in the economic field, we are aiming to develop joint initiatives and projects with the countries of the southern mediterranean through a new financial institution, around the eib - in particular, this morning we approved the hypothesis that it is an institution in which the eib has a majority - on the basis of the guidelines that the commission has adopted. we will spare no effort to contribute to the settlement of the conflict in the middle east, where the latest developments finally open a small window of opportunity after months of tragedy. we will also pursue the process of association and stabilisation in the balkans and, in the international arena, support the reconstruction of afghanistan. the third priority for 2003 is a sustainable and inclusive economy. i'm counting on a close-up. however, much also depends on the commitment of the union to implement the lisbon strategy. the external dimension of this strategy is particularly important as a contribution to the governance of globalisation, with the aim of distributing its benefits to as many countries as possible. in this context, the commission will be involved in several areas: firstly, the negotiations in doha will enter the crucial phase not this year but in 2003. we must also ensure that the kyoto commitments are implemented. finally, we must improve the global partnership between the north and south of the world and reaffirm europe's solidarity with africa in concrete terms. these issues will be discussed in concrete form in monterrey in a few weeks' time. the situation is certainly not the best, and we cannot be optimistic about finally making a serious commitment to the third world, but the commission is committed to acting in this direction. the second point today is the examination of the commission's financial and human resources. the annual policy strategy does not simply identify the main political priorities; it aims to ensure that the commission has adequate resources for its tasks. this is the commitment i made at the beginning of my mandate and it is taking shape, based on consistency between policy decisions, activities to be undertaken and resources. this commission has not made any commitments and will never make any commitments without the necessary resources. we must therefore commit ourselves - and this is the plan we are working towards - to the optimal use of human resources. we have used every means to improve the situation, namely productivity gains, negative priorities - and therefore tasks to be abandoned - and internal restructuring. at this stage, however, we cannot adequately prepare for enlargement without asking for more staff. there is no doubt about that: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. as is well known, the commission must also be ready to ensure the application of the acquis communautaire from the first day of accession. this means that we must complete all aspects of the preparation for enlargement by the end of 2003. the commission has therefore, after careful consideration, included in its annual policy strategy the request for 500 non-permanent staff, precisely to prepare gradually for enlargement. it is well known that the current ceiling on administrative expenditure does not provide sufficient resources for preparing for enlargement. that is why the commission considers it essential to make use of the flexibility instrument it has proposed. the request for 500 non-permanent staff for 2003 is part of an overall package of staff for enlargement and follows a careful analysis of all the activities that the commission will have to carry out in the future. the full results of this analysis will be presented in the draft budget for 2003 and will be discussed here. the other two priorities - security and sustainable economy - are also additional responsibilities for the commission. however, in order not to require further staff increase, we have decided to approve only those initiatives which can be carried out by internally redeploying the existing forces and/or phasing out other activities. this is proof of the seriousness and commitment with which we take on the commission's priorities without forgetting budgetary discipline: i am not going to go into the details of the budget, but i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commissioner for the budget is here and is prepared to admonish me if i do not respect this commitment. as regards financial resources, the commission and the budgetary authority must urgently find a more structural solution to the chronic shortfall in heading 4, which relates to external relations. the current rigidities do not allow for optimal action: in other words, we're wasting resources. the international developments of the past year, especially the events of 11 september and the subsequent war in afghanistan, have once again demonstrated that the union needs specific mechanisms to rapidly release the exceptional resources it needs in the event of intervention in crisis situations. this is of paramount importance if we are to really strengthen the voice of the european union in the world. the breakdown of heading 4 proposed by the commission therefore includes some crucial political priorities, such as afghanistan, the euro-mediterranean bank and the world health fund, without compromising other external actions. i therefore urge parliament and the council to tackle the problem of resources as quickly as possible because the actions i enormous importance for the future of europe. the convention, of course - as we know - is open to contributions of ideas from civil society. in this way it will not be possible to say that the new treaty is the result of negotiations between diplomats and bureaucrats in brussels, of which the citizens are unaware. let us not forget that the desire for a convention was born the morning after the allow ourselves to speak for just five minutes per reporter here - five minutes in which we really cannot get to the point of anything sensible. we have to divide it even between the two rapporteurs, because formally we have only one directive, but because of the two dossiers we have two rapporteurs. the commissioner who is just coming in will then have the opportunity to comment on this, as long as she is funny! i am not saying that we should not do this, but i think it is a disaster that we have to limit ourselves to such a small number of people in the political debate. i just said we're going to change the market structures. what we have is not a single market, but 15 submarkets in the european union. 15 submarkets which are more or less open in themselves, but above all where the degree of openness varies widely. this is even more true for the gas market than for the electricity market. but if we want to take advantage of the efficiency gains of a single market, we do not need the addition of 15 submarkets, but we need an integrated single market. efficiency gains for the economy to improve its competitiveness, especially of small and medium-sized enterprises, efficiency gains for consumers in terms of low prices, and efficiency gains for the environment through the conservation of resources. the open market we want is not laissez-faire or 'everyone does what he wants'. what we need are rules for all the players in this integrated market, rules that they can understand, rules that they can apply equally. we need access to the networks and other systems that is absolutely transparent and non-discriminatory for all market participants, otherwise there will be distortions of competition. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we need a regulatory framework that sets objectives, makes binding commitments, sets mechanisms and uniform applicability. now we have the problem that we have, of course, 15 different member states, and these 15 member states have very different structures. a country with 700 or more network operators has a very different framework from a member state with only one network. the key is that the regulatory framework is binding, that its application is controlled and that infringements are punishable. that is the point, and in that respect we must correct a little of what the commission originally proposed with its amendment directive, so that the systems in the various member states are on the one hand harmonized in their objectives, but on the other hand remain somewhat compatible with their mature structures. and how the institutions and authorities of a member state guarantee this is a matter for the member state itself. it just needs to be clear and reliable for all market participants. so much for what we can actually regulate as legislators. i want to use the remaining seconds to simply ask the commission for something. we have different conditions for electricity and gas. we produce electricity essentially in the member states themselves, in the internal market. we are increasingly dependent on imports of gas from third countries. i believe that it will be an important task here, from the point of view of competition and competitiveness, to bring about competition among producers. i know that this is a difficult matter because these are essentially suppliers from outside the union; but this would be a task we all have to work on, because without this competition on the producer side we will always have limited competition here on the european market.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. first, the crossborder trade in electricity. as rapporteur for the committee, i can say that the committee supports the commission's proposal for a regulation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the market is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. there are five conditions. firstly, the costs of the networks which handle the transit must be reimbursed from a fund. secondly, this can only be done in a european manner, i.e. by regulation. thirdly, both producers and consumers must contribute to the funds. fourthly, these payments by producers must be harmonised in the member states so that unilateral competitive advantages are not created. fifthly, there are no internal customs duties, i.e. no payments by so-called exporters and importers, which is an aberrant concept in the internal market, and no tariffs based on the distance of the contracting parties. it's physics, not law. three final remarks on the subject. it is an important question where the electricity is produced. it depends on many factors. the committee will probably be open if, within the conditions i have mentioned, so-called allocation signals are also found and applied. in florence, the regulators, the networks and the commission are thinking about it. the committee does not propose to change the powers of the comitology procedure and the bodies. but since this is a codecision procedure, we propose that after four years it be reviewed whether the procedure envisaged here is in keeping with the spirit of the codecision procedure. finally, the regulators in the member states and the experts, such as the network operators, should be involved in a controlled process. the entry into force of this regulation should not be earlier than the directives, which also decide on the changes in the electricity and gas markets. i am therefore in favour of the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, which are intended to improve the quality of the information provided by the commission. firstly, those in the council who want to reopen the markets only partially - and we know exactly who they are - are in breach of the european treaties. i would like to make that very clear here, and it is also in the committee's proposal for a decision. these treaties guarantee freedom of establishment, freedom to provide services and freedom to move goods throughout the eu to all eu citizens. these freedoms will only be achieved when all electricity and gas consumers can choose their suppliers throughout the eu. only then is the legal status of the contracts established. secondly, if a member state wants to treat all households in its member state equally, for example between lille and the pyrenees, it can do so, it can decide so. however, he may put out an invitation to tender for the service and ask which competitor is most likely to be suitable and qualified for the job. there is no justification for a monopoly of suppliers on the road. dominant position in their own company. we are in favour of regulatory systems in the member states to ensure that. i am in full agreement with mr rapkay that this has not yet been satisfactorily resolved in any member state. i am in favour of a solution with the council which is appropriate to the very different national network structures.

minerals alone. the demand for food is constantly increasing, as people's lifestyles and dietary habits have changed dramatically. vitamins and minerals are involved in a wide range of biochemical processes in the human body. an optimal intake of these substances is crucial for human health and performance. i think that the possibility of supplementing our daily diet with vitamins and minerals is very positive. when we speak of dietary supplements today, we are referring primarily to vitamins and minerals that are sold in the form of tablets, capsules and powders. the directive on food supplements aims to approximate the laws of the member states. this will facilitate access for producers to all markets under uniform conditions of production and marketing. the directive clearly classifies food supplements as food. supplements are not medicines and cannot replace them. with the classification as food, all the rules applicable in the european union apply to food supplements, including those on quality, hygiene and safety. the consumer must be able to rely on the safety of all foods, especially substances such as vitamins and minerals, some of which have different stability. the new directive is aimed specifically at two areas: consumer safety and the completion of the internal market in food supplements. parliament welcomed the fact that the council was taking account of the inclusion of other substances in the directive. these are substances which are already on the market but have not yet been evaluated by the competent scientific committee. these should be included in the annex to the directive. the common position provides for 18 months for the preparation of a dossier. the committee on the environment has extended this 18-month deadline to 36 months in order to give small and medium-sized enterprises in particular sufficient time to compile their product data. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i myself am pleading for 30 months, because i believe that two and a half years should be enough to prove the safety of a product which has been sold to the consumer for years. i am very much in favour of scientifically tested substances before they are covered by community legislation. as regards dosage and thus the best possible supply to consumers, parliament welcomed the system of safe maximum quantities in combination with population reference quantities. the manufacturer must therefore not exceed the limits of human tolerance with his dosage. it is not necessary to limit the quantities to the recommended daily intake, which is usually very low. it is precisely in this respect that the directive takes account of the wishes of consumers, but also of consumer protection. the common our fundamental priorities. the political primacy of this undertaking was already underlined in nice and a road map was drawn up setting out our tasks for this semester. in gothenburg, a clear time aspects and provisions and, finally, the chapter on the institutions. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption, and the council will be consulted on it. we will make draft opinion of the consultative committee on legal affairs and internal market. - mr president, i have to go. i am the rapporteur on the market abuse directive for the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. we have of course tried to ensure that the main outcome of our discussions is that the directive is legally correct. the main problem we faced was the question of comitology. the original draft directive provided for a very general definition of market abuse and, in addition, confined the mass of details, the actual definitions, to the annex and made them available to comitology. we believe that criminal law - and this is criminal law - can only be decided by the legislator himself and not in a comitology procedure. we are therefore very grateful, first of all, that the rapporteur in the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the economic committee as a whole have made the necessary adjustments, which are also in line with what the committee on legal affairs and the internal market wanted. the second legal aspect, which is essentially what we are concerned about, is that although we understood that the commission was seeking a results-oriented approach and not a fault-oriented approach, we now have the problem, and that is a general principle of law that without fault no criminal sanctions can be imposed. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. so, without any fault, you will not be able to make such sanctions! we also looked at the degree of culpability. in our view, market abuse is a crime very similar to other crimes against property, such as fraud. there is no such thing as negligent fraud or negligent theft. it is only done deliberately. for this reason, one of the wishes of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market was that intention should also be required as a matter of principle. we are very grateful to the rapporteur for being willing to incorporate these considerations of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market into his draft in the spirit of compromise. we have now only one last appeal to the council to ensure that fundamental rights are respected in its decision-making. this appeal is addressed to the finance ministers who are responsible for this, and for good reason! european council has also asked the ministers for economic affairs to assess the transparency of our accounting, consultancy and audit standards. we will not have truly effective standards if we do sectors such as transport, energy and telecommunications, and towards a financial system which, in turn, allows for the correct allocation of savings and financing at the lowest possible cost. this is perhaps where the european council's progress has been most relevant. in the area of financial markets, following agreement between the commission, the council and parliament, it will be possible to meet the timetables for achieving an integrated securities market by 2003 and full integration of financial services by 2005. we have identified seven directives and a regulation which must be adopted this year to achieve this. the commission has also taken steps to improve the quality of the information it receives from the member states. as you know, it has been decided to open the gas and electricity markets in 2004 to all european companies, which means that approximately 70% of the european energy market will be open to competition. as regards the rest of the market, the european council has given a mandate to take a decision before the spring 2003 european council. these energy opening measures are also complemented by the objective of electricity interconnection between member states of at least 10% of installed production capacity by 2005. once this objective has been achieved, we will no longer be able to speak of fragmented national markets but of a genuine european electricity market, open and integrated. in the field of transport and telecommunications, we have drawn up a work programme which will make a substantial contribution to improving the efficiency of the internal market. this year, for example, we will approve the revision of the transeuropean transport networks, which will enable us to eliminate major problems, among other areas in the baltic sea, the alps and the pyrenees. we have also agreed to launch the galileo programme, which has not only a clear role in the development of european transport and communications, but also an important technological component. we also agreed to the introduction of the 'single european sky' in 2004, which will reduce flight times, reduce air transport costs and make air traffic management more efficient, and we agreed to give top priority to the development of broadband networks as a key element in the development of the information society. the second set of issues i would like to mention, ladies and gentlemen, is the sustainable development strategy which we adopted at the european council in gothenburg. the european council agreed that the energy taxation directive will enter into force in december 2004, in parallel with the opening of energy markets. as you know, the union and its member states have decided to ratify the kyoto protocol. the council has urged that all national ratification procedures be completed by june, before the johannesburg summit. finally, in the run-up to the monterrey summit, the fifteen have agreed to raise the average of official development aid in the european union to 0.39% in 2006 as an intermediate step towards the 0.7% commitment. the third block of the barcelona european council, ladies and gentlemen, covers employment and social matters. as you know, the afternoon before the european council a summit was held with the social partners. the express result of this social summit was the commitment of the social partners to the lisbon strategy and objectives. throughout the european council there has been broad agreement that member states should work to remove the obstacles which hinder the integration of europeans into the labour market. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. in this connection, we have approved the creation of a european health card, which will facilitate the provision of medical care to citizens during their travels, and we have decided to create the corresponding single european web pages, via the internet, for job vacancies. the emphasis has been on measures targeting two very specific groups of the population: firstly, the promotion of access to day care for the vast majority of children as a means of facilitating the reconciliation of family and working life, and secondly, in the light of the low birth rates and the ageing of our populations, we will put in place the means to increase the average effective retirement age in europe by five years - during this decade. finally, the council also devoted attention to matters relating to education and research, technological development and innovation, which should be important elements of european competitive advantage. the european council considers that quality education is one of the essential characteristics of prosperous and open societies. that is why we have approved the "2010 work programme" for education systems. as regards education, the european council has supported the teaching of at least two languages from other member states from an early age and the general introduction of computer and internet education from secondary school. in the field of research, development and technological innovation, i would like to stress the important commitment we made in barcelona, which you are no doubt already aware of: to increase investment in these categories to 3% of gdp by 2010, with two thirds of this investment coming from the private sector. ladies and gentlemen, it was decided in lisbon that each spring the european council would hold a working session on economic and social questions to ensure overall coherence and effective monitoring of progress towards the new strategic objective. the barcelona european council, in accordance with this mandate, has devoted its work mainly to the lisbon strategy. this does not mean that other matters relating to the european union's external policy or other institutional matters could not be dealt with. among the latter i would like to highlight the debate which, at the initiative of the irish prime minister, was held by the european council on the ratification of the treaty of nice by the republic of ireland. the european council welcomed the approach presented by the irish prime minister and reiterated its willingness to support the irish government in the process of ratifying the treaty of nice, agreeing to take up the matter again in seville. this same european council will also be the first to dedicate a working session to examining the progress of the debate on the future of europe. a report by the president of the convention will enable us to see firsthand the progress of the discussions in this preparatory forum for the future intergovernmental conference. finally, on institutional matters, we have fulfilled the mandates of the european councils of gothenburg and laeken. in accordance with the last european council, the secretary-general of the council has presented us with a report from which we shall draw the operational conclusions at the seville meeting for the reform of the european council. in the coming weeks, the presidency and the general secretariat of the council will establish the necessary contacts to achieve and attain this goal. ladies and gentlemen, the debate on foreign policy has had an important chapter on the situation in the middle east. we also discussed the agreements reached between serbia and montenegro, relations between the european union and the atlantic alliance and the future role of the european union in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. on the other hand, i would also like to stress the european council's special support for the brussels process on gibraltar. the european union, through the adopted 'barcelona declaration', has reaffirmed its condemnation of all terrorist attacks, while stressing that it is the palestinian national authority, as the sole legitimate authority, which must fight terrorism. the european council has therefore called for the immediate lifting of all restrictions on the freedom of movement of the president of the palestinian national authority, yasser arafat. the european council also stated that israel must withdraw its forces from areas under the control of the palestinian authority, stop extrajudicial executions, lift the blockades and restrictions, freeze settlements and respect international law. the european council reiterated in this declaration the union's traditional dual objective in the region: the creation of a viable and independent democratic state of palestine, ending the 1967 occupation, and the right of israel to live in peace within secure and recognized borders, guaranteed by the commitment of the international community and in particular of the arab countries. only through close coordination between the union, the united nations, the united states, russia and other countries in the region can we make an effective contribution to the settlement of the conflict. ladies and gentlemen, european policy towards the balkans is also based on a clear principle, which is the principle of the inviolability of borders and respect for the territorial integrity of states. the agreement reached on 14 march by the leaders of serbia and montenegro is a good step in this direction, as it commits the two countries to maintaining their constitutional unity and territorial integrity. this agreement will be a good test against the european aspirations of the union of serbia and montenegro and, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. unlike my predecessor, who has not taken enough action, i must say that as a member of parliament and vice-president of the constitutional committee i am very concerned about the measures proposed by the governments. the european council sets objectives in these areas, some of which clearly fall within the competence of the member states. the fact that open coordination is no longer explicitly mentioned as a particularly appropriate policy method for these policy areas should not be allowed to obscure the fact that the procedure of objectives and guidelines, the implementation of which is subject to review by the member states at european level, should continue to be applied. the result is open coordination. this procedure is profoundly undemocratic. neither the european parliament nor the national parliaments are involved. this is a breach of the existing treaties. but this is also an affront to the objective of the next intergovernmental conference, and the main theme of the convention, the delimitation of competences between the european union and the member states, as formulated by the governments in laeken in december 2001. the barcelona council's conclusion that the european employment strategy requires a simplification of the process, and that this requires in particular a reduction in the number of employment guidelines, is revealing from a constitutional point of view. yes, who initiated this process? the need for a clear division of competences can hardly be more clearly documented. i can only ask the heads of government of the member states to respect the powers conferred by the treaties in force and not to assume rights which are not covered by either the national constitutions or the european treaties. the council's call for member states to make their national labour markets more flexible will certainly have a greater impact than utopian european objectives and guidelines. in addition to inflation of targets, the heads of government of the member states should also avoid inflation of councils and focus on realistic tasks of the european union covered by the treaties.

the commission has already made a number of proposals. the dismantling of our internal borders and the police cooperation that goes with it, as well as the securing of our external borders, will be one of the greatest challenges for the european union in the new century. in his report, my colleague mr oostlander thankfully pointed out the need for a common border regime at the external borders. my report now deals with the development of the schengen convention in the field of crossborder observation. where internal borders have already been dismantled, the national police have the possibility of cross-border surveillance of suspects, in consultation with the police of a neighbouring state. the instrument of crossborder observation is thus, together with the nacheile, the most effective instrument of crossborder law enforcement to date. the need for such a system was demonstrated in germany just last week when hostages were taken after a bank robbery and the perpetrators fled across the border to poland and then on to ukraine. although cooperation was good, a system such as the schengen convention would certainly have made it easier to prosecute in this case. the council proposal now aims to extend the range of offences for which crossborder surveillance is possible to organised fraud, organised crime, money laundering and trafficking in radioactive material. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i think that was a very important decision and we should include it in this proposal. that is why i regarded the proposal by mr buijtenweg and others as a positive addition. we are otherwise increasingly entangled in a thicket of innumerable different rules of criminal cooperation. in future we must do much more than in the past to achieve a uniform framework for penalties. at the same time, it is unfortunately ignored that the schengen convention has not only been restricted in scope, but that it has been hampered by bureaucratic obstacles. i have therefore proposed some systematic clarifications which have found broad support in the committee. we should have the courage to make real progress and developments in this schengen convention. since the introduction of crossborder observation, the number of applications has tripled. the most common obstacle is often cited by enforcement officials as the lack of a right of retention. until now, observers in a foreign country have had to watch crimes unable to do anything. they are not allowed to intervene, but can only inform their colleagues, who are already fully employed at national level. until they intervene, the perpetrators are usually way over the top. i therefore propose that foreign police forces carrying out crossborder surveillance should also be given the possibility of detaining offenders until the arrival of national police forces, if, firstly, the offenders have committed an extraditable offence and, secondly, the national police are no longer able to prevent this offence themselves. it is difficult to explain to our european citizens why foreign police forces are allowed to observe but not to intervene in the case of an emergency. we should be much more careful in adapting our laws to the realities of our europe which is growing closer together. but i am firmly convinced that, with all the development of this schengen convention, the european union needs real police powers in this europe which is growing together. we will not only be able to discuss in the the commission has already made a number of proposals. we are now in the second reading of a proposal for a regulation which, in my view, is of great importance and which makes one thing clear in particular, namely that in recent months, thanks in particular to the commitment of the commissioner responsible, we have finally succeeded in catching up in the field of air transport with what should have been a matter of course for a long time, namely that air traffic must be free of frontiers, and that is why the regulations and safety measures relating to air transport are also free of frontiers, that is to say, in this case, uniformly organized throughout europe or at least in the member states. the present regulation establishing an air safety agency, which we are considering in second reading, will ensure that in future there will be a uniform assessment of the criteria for the construction and subsequent certification of aircraft for use in air transport. i think that this step is not only important, and this is obvious, for safety in the skies, because the designs are assessed uniformly, but it is also of course essential for the aircraft industry, which has hitherto had to apply for approval in each member state individually, but which will in future be able to deal with an authority, an agency, on this problem and obtain the appropriate certification here. the air safety agency will be responsible for the licensing, certification and monitoring of aircraft. at the same time, and this is the wish we made clear during the discussions in the committee and in the preparation of the second reading, the appropriate monitoring of flight personnel, but also maintenance and other measures, all of which have an impact on aviation safety, should be regulated by law in future. i repeat the clear message: the main objective of this regulation is to establish a uniform high level of aviation safety in europe. there are, of course, other corresponding aims or reflex effects which can be briefly described. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the committee was concerned with the broad independence of the aviation safety agency. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it was also important to ensure the autonomy of the agency, i.e. that the executive director is the de facto head of the authority and that the management board is also able to determine and influence the policies and the way the agency operates. i know that we have been in a conflict with the council and the commission. i believe that in the many discussions we have had, we have come to solutions which ensure that the commission's responsibility is clear, of course, that it continues to monitor the aviation safety agency, so to speak, but that it is also clear that the aviation safety agency has its own responsibility in the area in which it is competent. i am confident that we will be able to avoid a conciliation procedure, that we will be able to put this regulation into effect with the council's approval and that the agency will actually start work 12 months later. i think that we have taken a great step forward in this area of aviation safety. i would like to thank all those who have initiated and supported this bill, in particular my colleagues on the committee on transport. i also thank the commission and the council for their willingness to seek compromises and i hope that with today's vote we can conclude this report and then open a new chapter in the history of aviation safety in europe in this area. - the next item is the report (a5-0059/2002) by mrs palacio vallelersundi, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a council regulation on the community patent (com (2000) 412 - c5-0461/2000 - 2000/0177 (cns)).

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. in my view, the question of which national courts have jurisdiction over a european patent is not the crucial question in this report. i am more concerned with the purpose of this design and what exactly such a patent regime does. this report and other planned changes to the eu patent regime are intended to make patent applications more attractive by extending patent protection directly in the eu. a patent suggests that the patent holder has invented everything that she wants to patent. but in general it draws on all kinds of knowledge that people before it have developed and developed further and that it can only use, and that free of charge, if it does not fall under the patent regime. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the patent is not infringed. even algorithms in computer programs are no longer to be freely available. this takes away the basis for any developer to create a new computer program. the argument often advanced by the patent advocates is that patents would benefit women inventors who do not work for a corporation but make their inventions privately or at least with few financial resources. a patent would protect these people from companies using their invention without paying the inventors, and thus not paying them for their work. the problem with this idea is that this image is far from the reality of patenting. in germany, at least, corporations hold most of the patents and are continuing to expand them. access to the internet is often denied to private individuals because of high patent fees. as the term intellectual property suggests, patenting is nothing more than the valuation of intangible things such as ideas, inventions and even discoveries. the fact that the proponents of capitalism are doing this to themselves, at least if they believe in their creed of innovation and competitiveness, does not interest me. because my goal is the free access and exchange of information and knowledge and their further development. this is precisely the prerequisite for a self-determined life and an emancipatory political approach. in contrast, the palacio report aims to convert an increasing proportion of the world's knowledge into commodities, thereby making it profitable for industry.
commission. – the commission welcomes the report prepared by mrs palacio vallelersundi. at a moment when the council is still struggling with the community patent, it is important that parliament should deliver its opinion on this difficult and complex issue. the report of mrs palacio vallelersundi addresses all the key issues that are relevant to the community patent. several of the proposed amendments enshrine principles that the commission is ready to consider favourably. firstly, there is the principle enshrined in amendment no 8 to allow testing for the sole purpose of receiving market authorisation after the expiry of the patent – the so-called bowler exception. the commission has already proposed a similar line in its revision and whilst not committing myself to the exact wording, i can inform parliament that the commission will carefully consider the issue, taking into account the need for the community patent and member states' national patents to produce identical rights. but amendment no 18 on the same issue goes too far and cannot be accepted. a second example regards amendments nos 1, 6, 7, 21, 27 and 39. these amendments refer to the national patent offices. the commission recognises the important role of those national patent offices. the commission can also agree in principle that they should participate in the processing of community patent applications provided that four conditions are met: first, to ensure the quality and uniformity of community patents, national patent offices and their participation should be set in a properly defined framework. partnership agreements with the european patent office, with quality criteria and mechanisms for quality control would constitute a proper framework. secondly, national patent offices' participation could go as far as doing the prior search – a suggestion made earlier this evening by mrs palacio vallelersundi. thirdly, the applicant should always be free to ask that his application should be processed exclusively by the european patent office. finally, national patent offices and their participation should be restricted by clear quantitative limits. but even with this clarification, i should like to stress that the participation of national patent offices is a matter on which the community alone cannot decide. it is thus not an issue for the regulation but should be negotiated in the framework of the european patent organisation. a third example is amendment no 9 on the distribution of income from renewal fees. while the commission can agree to the principle of distribution of part of the fee income to member states or their patent offices to be used for innovation promotion purposes, it nevertheless considers that this issue should be dealt with in the context of the european patent organisation. it remains to be discussed whether the importance of the patent office is the right distribution key. some of the proposed amendments are not in line with the objectives of the community patent and cannot therefore be accepted. today the driving force for a community patent is the competitiveness of european industry at a global level. there is no point in creating an instrument unless it is affordable enough and offers a sufficient level of legal certainty for it to be used by our inventors and our industry. the commission continues to believe in affordable language and translation regimes. here two different issues are involved. the first one is the language for the processing of patent applications and for the granting of the patent, including translations of applications. the european patent office functions well with a three-language regime. it is not necessary to modify it, whether by reducing the number of languages, as has been suggested by some, or by adding more languages. in particular, adding two or more working languages to the european patent office would considerably complicate its work. it would put a heavy burden on its cost-effectiveness. the european patent convention allows, in principle, eu citizens to submit the initial application in their own language and compensation is provided for those applicants who must translate their applications into one of the working languages of the european patent office. i should also like to add that the language regime of the european patent office cannot be decided by the community alone. that is the first issue. the second issue concerns translations of the patent once it has been granted. if the amendments imply that the patent would have to be translated in its entirety into all official community languages which soon will be either 19 or 20, depending on whether maltese becomes an official language, this would make the patent so expensive that the community patent system would simply not be used. i remind parliament that we have been here before. there has been a luxembourg convention which required translations of the whole patent into all the official languages. that convention has remained a dead letter – it has never been used. surely we do not want to repeat the same mistake. let me give some examples of the costs that would be involved: there would be eur 17 000 for translations just in the community of 15 member states. last but not least, costs must be evaluated, taking account of enlargement. translations into 19 community languages, excluding maltese, would cost around eur 31 500 per patent. for all these reasons the commission cannot accept the following amendments: amendments nos 2, 22, 31, 32(2), 32(3), nor amendment no 36. the commission would like to accept amendment no 34. this does not mean that the commission would systematically oppose any translation requirements of a part of the patent or patent application or of other information. after all, there is the patent in its entirety, a summary and the claims. so we may be talking about different requirements for translation. the commission could accept such translations of parts of the patent provided that they were truly useful and that the overall community patent system remains affordable, simple, cost-effective and legally certain. in this respect amendment no 25, part of amendment no 19(1), 30 and parts of 32(1) and 32(4) merit closer evaluation. but parts of amendments nos 19(1), 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4), part of amendments nos 20, 28 and part of amendment no 31(4) are unacceptable. firstly, there is no reason to require a translation of the patent into the language in which the initial application has been submitted. that already exists. secondly, the community budget should simply not be used to finance translations, nor should applicants be obliged to use the translation services of the european institutions. thirdly, the patent should be published by the european patent office in the community patents bulletin and not in the official journal of the european communities. fourthly, article 44(3), as proposed by the commission, offers sufficient guarantees to protect third parties in good faith. there is no reason to require further formalities from a patent holder who wishes to enforce his patents. on the other hand, article 11(3) cannot be deleted because it corresponds to article 44(3); it just applies in the pre-grant phase. finally, the procedural languages of the courts will have to be determined in a separate context and not here. the commission also has difficulties with amendments nos 23, 24 and 38 on the relationship with the european patent organisation. the commission continues to believe in a user-friendly system where applicants can obtain a european patent and a community patent in one go from the european patent office. the accession to the european patents convention will enable this. it will also enable sufficient legal and political control over the european patent office, taking into account that the european patent office is not a community body. as far as the judicial system, about which a number of members have spoken, is concerned, the commission is prepared to consider amendments nos 26 and 29 in principle, but in the light of the new ec treaty provisions – namely articles 225a and 229a – adopted by the nice treaty. the treaty introduced the possibility to set up community judicial panels to handle cases in first instance with the possibility of appeal to the court of first instance of the european communities. the setting up of such a system would naturally be possible only once the nice treaty has entered into force and it requires a separate commission proposal. however, the commission has major difficulties with amendments nos 3, 4, 5 and 10 to 17. there should be a high level of expertise and unitary case-law right from the start. that pleads for a centralised community jurisdiction. the system proposed in the amendments would not provide this, because some national courts would have so few cases to handle that they could not build up or maintain the necessary expertise. that could result in divergent case-law and quasi-systematic appeals to a higher court. this would imply higher litigation costs and also that parties would have to wait longer for the final decision. i should also like to recall that it is highly doubtful whether the articles of the ec treaty, to which the amendments refer, would allow a system as proposed in those amendments. as regards reporting on the application of the regulation, the commission is ready to prepare the first report at the latest within five years of the entry into force of the regulation. should the commission believe that earlier reporting is required, it will do so. moreover, the formulation in the commission proposals, which focuses on the costs for obtaining and renewing the patents, should already cover all relevant cost factors. it also goes without saying that the commission will propose amendments whenever this is appropriate. therefore the commission cannot, regrettably, endorse amendment no 33. finally, the commission considers that amendment nos 35 and 37 are unacceptable. the commission has presented a proposal for a directive on the patentability of software-related inventions, which is now before parliament and the council. therefore a debate on this question should be carried out in that context and not in this. i would like to thank members for their support and collaboration on this important regulation. i hope that europe will soon be able to improve its performance at the global level by offering its industry a competitive, unitary, affordable and legally secure community patent.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

the cost is involved. i am convinced that in many cases this will lead to mediumsized enterprises throughout europe suffering very badly. i therefore believe that in future the costs for businesses - the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0090/2002) on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council (c5-0638/2001 - 2001/0018 (cod)) with a view to adopting a european parliament and council directive amending for the 24th time council directive 76/769/eec on the restriction of the placing on the market and use of certain dangerous substances and preparations (pentabromodiphenyl ether) (rapporteur: mrs ries).
the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i would first like to thank members for their interest in this proposal and i would of course like to thank the rapporteur, mrs ries, in particular for her constructive work. this is definitely an important directive. it prohibits the use of pentabromodiphenyl ether, pentabde, which has been identified by a risk assessment as posing an environmental risk. the substance accumulates in nature and, as already noted, has been found in breast milk. the directive is far-reaching, covering all uses of pentabde and all types of articles containing this substance. the directive is based on the precautionary principle. the proposed directive will not increase the risk of fire or the risk to the environment, as there are already suitable alternatives available. i can understand and share the concern of members with regard to other closely related subjects which are not within the original scope of the proposed directive, and i would like to comment on this as well as the question of timing. the commission is actively investigating the risks of the two closely related substances, octabde and decabde, as well as the risks that could arise from fire if these substances were to be banned from the market. the commission's position is that we should minimise the overall risks. we are close to completing this risk assessment for octabde and decabde and we expect to have information on the consequences of banning these substances before the end of the year. this concerns both the limitation of chemical risks and the possible increase in risks from fire. on the basis of the results of this work, the commission will present a new proposal at the beginning of next year, i.e. at the beginning of 2003. the commission will also give clear instructions to all parties concerned to speed up the completion of the assessments if possible before the end of the year. in view of this, it is not possible for the commission to accept the amendments tabled by parliament which would extend the scope of the proposed directive to include a total and immediate ban on octave and decable audio. this concerns amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 10. the commission also cannot accept the amendment which would ban decabde altogether from 1 january 2006 if the outcome of the risk assessment showed that the substance posed risks. the commission notes that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the compatibility of the aid with the internal market. i assure members that the commission will act on these matters at the earliest possible opportunity, taking account of the precautionary principle. i also hope that members are aware that the commission has proposed a ban on these three substances - penta, octa and decadiphenyls - in our proposal for a directive on the restriction of dangerous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. this is the case with the florenz report, which was also discussed at this sitting. let me stress that the commission will ensure that the proposal we will present early next year on octabde and decabde will be compatible with our proposal on the restriction of hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. as the risk assessment for octabde and decabde is well advanced, it will be possible for the commission to take action much earlier than 2006 if necessary. the completion of the risk assessments and the examination of the availability of safe substitutes should make it possible to identify the cases where the use poses risks. appropriate measures can then be taken immediately. as the assessments will be ready shortly, the measures decided on can be implemented well before 2006. on the basis of the assurances i have now given on behalf of the commission, i look forward to the swift adoption of this very urgent legislative proposal. i thank the members for this debate.
