- the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the situation in chechnya. i call minister de miguel on behalf of the council.
council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, since the resumption of russian military operations in the russian federal republic of chechnya in september 1999, the situation in the chechen republic has been the subject of the european union's primary attention. the conclusions of the helsinki european council in december 1999 and the actions taken by the successive presidencies since then are proof of this. contrary to what some predicted, this position has not changed since the attacks of september 11. the spanish presidency has been acting and will continue to act in the course of this six-month period with full consistency in relation to this concern of the union. the presidency's work plan for the development of the common strategy for russia already included a paragraph stating the will to 'continue to express the union's wish for a speedy peaceful solution in chechnya within the framework of the principle of territorial integrity, the rule of law and respect for human rights, and to promote the improvement of conditions for the distribution of more secure and effective humanitarian aid'. in the months since january, this declaration of intent has been translated into a number of concrete actions. the presidency has put the chechen question on the agenda of all the meetings of political dialogue between the european union and russia at various levels, both between political representatives, such as the ministerial troika, the eu-russia troika, the eu-russia troika of political directors and the psc-russia troika, and at expert meetings, the so-called coest troika. the presidency raised the matter again at the recent troika meeting at ministerial level with the russian foreign minister, mr ivanov, on 2 april. the troika of heads of mission of the union in moscow also met mr gusarov, deputy foreign minister of the russian federation, at the beginning of march to express the union's concern about the human rights situation in the region. all these actions, which have served to convey to the russian authorities the european union's view of developments in the caucasus, must be supplemented by the request for and subsequent obtaining of the support of these authorities for the trip which the troika of heads of mission is planning to make to the region this april and which will enable direct information on developments to be obtained. for the same information purpose, the troika of heads of mission maintains frequent contacts with representatives of ngos and competent authorities such as mr calamanov, the kremlin's special representative for human rights in chechnya, and mr yastrzhembsky, the presidential spokesman. in this list of specific measures, although not limited, in this case, to those developed specifically by the spanish presidency, it must be remembered that the union's concern has translated into a significant financial commitment. the european union is now the largest donor of humanitarian aid to the region. the amounts allocated to it amount to eur 65 million for the period from the resumption of military operations in 1999 to the present. of these funds, 40 million correspond to the year 2001. as regards the current situation in chechnya, i would like to highlight a few points. in the field of human rights, all the reports from the osce support group, the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe and various ngos continue to give cause for concern. lord judd noted in his report to the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe that little progress had been made in this field during the past year. the reports of the osce support group in the first months of this year in relation to the military operations conducted during this period reported on the disappearance of civilians, looting, indiscriminate use of force and other violations of the rights of the civilian population, all of which occurred in contravention of what had been agreed previously. not all operations were attended by the representative of the public prosecutor's office. the steps taken by the russian authorities to improve this situation must be acknowledged. president putin - it is fair to say - has expressed his commitment that those guilty of human rights violations, even if they belong to the military establishment, should be tried and convicted. these statements have been repeated by other official representatives. the office of the kremlin special representative for human rights in chechnya has continued its work, channelling complaints about alleged human rights violations. the russian authorities cooperate with organisations active in this field. as regards intergovernmental organisations, in addition to cooperation with the united nations high commissioner for human rights, the mandate of the osce support group in chechnya was renewed until 31 december 2002; three representatives of the council of europe continued to participate in the work of the same office and the joint working group consisting of representatives of the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe and the state duma continued its work. as regards the ngos, it was agreed last january to set up a council for the protection of human rights in chechnya, comprising representatives of these non-governmental organisations, the prosecutor's office, the security forces and local authorities, with monthly meetings. the presence of chechen police at the checkpoints on the country's roads is also one of the positive measures. however, as the present situation has been diagnosed, these measures are insufficient. as regards the humanitarian situation, the plight of hundreds of thousands of displaced persons, whose main obstacle to returning to chechnya is the persistence of insecurity, and some of the difficulties faced by humanitarian organisations in carrying out their work, continue to exist. in this area too, it must be acknowledged that the russian authorities have taken various measures: apart from the setting up of the working group with ngos, which will provide a forum for dealing with these issues, the authorities of the russian federation have implemented various measures to normalize life in the area. these measures are not limited to socioeconomic development plans, the reopening of schools or the re-establishment of the public pension system, but also extend to the preparation of a draft constitution to be submitted to a referendum. this will be the first step towards holding new elections in which the people of the region can elect their representatives. in view of the persistence of the problems i have just described, the european union has used - and will continue to use - all channels of dialogue to convey to the russian authorities its position, which is based on the following points: firstly, the european union recognises the territorial integrity of the russian federation and the right and responsibility of its authorities to protect its population from terrorist acts, which the union condemns in no uncertain terms. this recognition is accompanied by a twofold statement: firstly, the union expresses its firm conviction that this responsibility to protect the population must be exercised within the framework of the rule of law and the strictest respect for human rights and international humanitarian law, enshrined in numerous treaties to which the russian federation is a party. the european union therefore calls on the russian authorities to bring to justice and punish those responsible for human rights violations, thus eliminating any risk of impunity, which unfortunately existed in the past. it also urges the authorities to provide federal officials with adequate human rights training, which will prevent such events from occurring in the future. i would like to point out the contribution made in this area by the council of europe and the office of the united nations high commissioner for human rights and to take this opportunity to express the european union's full support for the work that both these organisations and the osce have been carrying out in chechnya. the union also hopes that the russian authorities will continue to cooperate with international bodies and ngos in order to remove the obstacles which still hinder their work. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the european economic area. the improvement in the human rights situation will undoubtedly favour the return of displaced persons. the removal of restrictions, which currently make it difficult for media to access the area, should also help to build greater confidence, both among the civilian population and at international level. secondly, the second major point in the union's position is that terrorist acts perpetrated by armed chechen factions are certainly part of the problem but are far from the problem. the european union is also committed to the peace process, and we are convinced that the peace process in chechnya will be successful. this result must be achieved through dialogue with the various sectors of chechen society. the european union welcomes the progress made in the negotiations on the accession of the republic of moldova to the european union. thirdly, the european union considers that its position on this issue is equitable, since, on the one hand, it does not hesitate to acknowledge the progress made, but on the other hand, it should not hesitate to continue to point out those areas where serious deficiencies persist. the union is thus acting in full accordance with the set of values on which its very existence and its relations with third states, and within these the strategic relationship between the european union and russia, are based. the core of these values which the union and russia share is respect for the rule of law and the safeguarding of human rights and fundamental freedoms. this attitude of equanimity and consistency will also guide the european union's action on the treatment of chechnya at the 58th session of the commission on human rights. the union has expressed to the russian authorities its full willingness to negotiate a statement from the presidency incorporating both progress and shortcomings in terms analogous to those which i have set out before this house. the european union has also informed the russian authorities that if this goodwill of the union is not reciprocated by russia, the european union will not hesitate to resort to the adoption of a resolution, as was necessary to do at the 2001 partsession. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i can only stress the firmness and consistency of the union's position, which will continue to regard the situation in chechnya as a priority in its relations with russia and will continue to devote all its attention and efforts to it when events require it, and also to affirm that this issue will be an important part of the dialogue at the highest level to take place on 28 may on the occasion of the summit between russia and the european union.
commission. – mr president, the commission shares parliament's concern about the deterioration of the situation on the ground in chechnya, as shown by a number of recent solid reports of serious violations of human rights over the past few months. in view of these reports, including from the council of europe, the european union has continued to express its concerns on the matter to the russian authorities through the appropriate diplomatic channels. as you are aware, the eu-russia political dialogue offers an intensive calendar of high-level meetings, including last week’s ministerial troika with foreign minister ivanov in madrid. the position of the european union on this issue is quite simple, and quite firm. the eu supports russia wholeheartedly in its legitimate fight against terrorism, in chechnya and elsewhere. there should be no doubt about this. our calls for a political solution which, without prejudice to the territorial integrity of the russian federation, satisfies the majority of the chechen people, do not in any way undermine such support. equally, there should be no doubt about the eu commitment to uphold human rights in the fight against terrorism world-wide, including in chechnya. in this regard, i am confident that the european parliament fully shares the view that the fight against international terrorism cannot serve as justification or excuse for the violation of the most basic individual human rights, be it in the west bank, in afghanistan or in chechnya. this should not change – and has indeed not changed – due to the horrible terrorist attacks of 11 september last year. against the background of our joint efforts with russia to establish closer political and economic relations, the european union has repeatedly made clear to russia that it expects her to act in full accordance with the values that russia undertook to respect when it entered the council of europe and the osce. these basic principles of full respect of fundamental human rights and the rule of law, including international law, constitute an integral part of the strategic partnership that we are trying to build together. as you are aware, the human rights commission is currently meeting in session in geneva, and chechnya remains an important item on the agenda. the european commission is fully participating in the internal deliberations of the eu in this forum. while the european union is prepared to engage in good-faith negotiations with russia, in order to acknowledge all positive efforts undertaken by russia during last year, there are still too many very serious issues that have yet to be addressed in chechnya. on the positive side, we have acknowledged some positive russian steps towards a political solution that could guarantee long-term peace and stability in chechnya. we welcome these steps and are prepared to support them in any way necessary. in the same vein, we must also acknowledge that there has been progress on a number of issues during the last year, including on physical reconstruction, setting the conditions for economic development, supporting the reestablishment of the chechen judiciary to restore the rule of law, and so on. clearly, a lot more has to be done in all of these fields, but there has been progress and credit should be given where credit is due. also, we have noted that the number of reported violations of human rights that have been followed up by prosecutors has increased. however, we must still regret the excessively low number of follow-up convictions that these reports have resulted in. it is clear that, by dispelling any notion of impunity, the punishment of those guilty of human rights violations is crucial to avoid further violations in the future. more must be done here. another area where progress is warranted is in the provision of and access to humanitarian assistance. as you are aware, the european union, through the european commission humanitarian office echo, is by far the largest donor of humanitarian aid to the northern caucasus. since october 1999, we have provided some eur 65 million in aid to the victims of the chechnya conflict and last year alone more than eur 40 million. our funding is crucial for the presence of international humanitarian ngos in the area, as well as being crucial also for the work and presence of un organisations, notably the unhcr. in our view it is essential that representatives of the international humanitarian community are present in chechnya. we remain concerned about the persistent difficult operating conditions for humanitarian organisations in the northern caucasus, notably the opaque and time-consuming system of access and work permits for chechnya, and also the denial to humanitarian ngos of the right to use vhf radio communication which is very important for their safety. we have been constructively raising the issue of operating conditions with russian authorities at various levels for more than two years, with only very minor improvements so far. we have tried all possible channels; this is a discordant element in the ongoing discussion with the russian authorities, but we will not stop pressing these issues. security conditions in the northern caucasus remain difficult; indeed, one must expect a certain level of operational problems. but we expect more cooperation to be forthcoming from the relevant russian authorities. in this regard, we will continue to advocate concrete improvements, so as to facilitate the conduct of humanitarian operations according to the basic established normal international standards of safety, efficiency and independent monitoring and evaluation. in parallel, we will keep insisting that any repatriation of chechen displaced persons, from within neighbouring ingushetia and daghestan, and refugees from georgia, must take place on a voluntary and unconditional basis only. this is becoming a more and more serious issue. a massive return movement seems rather unlikely at present, given the persisting instability and violence in chechnya and the very limited progress in the implementation of the russian government's long-announced rehabilitation and reconstruction programme.

mr president, while chancellor schröder and president putin are sitting together in weimar today, doing business as if nothing had happened, a genocide is taking place in the shadows in chechnya. i really want to speak of genocide, because that is what has happened in chechnya in recent years: a fifth of the population has been displaced, tens of thousands have been systematically murdered, and the killing is not going to stop! i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i respect the rapporteur's efforts. the economic interests of the union continue to be the primary consideration in the assessment of its relations with the people's republic of china. this is understandable, since a market of some 1.3 billion people holds out almost inexhaustible profits for the companies and banks that operate on it. the accession of china to the wto will further improve the conditions for the recovery of capital. this will also increase competition between pacific economic powers such as japan and taiwan, and between the us and the eu and its member states. everyone wants to get the biggest piece of the big pie. this is accompanied by constant political pressure on china to respect human rights more. the fact that china is seeking to complement its long-running economic reforms with federal democratic structures, social security systems and economic governance mechanisms is overlooked or underestimated. china is continuing this process by joining the wto. but no one should be under the illusion that the separation of state and economy will solve china's enormous social problems. the much-vaunted market of global capitalism is - - report (a5-0092/2002) by mr kindermann, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the annual report from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the results of the multiannual guidance programmes for the fishing fleets at the end of 2000 (com (2001) 541 - c5-0007/2002 - 2002/2006 (cos)).
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the commission has postponed for another time the adoption of the proposals for the reform of the common fisheries policy, which was originally due to take place last week. the commission has a number of proposals to make, and i am sure that the commission will be able to make them. but now to my report, in which i have deliberately confined myself to the commission's report on the implementation of the multiannual fleet reduction programmes. as we are in the hot phase of preparing for the reform of the common fisheries policy in general and thus also of the fleet policy in particular, i would like to take a position on the maps in general in order to point out some problems which should definitely be taken into account in the reform. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. this shows that the fisheries committee agrees in its assessment that the commission's 2000 report, as well as the previous annual reports, showed above all one thing: the maps have not achieved their objective, namely a significant reduction in fleet capacity and thus in fishing effort. we regret that the majority of member states have failed to meet their map targets, for the first time. we call on them to make a massive effort to reduce their fleet, and at the same time we welcome the fact that the commission has opened infringement proceedings against several member states which have repeatedly failed to meet their map targets. we also urge the council and the commission to analyse the reasons for the failure to achieve the objectives and to develop more effective sanctions. we also call on the commission to take into account in its proposals for a new fleet policy the need to strike a balance between the fishing capacity and/or fishing effort of each member state's fleet segments and the fishing rights available to it. commissioner fischler spoke to the committee on fisheries last week about an overcapacity of some 40% of european union fishing vessels, and this figure is not only alarming but underlines all the more the urgent need for action. this high overcapacity is mainly due to the fact that the fleet reduction instrument did not reach its target and that fleet capacity has actually increased in recent years. this problem must therefore be tackled urgently. the commission must, however, ensure that fleet reduction is carried out in a socially acceptable manner by using community financial aid to alleviate social hardship. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. the previous system led to fishermen who wanted to give up their activities and who had given up selling their vessel's tonnage on the market, and thus the fleet was increasingly bought up by companies with a high capacity. this does not, however, lead to a reduction in capacity. finally, efforts to reduce fleet capacity must not be at the expense of working conditions on board and the safety of the vessel or the quality of the catch. the commission has therefore decided to continue to use structural aid to modernise the fleet. however, ways must be found to prevent a simultaneous increase in fishing effort. i am aware that it is not an easy task for the commission to come up with a balanced proposal, and we look forward to hearing their proposals for reform. i would like to thank all those who have helped us in this delicate task, and in particular the commission for its constructive cooperation. following, and i would like to put them forward because i believe that this is the real expression of the current situation in our relations with the united states: firstly, the density and importance of relations between the european union and the united states in economic terms is undoubtedly outstanding, since together we account for almost half of the world economy - 40% - of which, as i said before, only 5% is disputed, and it is the largest bilateral relationship in the world today in terms of trade and investment, and also the importance of these relations in political terms with the renewed impetus we have given jointly to the fight against terrorism. secondly, it was once again clear that there are common challenges and strategies which make the european union and the united states strategic partners, with terrorism naturally highlighted, as i said before, with the launch of negotiations for extradition agreements and judicial assistance in criminal matters, a mandate which was approved by the justice and home affairs council on 25 april, and the strengthening of cooperation on the freezing of the assets of terrorist organisations and in the field of non-proliferation. just before the summit, the new list of such organisations was drawn up to demonstrate our commitment to continue the fight against such organisations. thirdly, from the point of view of foreign policy, close cooperation and consultation on regional conflicts and reconstruction processes were stressed. the agreement on security in the middle east on the principles of ending violence, the recognition of states, the recognition of the palestinian authority as a legitimate interlocutor and support for the mitchell and tenet plans are clear examples of this concertation. at the same time, the improvement of the situation in the balkans was noted, with examples of us-european cooperation in areas such as macedonia, bosnia-herzegovina, serbia and montenegro; the effectiveness of close cooperation in the reconstruction of afghanistan and in the achievement of a political solution in the framework of the bonn conference. fourthly, both sides expressed their willingness to respect the rules of the world trade organisation in all trade issues and supported the inspiring principle of the positive agenda and the qualitative leap which entails the identification of areas of cooperation for concrete future actions. fifthly, in keeping with the above line, the willingness to cooperate in other forums and international processes was expressed, such as the doha agenda and the road to johannesburg, the conference on sustainable development. finally, it was noted that all these avenues of cooperation have been affected by internal changes in the union, such as the enlargement process or the establishment of the union's external security and defence policy, with a clear radiation effect that has been translated in a noticeable way into an intensification of relations with the united states. these, mr president, are the main conclusions to be drawn from the meeting which, as is customary in these cases, took place in a restricted session format, preceded by a plenary session devoted to the more political subjects, followed by a subsequent lunch in which the commercial subjects were discussed. without losing sight of the ideas we have just outlined, let me, ladies and gentlemen, analyse in detail the specific content of the negotiations on the various items on the agenda. first, there is the fight against terrorism. as has been said on other occasions, this is a central and priority issue for both sides, particularly after the events of 11 september. this chapter dealt with the draft agreement on extradition and judicial assistance in criminal matters which was reached after the mandate was approved - as i have already mentioned - by the jha council on 25 april and which was very well received by the north american side. secondly, there is the fight against the financing of terrorism. reference was made to the point on the extension of the lists of terrorist organisations in an attempt to harmonise the contents between the european union and the united states, and to the updating of union measures to implement un security council resolution 1373. this parliament is certainly aware that the presidency has made a considerable effort on this point. several meetings of the clearing house and an extraordinary coreper were called to deal exclusively with this issue and finally the formal adoption of the enlargement of the european union list was achieved on the same day of the summit. the united states was, unsurprisingly, receptive to this new effort, although it expressed some disappointment at the non-inclusion of hamas and hezbollah on the list. the two sides expressed their mutual commitment to intensify efforts to achieve greater consistency in the subject of lists in the light of future amendments. finally, there is the question of non-proliferation. american interest in this area was focused on the so-called 10+10, or "ten plus ten over ten", a ten-year program, estimated at ten billion dollars, aimed at reducing russia's radioactive and chemical material. the united states stressed the importance of the role which the european union could play in this matter, taking into account its relations with third countries such as iran. as part of the negotiating mandate for the trade and cooperation agreement which the union intends to conclude with the country, the european union has undertaken to include non-proliferation as one of the issues to be discussed in the political dialogue. the european union also took the opportunity to announce measures to strengthen multilateral instruments. secondly, the series of regional cooperation issues of mutual interest which were discussed at the summit. it's the middle east, the balkans, russia and afghanistan. the european union is also calling for the establishment of a european union-wide network of information and communication networks. on behalf of the united states, president bush and secretary of state powell recalled that the content of the presidential speech of 4 april was still alive, but that he had to acknowledge the constructive spirit that saudis, jordanians and other moderate arabs were showing. the need to rebuild palestinian infrastructure was reiterated by the high representative, mr solana, and commissioner patten, who also recalled the conclusions of the last ad hoc contact committee in oslo on the need to avoid a security vacuum in the palestinian territories. it is also worth noting that the high representative, mr solana, recalled the injustice of the accusations of anti-semitism by american public opinion against europeans. president bush has accepted the injustice of these attacks. it should also be recalled that the quartet, as i mentioned earlier, met on the sidelines of the summit, in a meeting which was described by the united states as a milestone, thus recognising the importance of international consultation in promoting a negotiated solution to the conflict in question. there was therefore a fundamental agreement on the importance of developing the political, economic and security bands in parallel, and both sides showed their determination to keep up the pressure on the two sides involved. the united states expressed its appreciation for the efforts made by the european union in this area and expressed that it would always act on the principle of caution to avoid calling into question american credibility in the area. in short, the washington declaration reiterates and reinforces the madrid declaration of 10 april. the european union also welcomed the progress made in the implementation of the un security council resolution on the situation in the middle east. the eu also reiterated its readiness to take on the amberfox operation in the republic of macedonia and the us welcomed the joint initiatives in this area, adding at the same time its interest in putting pressure on serbia to cooperate with the hague tribunal. the exchange of views on russia took place in the context of the us-russia summits of 24-26 may, the nato-russia summit of 28 may and the eu-russia summit of 29 may. the european union stressed the positive aspects of the political dialogue with russia, while addressing politically sensitive issues such as belarus and moldova, and also expressed concern about the human rights situation in chechnya. the united states welcomed the way in which the consultation process in this area was developing, as it gave added strength to president putin's western orientation, and expressed its commitment to reaching an agreement with russia before the next summit on nuclear arms reduction. we have already seen from yesterday's news that this agreement has been able to materialize. the european union added a mention here of the economic dimension and the steps russia is taking towards achieving full market economy status, a prerequisite for its membership of the world trade organisation, not in any case expected before 2004. the two sides reaffirmed their common position on afghanistan, stressing the importance of bilateral cooperation in the reconstruction of the country and acknowledging the important economic contribution made by the european union to that end. the principle of avoiding insistence on the current disputes, which often only obscure the importance of the great economic link between the european union and the united states, was maintained in the economic and trade issues. we are referring first to the doha agenda, to the summit that took place in monterrey and then to the one that will take place in johannesburg. this point was briefly discussed in order to confirm the mutual willingness to agree positions within the multilateral framework of the monetary fund, in accordance with the presidency's approach. references were also made to the nepad initiative as a topic to be discussed at the next g8 summit in kananaskis, and the possibility offered by johannesburg of developing joint cooperation projects on issues such as agriculture and drinking water. more specifically, as regards trade disputes, the exchange showed a willingness on the part of the united states to negotiate which can be translated, in concrete terms, into its commitment to the rules of the world trade organisation, in particular in the foreign sales corporation and restrictions on the import of clementines. as regards steel, it is already known that in this dispute it is envisaged that a negotiated solution on compensation may be reached in the medium term, without prejudice to the complaint which the european union will make to the world trade organisation. both sides made their position clear and once again expressed their willingness to comply with the rules of the organization. in any event, the european union has not failed to defend its intention to pursue compensation as a key instrument for protecting its rights. with regard to the foreign sales corporation, thanks to the favourable climate created by the delay in the panel's decision for june, this point was dealt with in a positive tone and bush undertook to change domestic us tax legislation to bring it into line with the world trade organisation. the united states also maintained its commitment to shortening the procedures on clementines in order to avoid, as far as possible, any damage to the next marketing year. it is clear that in those days the new law that has just been passed, which increases aid to american farmers, had not yet appeared, and this is another issue that may be the subject of confrontation between the united states and europe. at a time when we are all committed to reducing agricultural subsidies in the run-up to the doha round, it does not seem that the united states is sending a very positive signal, but i think that we will have to draw our own conclusions in this respect in our negotiating position in the doha round. the positive agenda includes all the subjects on which there is a basic agreement between the two sides and on which there is scope for medium-term agreements. the following points were included in principle: mutual access to procurement on the stock market, common approach on organic farming standards and controls and development of a common prototype for electronic customs. i would like to conclude, mr president, by reiterating the presidency's positive and far-reaching assessment of the summit between the european union and the united states held in washington on 2 december. the transatlantic relations are important, we are concerned about them, but the reality is that they now have - and i believe they will have in the future - a preeminent place in the whole of the union's external relations.
commission. – mr president, it is exactly a year since i presented to this parliament the commission’s communication on reinforcing the transatlantic relationship. few could have imagined then the horror of the terrorist attacks on the united states of 11 september , which have dominated international affairs and have greatly influenced the relationship between the united states and the european union ever since. those attacks brought home the vulnerability of open and democratic societies. but they also strongly underlined their enduring strength. the attacks demonstrated the extent to which europe and america are united by the values we share, as the scale of the outpouring of grief and sympathy in european countries in the weeks after 11 september made very clear. europe has displayed practical support as well as emotional solidarity. our cooperation with the us in the months after 11 september in the campaign against terrorism testifies to that. we have made significant progress in the field of police and judicial cooperation – through the us/europol agreement signed last september, the mandate for a us/europol data protection agreement and for a mutual assistance/extradition agreement, and through the decision to adopt a european arrest warrant. we have worked together to strengthen border controls, and we have made progress within the international civil aviation organisation and the international maritime organisation to strengthen aviation and maritime security. we have worked together to seize terrorist assets. the european union has played a full part in stitching together the coalition against terrorism. european troops are heavily engaged in afghanistan, both as the largest component of the international security assistance force, as well as in combat operations. and the european union is making a formidable contribution towards the reconstruction of afghanistan, which i am looking forward to seeing myself when i visit that country next week. on all these matters, we are working closely with the united states, and to good effect. we are showing how much we can achieve when we operate together with each other, and in partnership with other nations. we are doing so too in the balkans and, more recently, within the so-called quartet to try to seek a peaceful solution in the middle east. all of that demonstrates that the world is a safer and better place when the european union and the world’s most formidable power work in harmony. but, as honourable members are well aware, there has been for some time in washington a debate about whether the us – now so powerful – should focus on its own rather narrowly defined interests, the so-called unilateralist approach, or whether it should continue to give a lead to multilateralist efforts, at the head of the international community’s concerted drive to deal with common problems. this is not a new debate, though it has perhaps grown in intensity. i only want to say this about a debate whose existence is not an exaggerated figment of our european imagination. europe will necessarily be on the multilateralist side in this debate. that is in the nature of how we see the world and of our experience. no one has to apologise for that. but when we disagree over what seem to us to be unilateralist policies, what is the correct european approach? not to keep quiet, in my opinion. but, equally, not to stand around on the sidelines whingeing. where we disagree with the us – for example on their decision not to ratify the kyoto protocol – we should take the lead ourselves and press ahead with ratification, encouraging others to do so as well. similarly, we are opposed to the recent us decision on the international criminal court. but opposition is not enough, we will work hard to make the court a success. i hope that we will not get the disagreements out of proportion and that we can move to a relationship in which we are better able to celebrate the considerable areas in which the eu and the united states are working as one, and to find better ways both to manage our disagreements, and, where we fetch up agreeing to disagree, to do so in as sensible and as reasonable a manner as possible. it helps, in that context, to take a balanced view of events. for example, our disagreements on trade sometimes seem to overshadow our relationship. europe and the us are the largest trading partners. our conflicts account for a fraction of total our trade. the trade flow increases, but the number of disputes does not. too little attention is paid to the close cooperation we enjoy in protecting and developing the international trading system. eu-us cooperation was crucial to the success of doha in launching a new wto round focused on growth in developing countries. our cooperation to help developing countries has gone beyond trade; we have both substantially increased development assistance; we have agreed on a financing for development strategy in the "monterrey consensus"; we are now working very closely in preparation for the johannesburg summit on sustainable development. i hope we can cooperate as well there, too. i will not repeat pascal lamy’s recent words in this chamber on trade issues, but would only like to remind the house that the transatlantic economic partnership (tep) framework has continued to do what was set up to achieve. the partnership aims at preventing disputes from escalating and at accelerating activity in areas of mutual interest. these are precisely the results of our recent cooperation, in particular: first, the launching of a positive economic agenda; second, the reasonable management and prevention of disputes in the framework of the early warning mechanism (recent cases include spanish clementines and hushkits); third, a firm commitment at the highest level in the us on the necessary compliance with the wto decision on foreign sales corporations (fscs). it is worth keeping these points in mind – while not glossing over our profound disagreements on issues like steel and our new concerns about the impact of the new farm bill. i can assure parliament that we will continue to deal with the steel dispute and other disagreements entirely according to the wto rules and procedures. we do not intend to lose the high ground on these issues. i do not believe, against this background, that the appalling events of last autumn call for an entirely new framework for transatlantic dialogue and cooperation. the 1995 new transatlantic agenda (nta) is still valid. it has given us a strategy for the broadening of our relationship, which generally has been very successful. what has been lacking is a strategy to make our cooperation as results-oriented as we would like it to be. to establish such a strategy and to streamline an overly bureaucratic process was the objective of last year’s communication. the approach we suggested, which aimed at more stringent priority-setting, was endorsed not only by member states, but also by our us counterparts. i might add that – ironically, perhaps – counter-terrorism was one of the priorities identified at last year’s summit. this is not a structure set in stone, the priorities are reviewed on a regular basis, and it does not limit the overall scope of our dialogue. the positive economic agenda, which was agreed at the summit in washington early this month, is another good example of this approach. the report before us calls for the transatlantic dialogues to be strengthened and for a greater involvement for the european parliament and the us congress in the nta process. i am a strong believer in the role of parliament and of civil society. the commission has been supporting the transatlantic dialogues and listening to their recommendations. we are discussing with our us colleagues how to re-launch the transatlantic environment dialogue and how to give greater impetus to the consumer and business dialogues. we have been working closely with the european parliament in the past and will continue to do so. the transatlantic legislators’ dialogue and the inter-parliamentary meetings are important instruments and i would certainly encourage greater use of them. i will not add to the very full report on the recent eu/us summit by the presidency, save to note with pleasure that president bush promised to seek the necessary changes to us legislation to comply with the wto ruling on foreign sales corporation. and i emphasise once again that we were able to focus some discussion on those areas, like the balkans, like the middle east, like afghanistan, where we are working very closely together to produce a safer world. let me make one final point. occasionally, when an important relationship in international affairs hits a few problems, the reaction of critics is to say that what is required is a new vision or a new strategy. i have to say that i do not think that the problems we face in managing the european-american relationship result from a lack of vision. we have a pretty clear vision that we are better off on both sides of the atlantic, and the world is safer and more prosperous, when we cooperate and give the international community a clear lead in confronting the challenges of a new century. there are always likely to be problems, even in an important partnership, when national interests collide. national interest has not simply been erased in today’s world. but those differences will be magnified if we start to disagree too frequently about how "national" the national interest really is. it is our profound judgment in europe, the product of our history and experience, and not of some flabby prejudice, that the national interest is invariably pursued best through international cooperation, and we should not be ashamed to make that point loudly and clearly. one last point: mr elles has done a great deal to promote, to deepen our transatlantic dialogue and our transatlantic relationship. but i see from him an amendment on the order paper which causes, i am bound to say, and i am not a notoriously thin-skinned old hack, a slight frisson in the commissioner for external relations. the honourable member deplores the absence of strategic thinking from the commission. the honourable member's profundity as a strategist may be greater than mine and it may even be greater than dr kissinger's,(laughter)but i just want to say one thing to him: the steel dispute with the united states is not a result of a lack of strategic thinking on the part of the european commission. the lack of agreement on the kyoto protocol is not the result of a lack of strategic thinking on the part of the european commission. the farm bill, and i direct the honourable member's attention to this current edition of the economist magazine, is not a result of a lack of strategic thinking on the part of the commission. the biological weapons disagreement; the disagreement over small arms; the disagreement over the international criminal court are not a result of a lack of strategic thinking on the part of the commission. let me say something else. the view which is very strongly felt in the united states that europe does not do enough to defend itself, it does not spend enough on its own security – that is not a result of a lack of strategic thinking on the part of the commission. i stood here in this parliament a few weeks ago and asked whether there was anybody in the chamber who would tell me that their political party would fight an election, pledged to the sort of increase in defence spending that president bush recently announced. even the party to which mr elles and i are proud to belong would not commit itself to that. it is no problem of the european commission's making. where i agree passionately with the honourable member, is that the relationship between the european union and the united states matters profoundly. i deplore, as he does, anti-americanism. i deplore, as he does, those who seek to define their europeanness in terms of how hostile they are to the united states. if mr elles would like to see a development of that argument, i commend to him next saturday's edition of the guardian and the review by the commissioner for external relations of a recent book by will hutton. i equally deplore the mirror image of that: the visceral contempt that one sometimes reads about and hears expressed in the united states about europe. the relationship between the european union and the united states is of enormous importance to the future of the world. maybe some would argue that geostrategically the relationship between china and the united states is going to be more important in this century – over a fifth of humanity and the world's leading power – but our relationship is also important. what makes the relationship so difficult is that we are not just dealing with a superpower, we are dealing with what a recent us ambassador to london, ray seitz, has called a "super duper power". a "super duper power" which was responsible for 40% of the world's growth between 1995 and 2000. for all of us, managing this relationship with the world's greatest power is going to be enormously important. i do not think that we, in the commission, show an absence of strategic thinking in considering the importance of that relationship. but the problem is today that there are rather too many issues on which we disagree, and we want to work to reduce them and ensure that where we do disagree, we in the european union can fulfil our responsibilities of international leadership without that aggravating our relationship with our friends in the united states. (applause)
mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to thank not only the two speakers but also the two rapporteurs very warmly for their work. i would like to thank them because the transatlantic relationship is at a very difficult stage. we have to see that this community of values has been the most successful alliance in the history of mankind. it has secured and enforced welfare, democracy and human rights not only for europe and north america, but also in many other parts of the world, and it has contributed too much of a positive in this world. but we must now realize that after this triumph, some things do not work like that. on the one hand, there is the arrogance of unilateralism, which leads to difficulties, and on the other hand, there is weakness on our part, namely our inability to make a contribution in the military field, and this creates difficulties which we see every day and which have been partly listed here. the international criminal court, kyoto, trade issues or the fact that in the context of the response to the aftermath of 11 september nato is looking like a hollowed-out building, all these are causes for great concern and we must also see that it is right that progress is being made in the middle east quartet, but that we have not yet taken action together in jerusalem and ramallah, and i think that this is the appropriate starting point. i think that the approach of solving individual problems, such as the question of hushkits or bananas, cannot be the decisive starting point, because this is a race that you can never win, because once you have solved one problem, two new ones will come along. that is to say, this approach alone does not get us any further, and that is why i am so grateful to the rapporteur for proposing in his proposals, in particular, structural improvements, that we open the debate in a new direction, that we develop structural relations with the united states beyond nato, as was partly envisaged in the early and mid-1990s in the context of the transatlantic agenda. the question is whether we can find solutions involving bilateral dispute settlement mechanisms in the area of trade without disrupting multilateralism, whether we can discuss these issues in the context of the transatlantic market place, or whether we can conclude a treaty between the united states and the european union, a framework for how we can improve relations here, because such a treaty has the inestimable advantage of involving the american congress. the european union has a treaty with almost every country in the world, but we have none with our closest ally, the united states of america. we are moving from administration to administration, knowing full well that it is always only half the game and that the american congress has a great importance in this game, and that is why we must find a framework for the overall involvement of american policy, a structural frame of reference, and i hope that the council and the commission will take more intensive initiatives than perhaps has been the case recently. in writing. - (de) i welcome the commission's differentiated approach, which aims to guarantee a high level of health protection by means of specific hygiene rules in the field of foodstuffs. the fact that these rules also apply to game meat offered commercially and in large quantities to consumers cannot but be consistent. however, it is essential to distinguish between the commercial distribution and the private consumption of wild game slaughtered in small quantities. a hunter who offers small quantities of wild game after the hunt or who distributes it in local direct sales cannot and should not fulfil the same obligations as a large meat processing operation. as regards the special situation of hunters, practical solutions must be found. the new rules are just and desirable, but private hunters must be excluded from the regulation. our hunters already have a thorough knowledge of the hygiene and pathology of wild game. the trained hunter always bears full responsibility for health protection when distributing wild game and will continue to do so in the future. the european parliament's committee on the environment has adopted several amendments which provide for flexibility in the marketing of game and game meat without compromising food safety. i would ask you to support these amendments in plenary.

the council. - mr president, we are entering a completely different subject and we will have to adapt our mental chip to the new situation. i would like to briefly involve the honourable members in two matters. the first concerns a report which i had the honour of drawing up on behalf of the council, with the aim of examining whether, before the completion of the whole process of reform of the european union - above all institutional reforms - the council could function more effectively, of course within the legal and legal frameworks which exist today and at the expense of what the convention and, later, the intergovernmental conference itself might say. the proposals which have been on the table and which are being analysed at the moment, so that some of them can be adopted at the seville european council, are very simple and easy. the first would involve a change in the functioning of the european council. this, as you know, has a functioning which, in my opinion, is not the one it should have. the european council was created to be the driving force behind the major political strategies of the european union and therefore it should have a more agile, simpler and more targeted management mechanism. today the european council has agendas which are overloaded and which the heads of government themselves have no time to prepare. these heads of government spend a very important part of their time approving conclusions from a huge number of pages - sometimes more than 60 - which are very difficult to write and the effort put into their preparation is probably not commensurate with the number of people who read them. we must therefore do everything possible to ensure that the european council functions in a more agile and rational way, as a governing council operates in most or all countries of the european union, with well-prepared agendas and focused on decision-making in those councils that require it. this does not require major institutional changes: all that is needed is the political will to do so. we should also try - and that is my suggestion - to hold european councils in at least three different forms: a european council for well-prepared decisions, with a clear agenda and in which decisions could, in my view, be taken, even by qualified majority in the future; a second council which would be more of a monographic nature, that is, in which the heads of government would concentrate on one part or element of the great political life that is europe and in which they would not only try to give instructions but also, if possible, practical solutions which could help the european union to move forward; and thirdly, some european councils which would be more informal, where the leaders of the european union could sit around the fireplace - although there is no fireplace but an immense table - and discuss the issues of importance from the point of view of the present and the near future of the european union. i am sorry that we have not been able to reflect more deeply on some of the major issues which may have more to do with the future than with the present. this being said about the european council, the preparation of the european council can be discussed later. it is up to the council to decide which council to prepare and with what characteristics. until now, as you know, the tradition has been that the general affairs council, which is made up of the foreign ministers of the various countries that make up the european union, was responsible for this. but these ministers have an increasingly busy, dense agenda on issues that are strictly related to the foreign and security policy of the european union. if you look at the agendas, you will see that they are becoming more and more loaded and the question arises whether the general affairs council, in its present structure and composition, can devote sufficient time to the horizontal issues which are ultimately the ones that go to the european council. there are many solutions. i will not point to any one in particular: i suggested three or four which are now being discussed, but i do think that, in one way or another, we should have to choose between the separation of the councils or the separation of the sessions - it cannot be the same council with different sessions - the issues which have to do strictly with foreign and security policy, which are many, and those issues which have to do with the preparation of the european council's agenda. in the end, these issues are not prepared with the intensity that is required for the european council to be the effective body that we all want. there can therefore be two or three models of council: one in which there is a separation between a general affairs council whose main function is the preparation of the european council, which will represent an increasing workload; it could also be that the general affairs council itself has a formation of general affairs proper, where each government could send the person who contributes most effectively to the preparation of the european council, depending on the issues, and another configuration that would be strictly devoted to foreign and security policy issues. the third point raised in the report is one which will be dealt with by the convention and, in the end, by the intergovernmental conference itself. but it seems to me, mr president, that this is a subject on which we must start thinking. it is a difficult subject, no doubt, and it changes some fundamental element of our tradition in the european union, which is the concept of the rotating presidency every six months. in my long political life, which is becoming too long, in the european union, i have already chaired the european union twice as a minister and now i am watching this presidency from another position. i honestly believe that as the number of countries increases and international life becomes more complicated, it will become more difficult to maintain a rotating presidency every six months. in the early days of the european union, when we were basically dealing with internal problems that affected only the countries of the european union, we could do it, in that rotational way, every six months. as the union is assuming many more responsibilities, not only for us - for our countries - but also for third countries, i believe that the agility, the maintenance of certain common positions and the tenacity in defending certain elements of our own policy make it very difficult, if there is no adaptation in the presidency model, to achieve all those results which you repeat again and again in parliament that can be achieved. i know that this is a very difficult subject and that there are countries for whom the essence, or part of the essence, of the feeling of being part of the union lies in the fact that, every certain period of time, they have six months of presidency. i understand that, but all the countries should also bear in mind that when we are twenty countries, we will have to wait a long time before we can have the presidency again. so perhaps the value of holding a six-month presidency every so often is less valuable when the time taken for a country to move from one presidency to another is many years. however, i have only mentioned this as a personal reflection, because it is something that the convention will certainly have to deal with, as of course with the other issues, and which will ultimately have to be settled by the intergovernmental conference. the fourth issue to which i think we should devote some time from my point of view - which is why i put it in writing, so that it can be discussed - is the issue of the transparency of the council in general, but, very particularly, at the times when it acts as a legislator. i think we must think about how to involve public opinion more closely when the council acts as legislator; this is also a matter which should only be dealt with at the convention and subsequently at the intergovernmental conference, but i do think it is important that we create a certain atmosphere or culture so that sooner or later, and the sooner the better, this kind of approach will come to pervade the collective life of the european union. but, returning to the two fundamental issues, for which neither a convention nor an intergovernmental conference is needed, but only political will, the will to do things, i believe that more effective preparation and management of the european council, more focus on the fundamental issues, more rigorous analysis, more solid, more serious and more effective preparation, can be achieved without waiting for tomorrow. if there were political will today, it could be launched today, because nothing prevents it - the treaties do not prevent it - and it would not change the fundamental functioning of the european union in any way. this is, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, the kind of work we are engaged in at the moment. i have presented a first report in barcelona, as i said, which is very brief and deals with these issues in an almost schematic way. today the presidency - together with the secretariat team - is contacting the different capitals to see if there is any possibility that between now and the end of june, when the european council meets in seville, a consensus can be reached on some of these matters which strictly require the political will of the 15 heads of government sitting around the table, together with that of the commission. and that is very succinctly, ladies and gentlemen, what we are working on at the moment. there are many other things to be done in the reform of the council, which will be, without any doubt, on the agenda of the convention and on the agenda of the intergovernmental conference. we shall now have time to discuss them and, if possible, to reach agreements which will encourage a more flexible institution which can tackle the issues in a more rational and effective way in a europe which, fortunately, is new because the world is new; a better europe because the world is better.
commission. - mr president, mr secretary-general of the council, ladies and gentlemen, all the opinion polls on europe which we are analysing show that in the eyes of the citizens our institutions are very complex, too complex, not transparent, too distant. i think that this complexity, at least in part, must be borne by each of our institutions and explained, because this complexity is the price to be paid for a united europe which is not at the same time a uniform europe. this does not mean that for the rest, which is not nothing, there is no progress to be made, no changes to be made, especially at a time when we are about to put the functioning of the european union at great risk with 30 countries around the table - 25 at first - instead of 15. we know well, as javier solana has said, that essential reforms will require an amendment to the treaties. there have already been amendments, but they were far from sufficient, to say the least. this means that if we are to succeed this time, we must first discuss the union's tasks: that is what we are doing in the convention. this is the job of the convention on the future of the union. other reforms can, however, be carried out within the current legal framework, simply by changing habits or practices, if the will exists. as regards the european commission, on whose behalf i speak, we have, under the impetus of president prodi, embarked on a series of internal reforms. we have launched a fairly broad programme of administrative reforms which affect the working methods of all our departments. as for the council, it has made its own reflection, initially on the basis of a report whose recommendations, made in 1999, have so far not been followed up. the great merit of the report presented by javier solana, it seems to me, is that it has given a very concrete and even educational boost to the debate and, as he himself has said, has provided, already in barcelona and soon in seville, a basis for generating political will at the level of heads of state and government. these basic documents recall the need for more structured programming of the union's initiatives at the level of the presidency, and note the need for better horizontal coordination of the various council configurations. they envisage a european council focused on its role as a political impetus and, finally, they recognise the need for greater transparency in legislative work. this debate is very important to the commission. ladies and gentlemen, your assembly is making a very constructive and substantial contribution to this, thanks to the work of your rapporteurs, mrs maij-weggen and minister jacques poos. on behalf of the commission, i would simply like to express our support for four aspects of the debate on the reform of the council. firstly, we are in favour of introducing improvements to the council's functioning as soon as possible and wherever possible. the commission supports the council's intention to implement in the near future all possible initiatives which do not require amendments to the treaties, leaving it to the convention to draw up more comprehensive and definitive proposals for the future institutional system of the european union. secondly, we are in favour of the principles of coherence, efficiency and transparency on which the solana report seeks to base the reform of the council. as the commission has already had the opportunity to stress in the white paper on governance, each of our institutions must of course focus on its core tasks. but reform of the council is not only a necessity for the council itself. it is also a necessity for the other institutions and for the union itself. as regards the council's refocusing on its essential functions, i note in passing a convergence between the conclusions of the barcelona european council, the commission's proposals and those which parliament expresses in its resolutions, including those which you are going to adopt at the end of this debate. the council, for example, must organise itself differently when it legislates, with open debates and public votes. i have nothing to add to what i said to your house when we discussed the poos report last october on the subject of a possible legislative council. thirdly, i would say yes, on behalf of the commission, to what i would call the rediscovery of the community method because it alone offers us the chance of solving certain difficulties now. for example, one of the objectively important and sensitive issues concerning the functioning of the council is the rotation of the presidencies, which javier solana mentioned earlier. there are two ways of doing this: one way involves, in order to stabilise the presidencies, an amendment to the treaties, and then another way which would not require any amendment. as regards the second hypothesis, i would observe that continuity of the council's work and consistency in the programming of successive presidencies can be achieved by the classic dynamic: the commission proposes, the european parliament and the council deliberate. the annual political strategy presented by the commission will thus enable the council and parliament to engage in a genuine and stable dialogue on the political priorities and work programme for the coming year for the first time this year. we also support the idea of a council composition dealing with horizontal questions, without amending the treaties. we support this idea, which would lead to such training being included in the initial mission of the general affairs council, namely the coordination of the council's specialised training and, above all, the preparation of the european council. let us, ladies and gentlemen, rely on coreper, which must once again become the traditional channel for preparing council meetings. finally, i would like to conclude with javier solana on this point: we are saying yes to more transparency. this is now an obligation thanks to regulation 1049/2001 and the measures that parliament, the council and the commission have already taken and will take in the near future on access to preparatory texts. the community legislative process will become more readable. however, many documents are already available. the main aim is to help citizens to find the information they are looking for easily, more easily. a brochure jointly published by our three institutions should soon be available to help them do so. we shall achieve even greater transparency by giving the maximum publicity to the council's deliberations, particularly when it is legislating. that is the spirit in which we have welcomed javier solana's report, with its innovative and pragmatic proposals, and, of course, as mr solana himself has said on several occasions, in the knowledge that much of the progress, reforms and improvements will depend on the existence of an immediate political will at the level of the european council and, a little later, on the existence of a political will within the convention and then within the future intergovernmental conference, when we will have to talk about more fundamental and more substantial reforms.

council. - mr posselt will recall that, following the council decision of 22 december 2000 establishing the european police college, a network of european police schools was set up covering all the member states. the stages of this police school, called cepol, could be summarised as follows, in chronological order: in 2001, the network was launched. the members of the school undertake to organise 10 training actions on the priority themes defined in the council decision. in 2002, in the absence of a final decision on the location of the agency's headquarters, denmark temporarily hosts the cepol secretariat and a budget of eur 2.2 million has been obtained for 2002 to finance 17 training actions. during 2002, cepol's activity will increase. 21 training actions are planned, all of which are clearly linked to the priorities set by the council. as regards cooperation between the border control services of the member states, the council refers to points 24 and 25 of the tampere european council conclusions, which call for increased cooperation and mutual assistance between the border control services of the member states, for example through exchange programmes and the transfer of technology, especially at maritime borders, and calls on the applicant states to join this cooperation without delay. the council subsequently adopted a document entitled 'concept for european management of border controls' on 6 and 7 december 2001. this concept provides, inter alia, for the heads of the services responsible for border control to meet at least once a six-month period within the strategic committee on immigration, borders and asylum and allows the candidate countries to participate in its work at least once a year. the first meeting of the committee was held in brussels on 11 april 2002 and was attended by representatives of the services responsible for border control. this cooperation will constitute a first stage in the implementation of other forms of cooperation that may be envisaged, in particular in the light of the discussions on the future commission communication on border management and the outcome of the feasibility study carried out by the italian authorities in connection with the creation of a european border police service. this study, carried out under the odysseus programme, began in october 2001 and consists of four phases. the results of the study will be presented at a ministerial conference in rome on 30 may 2002. i would also like to draw mr posselt's attention to the content of the comprehensive plan to combat illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings in the european union, which was adopted by the council on 28 february 2002. this global plan aims to define a common and integrated approach to all issues related to illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings. it defines seven areas of action, including border management measures.

the committee also welcomed the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the definition of the term 'competition'. - mr president, i have to go. the present report is a contribution to the revision of the treaties, a contribution also to a european constitution. draft constitutions are always created in political contexts and include strategic and tactical objectives and considerations, but also questions of power. the spinelli report of 1984 already took account of the union's responsibilities and the division of labour between the union and the member states, as the lamassoure report rightly does today. however, the question of competence has become more important. this is particularly true in the area of economic constitution and legislation. the success of european economic policy and the survival of the european social model require that the union's own competence in the important areas of the internal market in its entirety, the four freedoms of financial services, competition, customs and monetary policy, be preserved. the report rightly emphasizes this. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy considers that the report does not provide sufficient democratic legitimacy for the delimitation of powers, particularly in the area of policy coordination. the experience of economic policy coordination underlines the need for a union-wide coordination capacity to address the shortcomings of the past. it is not just a question of democratic control, which should be exercised by the european parliament, but of finally moving from a negative to a positive coordination of policies in the coordination of policies - and specifically in the coordination of economic policies. positive policy coordination requires both clear democratic legitimacy and unilateral implementation. the broad guidelines of economic policy should therefore be defined jointly by the council and the european parliament, on the basis of a formal proposal from the commission. this would also serve as an example for other policy areas where coordination is needed and should be exercised. the power, indeed the moral obligation, to organise such a wide-ranging framework in the interests of economic well-being is enshrined in the chapter on the principles of the european union, if we include among the activities of the union the introduction of an economic policy based on the definition of common objectives, in which, in particular, a harmonious, balanced and sustainable development of economic life, a high level of employment and a steady, non-inflationary growth, but also social protection, can and must be organised. in the spirit of the lisbon process, i strongly urge the european parliament to advocate a policy coordination that is truly worthy of the name and that makes clear that policies of common interest can only be successful if they are also visible.
