the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. we are dealing today with a report which was unanimously adopted by the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. this shows that the colleagues in the committee felt that the line i proposed in it was the right one. but in january these colleagues had the opportunity to hear some of the albanian parliament's colleagues in committee speak for themselves. they could see the maturity of this country and its politicians. i do not want to repeat what my colleagues said during the debate there. but i was not under the impression that the comments of my colleagues and my own comments in this debate had led all the politicians in this region to finally realize that they really had to make policy for the albanian people, both the opposition and the government! that is why i think that we are presenting a report which is relatively strict, but not because we do not love the albanian people, but because we love them perhaps a little more than some politicians in this country who are not so much concerned with the welfare of these citizens as with their own pockets and their own position. i say this because i know the people there and i know the politicians. so i think we should not just stand behind the mountain, but really say, there was an election last year. this election was rigged. we then allowed it not to be repeated. but we then asked that - because this election was rigged in order to have a huge majority in parliament to elect the president in june - this election at least not be held. instead, politicians should come together and try to find a personality who could then be a president of all albanians, instead of becoming an albanian president thanks to a stolen majority. i am therefore very grateful to the honourable members who have followed me in paragraphs 4 and 5, in which we ask that, before the negotiations between the commission and the albanians are opened, at least once all the provisions laid down by the osce/odihr election observation commission be followed, namely that this commission should start its work in parliament and check that a new electoral law is also being put in place, and that the honourable members should consider who in albania can lead this country as president in such a way that it is united. now there are many who say that opening negotiations means, of course, that all this can be much better controlled. i can't believe you did that! we're there more than anywhere else. albania is the only country in the world that has a circle of friends, where states, organizations come together and meet several times a year to help this country. and what did that turn out to be? i know albania has had the worst fate in europe. we know. hoxha was not tito, nor was he honecker. hoja was hoja and it was terrible! but albania has been without hojza for some time now, and so we could actually expect things to get a little better. but there's an infinite amount of work to be done. what albania has to do, it does not do because it has to get closer to europe. albania must do this because it wants to become a proper democracy, because it wants the best for its citizens, and that is why it needs a proper jurisprudence, administrative practice and the possibility for people to get back to their property that they were deprived of, and for that it needs a proper infrastructure. all these things are needed to attract investors. it also needs the confidence of foreign investors and for that it needs good policy! i think the council would be well advised to consult us, because we must end up approving the treaty. i think the commission is basically thinking along the same lines as we are - we should not start until albanian politicians have shown themselves willing to take a step forward. we are therefore prepared to start negotiations with them immediately, which will then resolve all the problems they are now facing. i would remind you that we are there in the year of the many and we are trying everything to help this country, and what we say today is really only help for the people and not against the people. i am therefore very grateful that we voted unanimously in the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. i would be very happy if this were the case tomorrow!
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission is not the legal affairs committee and, after parliament has given its consent, parliament as a whole, shall submit to the commission a complete proposal for a directive, a legislative initiative on book pricing in the european union. why is this initiative necessary? in spring 2000, the commission decided that the crossborder book price link between germany and austria was not compatible with community law. we accepted that decision. austria has responded, has passed a law, germany has initially signed a contractual agreement, but the federal republic of germany will also pass a law on book price fixing before the summer. what are we aiming for? we do not want to impose this on member states which do not want a price-fixing system. each member state should be able to decide whether or not to accept this system. this is important! but the national systems of book pricing accepted by the commission are de facto threatened by the import of books, by exports and re-imports and by internet trade. there are many ways of getting around these roads. competition rules are therefore necessary in community law to ensure that the permissible national systems of book-entry pricing are not undermined. the national rules are also threatened by commercial companies which also trade in books and which have these national systems constantly attacked by national and european courts in the hope that they will one day actually fall. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. in fact, in the discussions i had with him at the time, commissioner monti recommended that very approach. he was in charge at the time and said: 'if we, the commission, have decided, we should think of a directive which makes this decision sustainable for the future.' it is a question of respect for the member states which have opted for these systems. they do this for the sake of cultural diversity. i will give just one example. in the federal republic of germany more titles are published in a year than in the united states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that is why the commission must ensure that we create this legal and economic framework so that the member states which have these systems can keep them de facto. that is the point of this proposal for a directive. it is not a question of enforcing the price of books throughout the european union. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i have also explained in detail why these coexisting systems can distort competition and why a legal basis is necessary for the european union to act. commission. – mr president, i shall begin by addressing some of the points raised this afternoon. firstly, mr miranda's wish that parliament be kept well informed about progress in our relationship with the united nations family and that this be included in our annual report. i agree completely. i am grateful to mr miranda for referring to the annual report, because it requires something of an emphasis on the operational side, even at the level of project selection with un organisations. basically, the way in which we prefer to work with others is project selection or the formulation of sector programmes, something rooted in the policy of the host government. the consequence will be that we and other donors provide some sort of basket funding enabling a government to carry out its education policy, its health sector policy, or whatever, rather than donors together deciding on a project. it has to be flexible to meet all kinds of circumstances, but basically this more problematic way of planning things is also what we are discussing with the un family. a big problem today is that the restrictions on how we can spend money in the existing financial regulation force the commission to fund specific projects only one by one, through un organisations. this makes us an inadequate and even sometimes unwelcome partner because we lack predictability and a more long-term perspective. on top of this, we are obliged, on the basis of existing rules and regulations, to insist on having reporting, accounting and auditing on funding through a un entity carried out under our rules. we are not allowed to accept their way of reporting, unlike our member states. this is the core of the changes that we presented nearly two years ago to member states. i will come back to this. mr mccartin, it is absolutely true that we still have a problem about the rate of implementation. however, at the end of 1999, when this commission took over, it took 4.6 years to spend what was committed at the then rate of spending. the following year this was down to 4.1 years and, at the end of 2001, the figure was 3.6 years. so we are eating into the mountain of unspent commitments. we have not finished yet, but things are moving. on the question of the development of a single policy, we have an overall development cooperation policy statement. it was adopted unanimously by member states in november 2000 and parliament has also endorsed this policy unanimously. we are very pleased with that. the main effect of this policy is to focus more clearly on poverty reduction or eradication as the guiding principle for whatever we do. we have never had anything like this before. it covers our global activities, so we have a guide as to what member states should do. however, reality can be different. let me applaud the positive and constructive report of mr miranda. we welcome the support given by that parliament to the commission’s approach to building a more effective partnership with the united nations. i liked the positive tone this afternoon in all the speeches. this has not always been the case. it is a sign of maturity and of healthy self-confidence on our part in europe that we now approach this in a more active manner. the united nations, due to its global mandate, its unique legitimacy and, in a number of areas, its operational strengths, provides an irreplaceable framework to address global challenges confronting the international community. enhancing dialogue and cooperation to build a strategic partnership between the community and the united nations will improve the effectiveness and efficiency of development cooperation and humanitarian aid, thereby strengthening the community’s contribution to poverty reduction and human security. there is, however, a limit to how far we can go. it is, after all, called the united nations – it is not called the "united commissions". our member states are the real owners of the united nations as an organisation. but there is large scope for improvement and a very strong interest on both sides to move in that direction. a more active and visible presence of the commission in the un also has a positive effect in enhancing the ability of the european union as such to act and speak with one voice on global matters. this is a very important, and also a very real, aspect. we saw this demonstrated in monterrey, and it is the intention of the commission to continue along the same lines. we aim at concrete outcomes at policy and operational levels. at policy level we will strengthen the involvement of the community in the upstream policy dialogue with the different members of the united nations system. at the operational level we will work towards a transparent, financially credible, predictable and easier to monitor strategic partnership with selected un agencies, funds and programmes. the follow-up to the communication we are discussing is already well advanced. commission. – the commission shares the concern about zimbabwe following the presidential elections, in terms of the legitimacy of the present government, the issue of freedom of the press, continued violence, the economic crisis and the associated food shortages. it is clear that the election results did not reflect the will of the people of zimbabwe. the process leading up to the elections, as well as the conduct of the elections, were characterised by deliberate attempts by the authorities to prevent free and fair elections. we are particularly concerned about the continued violence and repression prevailing in zimbabwe, the crushing of the opposition, civil society and the independent press. putting an end to violence and the resolution of the political conflict through negotiation is the highest priority. only with a degree of social peace can the rule of law be re-established, and, with it, the impartiality of state institutions, such as the security forces. the eu has applied targeted sanctions against members of the ruling party and a moratorium on bilateral ministerial contacts. it is possible that the council may decide to further extend sanctions in view of the stalemate and lack of progress in inter-party dialogue and the continued repression and violence we see in zimbabwe. i would like to underline that the situation in zimbabwe has now become a very real emergency, and is likely to become a protracted one. we have anticipated humanitarian needs and are addressing food shortages and the needs of refugees and internally-displaced people. eur 18 million is available to cover immediate needs. this figure is not fixed, but it reflects the needs assessment we have made so far. this is the way we normally do things. we have to ensure that this is the basis of our decisions. these funds will be managed by the world food programme and by different ngos, reflecting the need to avoid political games. although prepared to make a major effort to assist the population, we are fully aware of reports pointing to the government of zimbabwe's use of the food crisis for political purposes. in our contacts with the zimbabwean authorities we have systematically stressed that all of those affected by a humanitarian emergency need to be assisted, regardless of their political conviction, and reiterated the need for non-partisan food distribution. unfortunately, about 18 months ago, one of our attempts to distribute food in an even-handed way was disrupted by violence. moreover, we have emphasised that in zimbabwe – once a food-exporting country – the present food shortages are mainly the product of misguided policies and only partly the result of drought. the drought problem is, however, a regional problem and has the negative effect of making it more difficult to buy food in the region in order to assist zimbabwe. thus, things are more complicated because of the drought, but the real problems we are faced with in zimbabwe do not basically stem from the drought but are a product of misguided policies. we believe that the international community should follow the situation very closely. a european union troika visit to the sadc region will take place next week to confer with sadc countries in looking for courses of action, and to support regional efforts to broker a negotiated political settlement in the internal zimbabwean crisis. we hope to initiate a real dialogue on zimbabwe and to promote coordination between the eu and the sadc region. in fact, we managed to establish a close political dialogue with the sadc region at political level during the difficult months – winter and early spring – this year, but we need to move that discussion further in order to try to create a positive influence on the situation in zimbabwe.as to mr mulder's suggestion of doing something about the assets in europe of leaders of zimbabwe, we have not been very good at delivering on the justified, legitimate demand from nigeria to identify and retrieve the money that was stolen by the previous military government. some progress has been made, fortunately, with a number of court rulings and this is important. i mention it to illustrate the difficulty of simply delivering something like this, but it is an area that needs to be investigated. we have a question of extraterritoriality to discuss with these kinds of sanctions, and this is not very easy. there are important principles at stake in those decisions and discussions. so, much as i welcome the thrust and the direction of the thinking in mr mulder's contribution, we have to be careful about what we do.

'very well tightened up', said a major monday newspaper about the emissions legislation we are going to adopt tomorrow, and indeed we have taken another step with this legislation towards reducing the combustion behaviour of engines in relation to air pollutants. the new legislation now on the table will make motorcycles and scooters as clean as a modern euro iii car in 2006. it was a long process to achieve that. the motorised two-wheelers have been left somewhat out of the emissions legislation in the past. in this respect, a situation has arisen where the permitted limits are currently many times higher than the limits for vehicles such as cars or lorries. there is no justification for a motorcycle with just one person on it, or one person on it, to emit 17 times as much as a car with maybe four people in it. it was therefore right and necessary that we should also have introduced sensible legislation here, and i believe that the result we have finally achieved is demonstrable. we have set limits which reduce the permitted emissions by an average of 75%. i think that is a figure that we can all be proud of. we will achieve this in two binding stages. we had a little bit of a fight, but we finally agreed on this second binding stage, so that in 2006 this substantial reduction can be achieved for all newly registered motorcycles and scooters. but we have added safety nets to the limitation, so that these limits are not only nice for the approval process, but actually on the road, they actually reduce the emissions of motorcycles and scooters. we have agreed that the limits must be given a lifetime of 30,000 km. so in practice, in the field, you have to make sure that the bikes stay clean. then we agreed that if there's a reasonable suspicion, authorities can do a field surveillance, control models of a type. is there a mechanical, engineering or perhaps maintenance failure that leads to higher emissions? in writing. - (de) i did not vote for the compromise amendment on article 15 (1) by my colleagues paciotti and palacio. the amendment to article 15 (1) and the related question of the obligation on member states to take measures, inter alia, to maintain national security, is not balanced in my view. the powers or obligations of national legislators with regard to the obligation to store data have not been limited or satisfactorily defined. with the amendments proposed by the council before us, member states can oblige the telecommunications companies to collect systematically all the data produced for all users and to make them available on request, subject to authorization. neither the important criteria specifying which data could be collected, and in what time period, nor those indicating who should bear the costs of data storage and processing (which in turn depend on the volume and time) were established. this remains a matter for the member states. furthermore, it was not specified what obligations, liability criteria and security measures were to be applied to the companies responsible for storing the data. at present, these issues are being addressed under the third pillar. i have been informed that a framework decision on the storage obligation is being prepared. in addition, the topic is being discussed in the cyber crime forum, set up at the initiative of the commission, where all relevant parties (e.g. judicial authorities, communications companies, data protection advocates) are represented. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. the rules of procedure are the instrument by which parliament regulates its work. it is, as it were, the calling card we give out. as the only institution with democratic legitimacy in this european union, parliament is obliged to work with the greatest possible transparency and clarity, so that citizens outside can understand and assess the workings of this house. only by making the procedures as clear and simple as possible will we be able to achieve the desired acceptance of our work among the population. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this right, which is of crucial importance for budgetary control, is laid down in article 197 of the ec treaty and in article 44 of these rules of procedure. it is an expression of parliamentary control over the administration and must not be restricted. however, attempts to restrict this right have been made in the past, such as the framework agreement of july 2000, which limits access to documents and information for every member. this is one of the reasons why parliament has decided to amend this framework agreement as soon as possible. i take this opportunity to remind the president of his duty in this regard. i am very pleased that the report before us, in an addendum to rule 44 for written questions, explicitly states that the content of the questions is the sole responsibility of the questioners. this means that there can be no prior review by the president or any other body, and this too has been questioned in the past.
the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the european sky is becoming more mobile, and fortunately so is european air transport policy. the effects of 11 september on the air transport industry seem to be almost over, with annual growth rates of up to 5% again expected; this means that by 2015, air traffic will double. our political response to this challenge is, on the one hand, the creation of a single european airspace, and on the other hand, we need greater capacity at the congested airports. so more airport infrastructure is needed, and yet none of us can seriously imagine that we might double the number of taxiways by 2015. that is why we must generate additional capacity. the key to this is an optimal system of allocating take-off and landing rights at congested airports. the old slot regulation of 1993 is no longer able to meet the challenges of the present day, and it has not been uniformly applied by the member states because it was imprecise. it did not ensure fair and transparent allocation of the time-sharing, disadvantaged recruits and allowed for abuses such as grey market trading. the commission's proposal to re-regulate the award of slots is a necessary intermediate step. the final settlement must be the subject of discussion for the next few years. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the products and the quality of the products, and it is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the measures to include the production of certain products. i would like to take this opportunity to thank the members for their good and thematic cooperation in the committee. we have succeeded in keeping the balance of the whole system in view, despite the differences of opinion. our improvements to the commission proposal are aimed at clarifying the commission text, at establishing uniform european criteria for the recognition of coordinated airport status, at further strengthening the powers and independence of the coordinator, at maintaining flexibility and planning security for the established airlines and at promoting flexibility and market access opportunities for new entrants. i would like to say something about the individual points. first, the crux of the regulation is the redefinition of slots as a right of use. so slots are not owned by airlines or airports, but are a public good. the committee also established that the definition of the right of use includes all airport infrastructure necessary for a flight. for the first time we have identified the link between airway slots and airport slots in order to allow better coordination between the two in the future. secondly, this is indisputable, but not without significance: we have further strengthened the position of the coordinator. we have relieved him of any liability for damages, and i believe that is essential for his independence. we have defined its powers more clearly vis-à-vis the coordination committee, it has the right to withdraw slots when airlines do not comply with their duty to provide information, and it has the right to cross-check its data with other coordinators and flight-scheduling intermediaries in order to disclose irregularities in flight schedules. thirdly, we should talk about the legitimate interests of the established airlines. the commission's proposal is not acceptable, but we are in favour of continuing to allow them to retiming in order to gradually optimise their flight plans. we have extended the use-it-or-lose-it exemptions to cover events such as 9/11, and we have withdrawn the commission's proposal to link a 'grandfather's tax' to aircraft size, because we believe that companies need more flexibility. this is good both from an economic and an ecological point of view. otherwise, it would have been contractually productive. fourthly, the legitimate interests of the new airlines. the commission's definition of newcomers has not been to the liking of many of the established airlines, but we think it is in principle correct. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's air transport market is not affected by the introduction of new technologies. to further empower new recruits, we have clarified their definition and facilitated their access to transmission and exchange of timesheets. fifthly, where there are clear rules, there must also be sanctions. we've established that slots are revoked after a single warning in case of misuse. member states may also impose fines. let me conclude by giving you a little perspective. many members of the committee wished to see a fundamental reorganization as soon as possible. i can relate to that. the need for renewal is not yet met by our interim measure today. however, first of all, the impact of the present regulation needs to be assessed, because the air transport market is a highly sensitive area and at the same time of considerable economic importance. that's why the quick-fire is inappropriate. we also have time and need time to reach a broad consensus among the main players in the air transport market. the commission has accelerated this consensus process with the study it commissioned on slot allocation models, but it is far from complete. the approach of including air transport in the logic of optimising overall traffic was unfortunately not incorporated in the slot regulation. i am sorry to say that, but we should nevertheless keep this aspect in mind when we are preparing future legislation. i hope that the report will receive the same majority in the plenary tomorrow as it did in the committee.

the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the amendment of the 2013 food labelling directive that we are now dealing with is an important step towards optimising consumer still cook according to basic recipes - have made more and more finished products part of our diet. policies must respond by introducing new rules for improvement and consumer safety. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. already today, 8% of adults and 3% of children in the european union suffer from allergies. the effects can range from respiratory illnesses to life-threatening conditions. the only way to ensure a high level of safety for the people concerned is to avoid foods that are dangerous to them. this is why information on allergenic ingredients is so urgently needed. the labelling should strike a balance between practicable and clear labelling on the one hand and the legitimate right of consumers to full information on the other. the commission proposal has provided a good basis for this. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive. the abolition of the 25% rule is particularly noteworthy. but what is absolutely new, or rather what i see as the main focus of the amendment to the directive, is the list of allergenic substances based on the codex alimentarius. for the first time, it is proposed that allergenic substances should be labelled in all cases and at all times. this list of allergenic substances must, however, be kept under constant review to ensure that it is up to date with the latest scientific knowledge. in this context, a way must be found to keep this list up to date in cooperation with the european food safety authority, the commission and the european parliament. this means that new substances must be able to be absorbed, but in the light of new knowledge it must also be possible to remove substances. i therefore ask for your support for my amendment to the continuous monitoring of the list. in addition, this list requires detailed guidance for interpretation in annex 3. for example, what is meant by nuts when they are also called nuts? what products are referred to as crustaceans? does that include the snails? the commission proposes to abolish the 25% rule and to introduce small exemptions for labelling of between 5% and 2%. these apply to foods already regulated by the community, such as chocolate, sauces and mustard preparations, and to foods which do not require a list of ingredients, such as milk. mixtures of spices are subject to a 2% labelling exception. in the context of seasonal changes in supply, it is particularly important for smes to be able to react quickly to changing market conditions through regulation and/or regulation. all these facilities, contrary to the view of some critics, do not represent a weakening of consumer protection but a reasonable system and an alternative to the abolition of the 25% system. this does not affect the basic obligation to label all allergenic substances. i have been very much involved in labelling and in its practical implementation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the labelling of foodstuffs is not distorted. the commission's proposal will improve consumer protection in the european union and provide consumers with more transparency and information. this is an important message for the people of europe, especially in the light of the current difficulties. in conclusion, i would like to thank all of you for your help and support. i would be glad if the amendments i have proposed were accepted by a large majority of the members of this house. commission. - mr president, the white paper on european transport policy foresees that, unless major new initiatives are taken, heavy goods vehicle traffic will increase by 40 to 50% by 2010 compared with 1998. experience shows that transport growth, especially in border regions, will accelerate as a result of enlargement. in order to tackle the bottlenecks resulting from this situation, the white paper sets out a policy to ensure the rebalancing of transport modes. a considerable part of this transport growth should be recorded in infrastructure other than road, i.e. either rail, inland waterway or maritime transport. the commission proposal to revise the decision on the guidelines for the transeuropean transport network has the general objective of reducing bottlenecks. in this context, the commission has proposed to add a number of links with the candidate countries. in order to strengthen the east-west corridors, it has also proposed two new priority projects: the combined transport project, the stuttgart-vienna high-speed railway and the danube improvement project between vilshoffen and straubin. the commission has also proposed to amend the regulation on the granting of community funds in the field of transeuropean networks, raising the maximum ceilings for co-financing from the current 10% to 20% of the cost of investment in exceptional cases, including projects carried out on the borders with the candidate countries. the commission is planning a wider review of all the transeuropean networks in 2004, taking account of the new configuration of the european union, that is, the one resulting from enlargement. as far as rail freight is concerned, we have already presented not only the first railway package, which was approved a year and a half ago, but also the second railway package, which aims precisely to boost rail freight transport by creating a railway of the 21st century, dynamic, competitive with the road, customer-oriented and therefore providing a quality service. i hope that the work of this parliament and the council of ministers will soon give the green light to these very important measures. finally, in the field of logistics, thanks to the new marco polo project aimed at promoting interoperability and subsidising the development of alternatives to road transport, companies in the candidate countries will be able to obtain financial aid if they apply for it together with a company in the european union.

- the next item is the continuation of the debate on the report (a5-0207/2002) by mrs hautala, on behalf of the parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending council directive 76/207/eec on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions (pe-cons 3624/2002 - c5-0185/2002 - 2000/0142 (cod))
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the outcome of the conciliation procedure for the equality directive is now in sight. i would like to thank our rapporteur, mrs hautala, very much. i am convinced that this amended directive will prove to be a milestone in improving career opportunities for women. we have managed, literally at the last minute, to reach a compromise on the definition of sexual harassment in the workplace, which prohibits all forms of unwanted sexual behaviour, verbal and non-verbal expressions that offend the dignity of the person concerned. direct and indirect discrimination have also been enshrined in eu law for the first time, making them binding in 15 member states and soon in 10 more. a qualitative breakthrough of enormous importance is that women are not to be placed at a disadvantage in connection with pregnancy and motherhood and are entitled to their previous jobs or to equivalent jobs after parental leave. it has been a hard fight to get fathers on parental leave and adoptive parents under the protection of the directive. by 2005, member states, including the candidate countries, must ensure that independent bodies are set up in enterprises to draw up equality plans and to take preventive action and have the necessary resources. there are real sanctions for violations. it is not clear whether this voluntary commitment between the federal government and employers' associations in germany, which is moving in this direction, will meet the high requirements of our eu directive. if companies do not significantly increase their efforts to promote women, the way forward is to take them to the european court of justice.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the amendment of this directive had become urgently necessary in order to take account of the treaty of amsterdam, which contains new provisions on equal opportunities for men and women. however, many extensive judgments of the european court of justice - such as the kalanke and marshall judgments - also give rise to an adjustment. we have been arguing long and hard in both the european parliament and the council for a workable compromise. we have never lost sight of the objective of ensuring equal treatment for men and women in access to employment. the definition of sexual harassment has been refined to the last, although there is still some disagreement on whether it should be included in legislation. a compromise was reached on the establishment of one or more independent bodies to analyse and monitor the implementation and application of the directive. such places, which may also be part of existing institutions, are worth supporting. the directive also refers to the rights of adoptive parents in the member states where adoption leave is recognised. the right to return to the original job or to an equivalent job after maternity leave has also been restored. the directive now obliges member states to introduce a number of binding measures on equal opportunities. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. you need support for this too. only when we have achieved that family, that childrearing, that elderly care is equally the responsibility of men and women, and only when it has become a matter of course for men to take parental leave for family responsibilities, only then have we moved closer to the goal of equal opportunities, equal rights, equal responsibilities.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. the forthcoming enlargement, which we are talking about here, is of course an unprecedented challenge for the european union. the number of members will almost double. the eu's population will grow by almost 50%. what will not increase substantially, however, is the gross domestic product of this new large eu. it will only increase by about 10%. the wealth gap between the current eu-15 and the enlargement countries is enormous. this enlargement will be a great burden for all of us. but we agree: what do they matter in the face of the historic opportunity of the political and economic reunification of europe in peace and democracy, in political and economic stability. but already now many of our regions bordering the candidate countries are feeling the harbingers of enlargement. it is precisely these border regions, which are facing enormous pressures directly in the wake of enlargement of the union, that must bear the brunt of enlargement on behalf of us all. these border regions need our solidarity. we must help them to cope with this difficult situation. of course, not all border regions are the same. one is better, the other is worse. but many have not been doing well for a long time. for many decades these regions have been on the absolute fringe, almost at the end of the world in our view. this is not a particularly attractive situation, which is also explained by the fact that a number of these regions are still objective 1 regions. they still have a large deficit compared to the eu average. the situation in these difficult border regions is characterized by high unemployment, a lack of prospects, including resignation, the emigration of young people, the devastation of the inner cities, the devastation of the villages in the countryside, and the consequent loss of infrastructure, for who would think of building roads, for example, when it seems that no one needs them anymore? the loss of infrastructure, but also the loss of quality of the site, of attractiveness, of quality of life: a vicious circle. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is a fact that borders have long been semi-permeable, semi-permeable. this is not necessarily a fair competition, because we know how wide the wealth gap is between these neighbouring regions on this side of the border and on the other side. this means completely different living, working and social costs, and, incidentally, very different environmental standards for a long time to come. a situation which distorts competition to a great extent. it is particularly difficult for small and medium-sized craft and service enterprises, smes, to manage. this is why i have paid particular attention in my report to the support for smes in border regions. i would have liked to have set up a separate budget line for this purpose, to guarantee this support. however, i had to realise that this position was not a majority position, because it is also true that setting up a new funding instrument, for example, takes a lot of time. the time is running out for the smes concerned. they need help fast. i therefore decided not to pursue my idea and to use the proven and long-established support instruments such as interreg. finally, i have the impression that the commission recognizes the absolute need for strong support for smes in the problematic border regions. we should also recognize the need for temporary transitional measures in the field of freedom to provide services and freedom of movement for workers. we need to open it gradually, risk of injury to pedestrians in the event of a crash by introducing passive safety measures at the front of the vehicle. the commission has instead submitted the communication on a voluntary undertaking negotiated with the automotive industry. however, this does not only include passive but also active security measures. since substantial parts can take effect immediately, it is a useful tool for achieving the policy objective of reducing annual accident deaths and serious injuries by 50% by 2010. however, i expect all parties to regard the negotiated commitment as a contract to be respected. the commission can certainly confirm to us that information indicating that the car manufacturers are already questioning their commitment on one point is incorrect. the motion for a resolution before us will encourage the automobile industry to intensify its research in the fields of passive and active pedestrian safety and will not contribute to paralysing development, as some lobbyists fear. the public interest is finally being taken into account in the area of pedestrian safety. the proposed two-stage improvement of pedestrian safety is in line with the objectives of the white paper on european transport policy. in phase a, which starts immediately and ends in 2005, there will already be substantial measures. these include the fitting of anti-lock braking systems to all new vehicles from 2003, the immediate technical fitting of daytime running lights to all new vehicles, the obligation to no longer supply vehicles with frontal protection handrails and the implementation of the european committee for the improvement of vehicle safety (eevc) 's modified pedestrian crash tests. however, in view of the importance of the eevc r & d programme, it is suggested that the four system tests be qualitatively developed for phase b. in order to ensure real legal certainty for phase b, the commission is invited to draw up a framework directive. in methods that take into account quantitatively more than the eevc test surfaces and that take into account the interaction of test bodies. this poses a broad challenge to the innovation and research activities of the automotive industry. the mature consumer will increasingly evaluate future cars on the basis of their safety-relevant values for occupants and pedestrians and will orient their purchasing behaviour accordingly. security is increasingly becoming a marketing and selling tool. this will benefit consumers and improve road safety. i recommend adoption as voted in committee.

commission. – mr president, the commission welcomes parliament's motion for a resolution on the abolition of the death penalty in japan, the republic of korea and taiwan. the eu works towards the universal abolition of the death penalty, which is one of the pillars of its human rights policies. in the process of attaining this objective and in accordance with the eu guidelines on the abolition of the death penalty, where the death penalty still exists the eu calls for its use to be progressively restricted and insists that it be carried out according to minimum standards. the eu also presses, where relevant, for the introduction of moratoria. the eu reaffirmed its commitment to the abolition of the death penalty by tabling a resolution at the commission on human rights in geneva this year. many activities which aim to contribute to the abolition of the death penalty have been supported under the european initiative for democracy and human rights. funding such projects has recently been reaffirmed as a priority in the commission's communication, or policy paper of 8 may 2001 on the union's role in promoting human rights and democratisation in third countries. the commission welcomes some of the recent positive steps taken by the three countries concerned, and, firstly, the frank exchange of views at a seminar in tokyo in may 2002 on "justice and human rights in council of europe observer states: the abolition of the death penalty" and the establishment of a japanese diet members' league for the abolition of the death penalty; secondly, the bill tabled to abolish the death penalty in the republic of korea which was supported by a majority of the national assembly last year; thirdly, the amendment to the penal code of taiwan which reduces the list of crimes for which the death penalty is mandatory. however, conscious that a great deal remains to be done to abolish the death penalty in the asian region as a whole, the eu decided in 2001 to enhance its strategy for abolishing the death penalty in that part of the world on the basis of the 1998 guidelines on the death penalty. the forthcoming eu annual report on human rights for 2001/2002 will provide an overview of the action taken in the region. the eu will continue its efforts to abolish the death penalty in the region.

commission. – mr president, the commission wants to thank the european parliament for this timely reminder of the risks of foot-and-mouth disease. the outbreak in the republic of korea coincides with the world cup when many thousands of europeans are present to support their football teams. clearly, we need to be alert to any potential risks that they may come in contact with the disease and return with it to the european union. we should not, however, focus our attention only on korea. the fact is that foot-and-mouth disease is widespread throughout the world. all foot-and-mouth-affected countries represent a potential risk to member states and therefore the problem must be addressed in a general way. although it would appear that the outbreaks in the republic of korea are at least 40 km away from the nearest football venues, the potential threat to member states cannot be ignored. therefore, this issue was discussed with member states at the meeting of the standing committee on the food chain on 8 may 2002. i also understand that mrs redondo, chairperson of parliament's committee on foot-and-mouth, raised the issue directly with my colleague david byrne. this is no doubt in the context of the ongoing work of parliament's temporary committee on foot-and-mouth disease. i understand the issue of controls, including on passengers at points of entry to the eu, is the primary focus of the committee's work. the commission has subsequently reminded all member states that, in accordance with eu law they are not authorised to import from the republic of korea foot-and-mouth disease susceptible animals and their products (fresh meat, meat products, meat preparations, milk, milk products, etc.). they have also been advised that imports of foodstuffs from korea by passengers are not allowed under eu legislation. the commission has requested that all member states ensure that public awareness of travellers visiting korea is specifically addressed at airports and that controls at points of entry into the community on goods coming from the republic of korea are reinforced. following the 2001 foot-and-mouth epidemic, the commission has been preparing a number of proposals addressing the issues related to foot-and-mouth, including measures to raise public awareness. the commission intends to present a proposal shortly to raise public awareness and reinforce controls on passengers at points of entry. however, the technical and logistical problems, and consequently the financial implications associated with such procedures, should not be underestimated. it must be borne in mind, that unlike australia or new zealand, the eu has a long land border. there is passenger traffic of millions each year between our member states and third countries where foot-and-mouth disease is endemic. in addition, there are air-traffic links with 90 countries that are not internationally recognised to be free of foot-and-mouth disease and infection. the extent of the challenge is also highlighted by the existing difficulties in combating drug smuggling in international transport. in conclusion, i wish to thank the european parliament for raising public awareness of the risk from foot-and-mouth disease. i am sure that the issue can be addressed in greater detail following the report of the committee on foot-and-mouth disease and in the light of the commission's forthcoming proposals on foot-and-mouth disease. i shall pass on the record of this debate to my colleague david byrne.

- mr president, madam commissioner, i would like to thank you for your reply. i fully support the savary report on the prohibition of heavy goods vehicles. it is a good compromise, which i support. firstly, member states have the possibility of imposing restrictions on the movement of heavy goods vehicles during the usual periods of time: saturdays, sundays and national holidays. secondly, the scope of the directive was established in accordance with the principle of non-discrimination between national and crossborder transport. the directive covers only crossborder traffic on the transeuropean road network, with the member states having the right to adopt additional legal restrictions on national traffic on the entire road network. thirdly, in addition to the general law derogations, national authorities have the discretion to adopt additional derogations for the ten road networks in cross-border traffic. fourthly, the sanctions and controls of the driving ban system remain the responsibility of the national authorities. the rapporteur has tabled two important amendments. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are respected. mr ferber, we have a difference of opinion on this very important point: the adoption of this directive will create legal certainty and will make it impossible to argue differently before different courts. road safety will be improved and the impact on people and nature will be minimised. member states which already have more liberal solutions will not be forced to introduce more restrictive measures, and member states which have more restrictive heavy goods transport will not be forced to liberalize them.

- the next item is the report (a5-0220/2002) by mrs kauppi, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the 2001 annual report of the european central bank (c5-0196/2002 - 2002/2092 (cos)). i would like to welcome the president of the european central bank, mr duisenberg. we are very happy and proud to have you among us. we are all eager to hear your explanations in view of the rise in the value of the euro! the composition of parliament: see minutes.
ecb. – mr president, six months ago we witnessed a milestone in european history: the launch of "the euro, our money", in its visible form. european citizens are now able to perceive – and to benefit from – the tangible reality of the euro, and the rapid substitution of what we call the legacy currencies at the beginning of this year bears witness to the successful launch of the euro banknotes and coins. the year 2001 provided a particularly challenging environment for the monetary policy of the european central bank. the worsening economic outlook was accompanied by short-term upward pressures on prices from various sources, which complicated the conduct of monetary policy. this task was made even more difficult by the extreme uncertainty which followed the terrorist attacks in the united states on 11 september. as usual, the monetary policy response of the ecb to such a situation had to look beyond short-term developments, focusing on the risks to price stability over the medium term. from this perspective, we could see that medium-term inflationary pressures were in fact receding. the ecb took account of this by reducing interest rates four times in 2001, by a total of 150 basis points. as a consequence, the minimum bid rate on the main refinancing operations of the ecb – the most important amongst our key interest rates – reached 3.25% in november 2001. the key ecb interest rates have remained unchanged since november and short and long-term real interest rates have been, in a historical perspective, very low. the average annual inflation rate in 2001, as measured by the harmonised index of consumer prices, was 2.5%. inflation in 2001 was affected by the lagged effects in import price increases in 2000, and by the new impact of livestock diseases on unprocessed food prices. we are not satisfied with such an outcome, which is not in line with price stability. however, it has to be recognised that the factors which contributed to shaping this outcome could not be controlled by the ecb. in fact, monetary policy only affects inflation with a lag and cannot control it in the short term. we are satisfied that our policy last year was very well understood by our observers and by the markets. in fact, the level of bond yields, as well as various other indicators of inflation expectations of economic agents, pointed to continued confidence throughout 2001 in the ecb maintaining price stability in the medium term. there were – and there still are – some concerns about the possible impact of the cash changeover on euro area inflation, which have also been echoed in the draft resolution on the ecb's annual report prepared by your committee on economic and monetary affairs. indeed, the increase in annual consumer price inflation in the euro area from 2.0% in december 2001 to 2.7% in january 2002 has unfortunately been associated, in many people's minds, with the cash changeover. in reality, other factors contributed to this increase, such as the rise in vegetable prices related to adverse weather conditions, particularly in southern europe, and higher tobacco taxes in several euro area countries. but it has also to be recognised that, in particular in some sectors with a low level of competition, some upward price adjustments might have occurred in connection with the cash changeover. however, there were also price reductions in the euro area associated with the cash changeover and statistical evidence has so far confirmed that the effect on the overall price level has been contained. turning now to the current economic situation, over the past few months economic conditions have gradually changed. the impact of the terrorist attacks on economic confidence has gradually faded away and economic activity has stabilised. while the strength of the ongoing recovery is still subject to uncertainty, the most likely scenario is for economic activity to gradually accelerate and reach levels in line with trend potential growth later this year. regarding monetary developments, we saw a high demand for liquid and safe assets in the autumn of last year, particularly associated with financial market uncertainty following the terrorist attacks. we saw some moderation in early 2002 but recent data indicate a new increase in the demand for liquid assets. in addition, the decline in the growth of loans to the private sector has come to a halt and credit demand has recently strengthened. these developments need to be closely monitored, as they may start to point to upward risks to price stability, in particular during a period of economic recovery. overall, the outlook for price stability is now less benign than it was in november 2001, when we last adjusted the key ecb interest rates. inflation has so far declined less steeply and less rapidly than we expected at the turn of the year. this again has been partly due to the temporary factors i mentioned before, and to the renewed increase in oil prices in the first quarter of 2002. at the current juncture, even though the appreciation of the exchange rate of the euro will contribute to easing inflationary pressures, we will continue to closely monitor all relevant developments, against the background of the risks that the deviations from price stability, which followed the exceptional clustering of upward shocks on inflation over the past couple of years, may be transmitted into longer-term inflation expectations, thereby potentially affecting wage and price-setting behaviour. in order to maintain price stability, it is crucial that wage moderation prevails also in the future. in this respect, we are concerned about recent trends in wages here and there. the importance of wage developments in line with our definition of price stability cannot be overemphasised. wage moderation is a key factor in favouring the expansion of employment and in helping to create the conditions for a sustainable increase in the potential growth rate of the euro area economy. current estimates for trend potential growth in the euro area are in the order of 2-2½% and there is much scope for raising potential growth in the euro area. the ecb will make its contribution by focusing on maintaining price stability in the medium term. but other policy actors also have to take up their responsibilities. the broad economic policy guidelines for 2002, which have just been approved in seville, place the emphasis quite rightly on the need for further structural reforms in the euro area. i understand that this view is also shared in the draft resolution. the future welfare of euro area citizens will also depend to a large extent on the prudent conduct of fiscal policies. the solidarity pact of our monetary union requires all participants to maintain a medium-term perspective in compliance with the framework of the stability and growth pact. this implies that budgetary positions in all countries should be close to balance or in surplus over the business cycle as a whole in order to allow sufficient room for a smooth functioning of automatic stabilisers. we have seen some worrying developments in fiscal policy in some countries over the last few months. we therefore recall the importance for those countries that still have not achieved a balanced budget position to honour their commitments to catch up with the other countries of the euro area by 2003/2004. let me now turn to some other issues raised in the draft resolution on the ecb's annual report. we welcome the draft resolution's clear support for the ecb's monetary policy strategy. the draft resolution concludes that short-term movements in monetary aggregates should not be overemphasised and that there should not be any mechanical reaction to deviations of m3 growth from the reference value. this is fully in line with the ecb's monetary policy strategy and practice. the first pillar of our strategy, which gives a prominent role to the analysis of monetary developments, is based on the empirical evidence of a close and stable relationship between money and prices in the euro area over the medium term. there is no evidence yet to suggest that this link has weakened over time. the ecb is fully aware that monetary developments may be subject to portfolio shifts in the short term, which are not directly related to future spending decisions. indeed, what matters is to identify and understand the underlying reasons for monetary developments in order to assess the implications for the risks to price stability over the medium term. in this respect, the analysis of monetary developments has provided useful guidance to the ecb's monetary policy also over the past year. this then leads me to another point mentioned in the draft resolution, namely the importance for a central bank to take account of asset prices when assessing risks to price stability, while not introducing moral hazard in financial markets through inappropriate reactions to excessive asset price developments. the ecb fully shares this view. it closely monitors asset price developments as indicators for monetary policy but it does not target them or react to them mechanically. as regards the proposed endorsement of macroeconomic projections by the governing council of the ecb, allow me to clarify once again the role of those projections in the process of monetary policy-making at the ecb. these projections play an important role for us, but they have by no means an all-encompassing role. they are an important technical input by ecb and national central bank staff in summarising and assessing the implications of a large body of information for future inflation in a consistent way. however, we are also fully aware of the difficulties of making projections. in particular, we recognise that it is impossible to summarise all the relevant information for assessing the maintenance of price stability in one single projection. given the difficulties of forecasting over the longer term and the uncertainty regarding the appropriate economic model, we do not advocate the use of a single projection to analyse the risks to price stability. we therefore explicitly look at many other indicators and analyses in the context of our two-pillar strategy, and we do not try to hide the complexity of monetary policy-making behind the production of a single governing council forecast. the projections reflect the expert judgement of eurosystem staff and we prefer to keep this distinct from the judgement of the governing council regarding the overall assessment of the risks to price stability. therefore, our decision to clearly separate the production of the projections from the analysis of the governing council is fully transparent as it honestly reflects the decision-making process within the ecb. as regards communication, we have always taken an approach that ensures a high level of transparency and clarity of our message. our monthly press conferences are key in this respect. the timeliness and the detail of our communication are without comparison. at the same time, we have not changed our view regarding the publication of minutes. we fear that, given the multi-country context in which the governing council works, published minutes – or a procedure in which dissenting views of council members are published (even without mentioning names) – could lead to undue pressure on national central bank governors to deviate from a euro area perspective. this cannot be in the interest of the euro area, no more than if the governing council were to end its approach of speaking with one voice. the draft resolution also suggests that the balance of votes within the governing council should be published anonymously. as i stated in my last testimony, i have some doubts whether this would give more clarity to the markets or more transparency than is the case now. in any event, i believe it is crucial that we continue to place the emphasis of our communication on the economic rationale behind monetary policy decisions, rather than on a pattern of differing views in the governing council. to conclude my statement, i should like to briefly refer again to the euro cash changeover. with a single currency, our citizens now have a common symbol of european identity which they use in their daily lives. indeed, the euro has created the foundations that may stimulate further integration – in the political, economic and financial fields. in this sense, "the euro, our money" can provide a new and more solid basis on which to build an "ever closer union". (applause)

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. why do you need genetically modified plants? by changing fewer building blocks of genetic material, a plant is better adapted to adverse environmental influences, such as pest infestation or weed competition. it's inherently more resilient. the use of herbicides and insecticides can be greatly reduced. the environment is relieved. in quality and nutritional value, these genetically modified foods are no different from conventional foods. this is confirmed by extensive testing. the commission's proposals on traceability and labelling are widely divided in parliament. we know that. we agree on one point: the proposals have had little success. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. despite these shortcomings, we do not want to reject the commission's proposals, because any further delay would be toxic to the status of genetically modified products within the eu. the de facto moratorium, which has been in place for some years, would continue. the two commission proposals aim to ensure that consumers are given clear and truthful information on genetically modified organisms in food and feed. i am of course in favour of full consumer information without any restrictions. that's for sure! but such information can only be obtained by labelling products as containing gmos which actually do contain gmos. scientific detection by means of genetically modified dna or proteins, or perhaps in the future by other new analytical methods, is a top priority. such product-specific labelling is the only viable option. the commission proposal is going in the wrong direction here. the so-called process-based labelling of food and feed, independent of the detectability of the genetic modification in the final product, is simply not feasible, it is an invitation to fraud. the consequence would be that europe would be overwhelmed by a wave of alleged scandals, and consumer confidence in our high-quality foodstuffs would be further shaken. for the same reason, the extension of the labelling obligation to animal products such as meat, eggs and milk products derived from animals which have been in contact with genetically modified feed should be rejected. such a labelling obligation would be just as abstract as that for food produced using genetically engineered or modified ingredients, such as enzymes, because in both cases there is no genetic modification in the food itself. there is no difference from conventional products. the same is true of highly refined products such as cooking oils and sugar. there is no evidence of any genetic modification in the product. so why label? such a procedure of labelling every product that the gmo has really seen would be contrary to the idea of consumer education or information. almost all foodstuffs would have to be labelled 'produced using or from gmos'. another key issue is the threshold for the accidental or technically unavoidable presence of gmos in products. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, against the vote of the epp group, has reduced the threshold for the accidental and technically unavoidable presence of gmos from 1% in the commission proposal to 0.5%. we agree that this threshold is purely a political value and has no scientific basis. but as a political dimension, this value must be guided by what is practicable, what is feasible. the feasibility threshold is, however, already more than reached with a lower limit of 1%. a threshold of 0.5% is simply not possible at the moment. it would be a prevention value, a prevention threshold. the commission proposal was, however, extremely unfortunate in its wording on this point, and i must say this too. of course, there is some unease when we talk about gmos that are not authorised in the eu. it's associated with something like helpless abandonment. in essence, this threshold is a necessary tolerance level, especially in the transitional period, for gmos which have not yet been authorised under the de facto moratorium but have already been examined by the relevant scientific committees in the eu and found not to be a danger to human health and the environment. they're ready for admission, they're in the queue. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i would like to say the following on the question put by mr posselt: the commission is not aware that the czech republic has requested a derogation from the community acquis on food law for 'utopenec' sausages. the commission therefore considers that the manufacturing and marketing practices of 'utopenec' are in conformity with community food safety rules or will be in conformity with community food safety rules at least from the date of accession. the czech republic has also not received any specific request for registration of traditional or local products for 'utopenec' during the negotiations, although such requests have been made for other products. however, the czech republic has indicated its intention to submit further applications for registration after accession, if appropriate. as regards sliwowitz, its manufacturing processes are not in accordance with the community definition of fruit spirits as laid down in article 1 (4) of regulation no 15/76, since ethyl alcohol, that is to say industrial alcohol, is added to sliwowitz. under that regulation, a drink to which ethyl alcohol is added may not bear the generic name 'brandy' in any form. the community therefore considers that a permanent derogation from the definition of fruit brandy for the czech sliwowitz is not acceptable. it would be possible to continue to use the name sliwowitz for this czech spirit but to call it either spirit rather than fruit brandy or to change the production process so that it complies with the rules for fruit brandy.
i am grateful to the commissioner for that very precise answer. the issue plays a major role in czech domestic politics and is a strong focus of eurosceptic forces. so thank you for the clarification on sliwowitz, which i must say is one of the best in the world. as for the utopenec, i'll look into it. i just want to point out that this is obviously a hygiene regulation. i would ask you to look into the matter further and, above all, to inform me from time to time of the specialties for which derogations have been requested.
the commission has already done so. mr trakatellis and mrs scheele have presented a comprehensive body of work which is clearly intended to contribute to improving information and transparency and to the freedom of choice of european consumers. the health of humans and animals is a priority. the most important criterion, however, must be that these legal frameworks are practicable. in particular, they must be in line with wto rules and must not hinder the development of biotechnology in europe by overbureaucratizing. firstly, we need a practical regulation on the accidental and technically unavoidable presence of gmos in non-genetically modified products. the 1% threshold proposed in the commission proposal is reasonable and realistic and a guide for producers and consumers. the threshold value is important for the coexistence of different cultivation forms, since in nature, for example, pollen flight can never be technically excluded. the second important point is that only products containing scientifically proven gmos are labelled, whereas labelling ingredients isolated from genetically modified plants is not meaningful, as gmos are no longer present in the final product, for example in oils, sugars and flavour enhancers. the labelling of meat, eggs and milk from animals that have been fed with gm feed should also be rejected, as it is misleading to the consumer. i am in favour of product-oriented labelling and i am expressly opposed to process-oriented labelling which cannot be controlled for technical reasons. labelling should only take place where it is possible to prove and thus control the labelling requirements.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the reports by mr trakatellis and mrs scheele are closely linked. a great deal has been said about this in this debate today. the public opinion in europe is largely opposed to the use of modern biotechnology outside laboratories. however, there are several aspects to this. studies show that most people feel too uninformed to make a clear judgment. some 86% of respondents in the european union said they would like to know more before consuming gmo food. the researchers conclude from their findings that food produced genetically in europe has a market if it offers clear benefits. the main emphasis should be on the freedom of choice for consumers. consumers want to be able to choose freely between gmo products and conventional products. we have already had a very heated debate today on the new labelling directives. in my view, labelling should only be carried out where it is possible to verify and thus control the labelling requirements. if genetic modification cannot be detected in the product itself, as is the case for example with meat, milk or eggs from animals fed genetically modified food, i am opposed to this demand. and what's very important to me is the incalculable liability risks for companies, and i don't want to say the word. it is therefore essential that practicable limits be set. that is why i am in favour of a uniform 1% limit. the commission's working document points out that zero tolerance is not feasible in practice, and many of my colleagues have already repeatedly mentioned the imponderables we have in nature. i do not want to add anything new to that.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. if genetically modified organisms were dangerous, they should be banned immediately. we agree, and we would do it immediately. today it is about labelling, about traceability. the consumer's right to information and freedom of choice is paramount, and we are all committed to this. the consumer should be able to decide for himself what he brings to the table, and for that we need labelling. within the union, a number of genetically modified organisms have already been evaluated by the scientific committees and found to pose no risk to health or the environment. however, information is also particularly important when it comes to the food sector, and we think that we will also find a better acceptance of the application of genetic engineering here. the commission proposes to introduce a maximum of 1% for the labelling of gmos. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. we must keep in mind the practicability and implementation of the regulations in all that we ask for. the question arises whether accidental contamination can be avoided at all. the reality is that zero tolerance is almost never guaranteed. and a particularly problematic one - and i repeat what the honourable members have just said - is the demand that all meat products, eggs and milk from animals that have been fed gmos or food that has been fed gmos. if the final product contains neither dna nor genetically modified protein, it cannot be that gmos still have to be labelled. it can only be what's on it, after all. what farmer, whose animals are out in the open, can guarantee that they will not ingest gmos that are spread by the wind? this fact, and also low levels in the feed, would then mean that all meat would ultimately have to be labelled as gmo. and this is an unacceptable situation for europe's farmers and consumers alike. for consumers, because they had to process meaningless information, and for farmers, this meant a technically insoluble problem. it is also unacceptable because farmers are not ultimately responsible for the introduction and spread of gmos.
