the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to speak here today for the first time in the european parliament. it is with particular pleasure that i do so as president of the european council, in order to present the priorities of the danish presidency of the european union. i look forward to the debate that will follow on the tasks ahead. the european parliament is an important and constructive force in the development of european cooperation, and i am sure that this will continue to be the case in the coming months, when we are faced with a number of decisions of crucial importance for the future of the european union. the danish presidency is therefore keen to work closely with the european parliament. the danish presidency wants to strengthen cooperation between the eu institutions. i know that the european parliament shares this wish. we will seek to promote contacts and cooperation between the institutions. we intend to hold summits between parliament, the commission and the presidency before the european council meetings in brussels and copenhagen. we are faced with important decisions in the context of codecision. the presidency will demonstrate efficiency and flexibility and looks forward to fruitful cooperation. we have to adopt a new budget. here too the presidency is looking for constructive and result-oriented negotiations. denmark attaches great importance to the work of the european parliament and the presidency will be well represented at all plenary sessions. a key role in this will be played by the minister for european affairs, bertel haarder, a former member of the european parliament. (applause from the centre) but a number of other danish ministers will also take part in plenary debates in the coming months. i myself will brief parliament after the european council in brussels and report to the presidency at the end of the copenhagen summit. i will also be taking part in the great debate on enlargement on 19 november. we have given our presidency programme the title 'one europe'. we are thus underlining the importance we attach to enlargement and wider cooperation on our continent. the programme contains a detailed statement of our objectives and plans in each area. today i want to concentrate on the main themes. the main headlines of the programme are: firstly, the enlargement of the european union - from copenhagen to copenhagen. we are to decide on enlargement of the european union at the copenhagen summit in december. secondly, freedom, security and justice - we must step up the fight against terrorism, crime and illegal immigration. thirdly, sustainable development - economic, social and environmental. we will work to ensure that economic growth goes hand in hand with environmental protection and the improvement of employment. fourthly, food safety. we will work for better food security, review the agricultural policy and renew the common fisheries policy. fifthly, the global responsibility of the european union. we must strengthen the common foreign and security policy, build stronger links between europe and the united states and work towards a global agreement between the rich and poor countries of the world. the seville european council adopted a number of decisions on the framework for the council's work in the light of enlargement. i welcome these decisions. we will try to implement them as far as possible under the danish presidency. this is particularly true of the decisions on greater openness in the council's work. on the whole, it is our ambition to ensure the greatest possible degree of openness about the whole of the work of the danish presidency. the enlargement of the european union is the main task of the danish presidency. i shall deal with this important subject in detail later in my speech, but first i will comment on the other items on the presidency's agenda. in addition to enlargement, the danish presidency is placing great importance on raising the important european agenda that is before us. we will focus on four areas in particular: first, we will work for greater freedom, security and justice. the danish presidency will give high priority to the fight against crossborder crime and to the implementation of the eu action plan to combat terrorism, and we will focus on developing strong international cooperation - not least with the united states. the presidency will also follow up on the conclusions of the seville european council on asylum, immigration and border controls. a number of forward-looking, concrete and balanced decisions were taken here, which form a good basis for the work of the danish presidency. secondly, the danish presidency will work for sustainable development. this is true economically, socially and environmentally. we will give priority to the completion of the internal market and the development of economic cooperation between the member states. a strong and competitive european economy is the prerequisite for growth, prosperity, increased employment and sustainable development. we must be able to keep up with the global competition - not least in relation to the united states. the danish presidency will then focus on food. we will work for safe food. food security - from farm to fork - is a very important task for the eu. under the danish presidency we will seek to make concrete progress in this area. the debate on the reform of the common agricultural policy will also be launched under the danish presidency. we will give this work a high priority and seek to take it as far as possible. but i would like to stress that this is a discussion which must take place independently of the negotiations on enlargement of the european union. we will not accept the creation of new conditions for enlargement. finally, the presidency will give priority to the work on a new common fisheries policy for the eu countries. it is a vast and difficult task. the commission's proposal provides a good and serious basis for further work. the eu's global responsibility is the last major theme of the danish presidency. the eu has a special responsibility for peace and stability in an increasingly interconnected world. this is particularly true in the fight against international terrorism and in efforts to reduce poverty in the world. the development of the common security and defence policy (esdp) will also continue over the next six months. as a consequence of the danish reservation on defence, the work on the military aspects of cooperation will be led by greece and i would like to stress that we will help to ensure smooth and effective cooperation between the two presidencies on this point. the danish presidency will be marked by a series of important international summits. the eu will and must play a central role at the world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg. we will work within the framework established at the seville summit. the danish presidency intends to ensure the most ambitious result possible. the aim is a forward-looking global agreement, binding both rich and poor countries, a global agreement where rich countries give poor countries better development opportunities through free trade and increased development assistance. in return, developing countries must commit themselves to good governance, that is to say, democracy, respect for human rights, open and free access to information. the asem summit in copenhagen in september will further develop relations between asia and europe. we will also seek to strengthen relations with russia and the eu's new neighbours to the east - ukraine, belarus and moldova. a new policy towards these countries is needed. the specific situation surrounding kaliningrad must be resolved - on the basis of the schengen rules. it should be possible on this basis to reach a reasonable understanding with russia. there is to be an eu-russia summit in copenhagen in november and this summit will be an essential step in this whole process. let me return to the most important task facing the presidency in this six-month period, namely to conclude the negotiations on the enlargement of the union to include up to 10 new member states. it was in copenhagen in 1993 that the conditions for accession to the eu were defined, and it may now be in copenhagen in 2002 that the enlargement negotiations will be completed. from copenhagen to copenhagen. our aim is to conclude the negotiations with all the candidate countries that are ready by the end of the year. this will enable these countries to become members of the european union in 2004, that is, before the next european parliament elections. at the same time, we will make progress in the negotiations with those countries which will only be ready for membership at a later stage, and we will strengthen the link with the eu's new and old neighbours. i will follow three principles in the negotiations on enlargement of the european union: firstly, we must maintain the requirement that clear criteria must be met in order to become a member of the european union. i hope that will be the case for 10 countries, but i will not compromise on the principle. secondly, no country should wait for another. there are differences in the size of countries, but not in their rights or obligations. if only some - but not all 10 countries - are ready by december, then we must conclude the negotiations with those who are ready in copenhagen, and no country which is ready should wait for a country which is not ready. (applause from the centre) thirdly, we will maintain december 2002 as a decisive and binding deadline. experience shows that the eu is best placed to tackle one big task at a time. the next six months are allotted to enlargement. then new tasks come along. in 2003 we are to conclude the discussions on the convention on the future of the european union. in 2004 we have the intergovernmental conference and the european parliament elections, and in 2005 and 2006 we have to define the framework for the next budgetary period. i am not saying that it is now or never, but if we do not take the chance now, we risk a substantial delay in enlargement. we have a moral and historical obligation to achieve a good and positive outcome. (applause from the centre) but there's a line of rocks in the road. we'll have to clear them out. firstly, there is the question of financing. this is particularly true of the negotiations on agriculture, the structural funds and the budget. in my view, the commission has put forward a well-balanced and sensible proposal. several member states consider the proposal too expensive. at the same time, the applicant countries are saying that the proposal is inadequate. i think the commission has struck the right balance in its approach. at the seville summit we adopted an ambitious timetable. it means that the eu must be able to communicate to the applicant countries by the beginning of november at the latest a common position on the issue of direct income support for farmers. the danish presidency will maintain this ambitious timetable. the second key issue is the cyprus question. cyprus is doing well in the accession negotiations, it is one of the countries that has closed the most negotiating chapters - 28 out of 31 - and as an applicant country, cyprus has a right to be included when it is ready. but at the same time, the problem is that the island is still divided. the helsinki european council stated that a solution to this problem would be an advantage but not a condition for accession to the eu. however, it was stressed that a final decision would be taken on the basis of all relevant factors. the danish presidency will continue to work on this basis and i would like to stress that all those involved - on both sides - should do their utmost to find a solution as quickly as possible. thirdly, the irish referendum on the treaty of nice is an unknown factor. the approval of the treaty of nice is a prerequisite for the enlargement to be completed within the deadlines set. the negotiations shall be conducted on the basis of the provisions of the treaty of nice. a new 'no' in ireland will jeopardise the whole process. in this context, i welcome the declaration of irish neutrality at the seville summit. a clear and positive message has been sent from europe to the irish people. i will not conceal the fact that we are facing considerable challenges. but no one should doubt the determination, commitment and will of the danish presidency. a good starting point has been created. this is not least the result of the tireless work of the applicant countries and the commission over more than 10 years. but the danish presidency is also building on the achievements of previous presidencies, including the great progress made by the spanish presidency. ten years of negotiations, ten years of hard work that have borne fruit, ten years of expectations that we cannot afford to disappoint. we must live up to the promises we have made to each other, we must meet the deadlines we have set for ourselves. we must seize the historic opportunity we have been given. more than 40 years of communist rule in central and eastern europe meant an unfortunate and artificial division of europe. it is this dark chapter in the history of europe that we now have an opportunity to close. the time for toasts is over. we must follow our words with action. this is the time to fulfill our promises. (applause from the centre) 'one europe' is the title of the danish presidency. one europe for all our peoples. one europe as the framework for future cooperation for the benefit of all. a europe of freedom, peace and prosperity. the danish presidency will do its utmost to carry out this and the other tasks entrusted to us. we can't do this alone, we need all our partners. after the second world war, great european thinkers such as schuman, monet and spinelli created the vision of a europe without war, a europe united in cooperation. that dream has come true for us in western europe. the enlargement of the european union is the opportunity to extend the freedom, peace, stability and prosperity that we know to the countries of the east. we must approach this task in the spirit of the founders of european cooperation. we must not lose sight of the details, but must have the courage and the will to maintain the historic vision and the task that lies ahead of us. i appeal to everyone to see the enlargement of the european union in this historical perspective. i call on us to seize this historic opportunity to reunite the formerly divided europe. i call for close cooperation with the european parliament in carrying out the most important political task of our generation: welcoming the new democracies of eastern and central europe into the european union. thank you, mr president.
president of the commission. - mr president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, today is the last plenary session before the summer recess. the european council in seville has come to an end and this very important six months of the danish presidency has just begun. so i think this is a good time to take stock of the situation. among the activities that will accompany us in the second half of present stage of the negotiations, and if there are no accidents on the way, it is likely that the commission will consider all ten countries in the first wave ready for accession. however, the in writing. -(de) i cannot share the optimistic assessment contained in the report on the world food summit. i think the results of the conference of 182 states are rather meagre, and the prospects for an effective fight against hunger as a world problem seem bleak. over the past six years, we have taken only a modest step towards the goal proclaimed at the previous summit in 1996, to reduce the number of hungry people in the world from 800 million to 400 million by 2015. while hunger has been contained in some states, new areas of famine have emerged in other regions, such as the former soviet union. the main reasons why the 1996 action plan failed to achieve its objective were mainly that it was based on a neoliberal policy, which does not eliminate the structural causes of hunger and malnutrition, but, on the contrary, reinforces them. instead of globalisation and market liberalisation, the strict removal of trade barriers imposed by the north on products from the south is just as necessary as the encouragement of small-scale food production for local markets by small-scale producers and the free access of producers to means of production such as water, land, forests or fisheries. only then can trade become a key element for global food security, if it is not seen as a one-way street, on which large agri-food groups or livestock feed producers have a free hand. the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. in 1999, the total amount of packaging waste generated in the european union was 63.5 million tonnes. this represents about 17% of municipal waste and 3% of the weight of all waste generated. directive 94/62/ec on packaging and packaging waste has led to a reduction in the environmental impact of packaging and packaging waste, in particular through increased collection, recycling and recovery of waste. packaging is now recycled throughout europe, not just in central and northern european countries. there is no member state which did not reach the minimum material recovery targets for 2001 in 1998. the aim of this proposal is to set new targets for material recycling and recycling in general which are much higher than those provided for in the current version of the packaging directive. the commission proposal more than doubles the minimum material recovery target by 55% and increases the overall minimum recovery target by 10% to 60%. the european parliament has repeatedly stressed the need to take account of the economic and environmental consequences of the recovery and material recovery targets. this was done in the most detailed cost-benefit analysis ever carried out for community material recovery targets. the additional financing needs are estimated at a total of eur 700 million per year. the alternative disposal costs amount to eur 800 million in comparison. in addition, the environmental benefits were estimated at around eur 350 million. however, there are significant differences between the different packaging materials, both in terms of environmental benefits and the cost of material recovery. the commission proposal therefore sets not only overall targets for recovery and material recovery but also differentiated targets for individual materials. this is intended to ensure that material recycling is focused on those materials where it provides the most environmental benefits in relation to the costs incurred. some member states have already reached the new targets proposed by the commission. however, for other countries that have not yet developed their material recovery programmes, they represent a significant challenge. i should also like to add that i introduced the proposal on behalf of my colleague, mrs wallström, who is in johannesburg today for the sustainable development summit.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur for the committee on the environment, mrs corbey, for her report and congratulating her on it. it has broadened the debate on the amendment of the packaging directive and brought it into a broader environmental policy light. in addition to the change in recycling rates, it has introduced considerations of environmental impact assessments, for example through the use of life cycle analysis. it has thus already - one might say - anticipated the discussions on the white paper on integrated product policy. it is of course never wrong to start thinking about environmental impact assessment methods as early as possible, as this will create wider awareness of such environmental policy concepts. on the other hand, we cannot prescribe results in the directive on packaging waste until we have dealt with the subject in detail here in parliament. the white paper on integrated product policy is designed to do this. the committee on industry, external trade, research and energy has almost unanimously agreed. that is why we in the committee on industry, external trade, research and energy voted by a majority to exclude amendment no 16, which already provides for the introduction of environmental indicators for packaging, from the report. amendment no 16 also provides for a general avoidance rate of 10%. does this mean that the production of packaging material should be reduced? how are we going to achieve this? we are not going to be able to do that, because we are not going to be able to do that. that is another proposal which we should not be getting too close to. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. the new targets are ambitious, but i think they are justified in the end, from an industrial policy point of view, in favour of the environmental objectives of the european union. we will therefore be happy to agree to mrs corbey's report to a large extent, with the restrictions i mentioned earlier. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. mrs corbey has presented a comprehensive, ambitious report, which i support on most points. it is necessary that in future all member states actively and constructively contribute to the systematic prevention, collection and recycling of packaging waste. we need optimal systems for the 58 million tonnes of packaging waste produced in the european union every year. we are thus improving environmental protection, but at the same time we are also giving important industries greater planning certainty. two amendments are extremely important to me in the vote. the first concerns ceramic packaging, which has been produced for decades in many member states, particularly in france, italy, the netherlands and spain, but also in family farms in my home region. ceramic bottles, ceramic pots and ceramic shells are now used mainly for food packaging, but also for the packaging of snacks, chocolates, pastries, etc. and they account for only 0.1% of the packaging waste generated in the european union. so that is 60,000 tonnes out of 58 million tonnes. these ceramic packages are made of pure burnt clay and therefore do not contain any harmful substances. the nature of the material makes it pointless to recycle the used ceramic containers. they cannot be thermally recovered or recycled. they are inert and do not pose an environmental problem. it would make no sense, either ecologically or economically, to collect such small quantities separately and transport them thousands of kilometres across the member states. i therefore ask for support for amendment no 68, which sets out a small number of targets for recovery. the second point concerns the recognition of the latest techniques for the recycling of plastics in the directive. if we are going to amend this directive, we should take the opportunity to update the legal requirements in technical terms as well. amendment no 43 provides for the physical recycling of plastics, which will allow the production of new-product quality plastics from contaminated plastic waste. this is a method which makes perfect sense both ecologically and economically and has been proven to be a great technology. in germany, for example, over 1.8 million tonnes of plastic waste have already been recycled. there is enormous potential in this technology. it offers another method of recycling plastics in addition to the melting of high-quality, pure packaging plastics and the purely thermal recycling of mixed plastics in waste incineration plants. it should therefore be included in the directive. in addition, consumer protection requires that packaging materials are safe and comply with the requirements, that the hazard of waste is minimised and that the manufacture of packaging is state-of-the-art. i do not think that the commission should develop environmental indicators for packaging. the commission should develop concrete criteria for assessing the environmental impact of packaging. we need this directive to establish a functioning waste management system for packaging in all the member states of the european union. today where one in four flights is delayed. part of the delay is because the airspace is overloaded, and it's overloaded because we have this catastrophic situation -- the fragmentation in the sky. 350,000 hours of flying are wasted every year, caused by planes having to take detours because the direct route is blocked by military zones that cannot be overflown. in addition, we now have 41 airspace blocks in 15 eu member states. i always like to illustrate this with an example: on a flight from rome to brussels, the captain has to fly through nine different airspace blocks, which means he has to check in nine times and check out nine times. if you are trying to tell me that this does not involve additional potential dangers, because of course there is always the possibility of misunderstanding, language problems can occur, you are wrong. this is a very important point, and i hope that the commission will take it up. i believe that the proposals are appropriate to create a new architecture in the sky, to set up functional airspace blocks and thus ensure that on the one hand we increase capacity, which is absolutely necessary in view of the increasing volume of air traffic, and on the other hand we increase safety by minimising potential dangers in advance, that we reduce costs and thus make flying cheaper, and that we ultimately also do a favour, especially to the environment, because the 350,000 unnecessary flight hours that i have already mentioned can be eliminated. so we have the right target in sight. i would also like to say that there are certainly some points which can be discussed critically, and i know that some of my colleagues have doubts about this or that point, whether it is the right way to go. we have tried to make certain additions in the committee. i mention the industry consultation body because we felt it was right to involve users and manufacturers more closely in the project, so that we do not produce something that is not needed later, or on the other hand the requirements are quite different from what is coming to market. because in addition to the fragmentation we have in the 41 airspace areas, we also have a fragmentation of technology in europe. i believe that this too must be modernised and brought into line as quickly as possible. i would have liked to have gone a step further - as mr stockmann did, who made a similar request - and created a european supervisory authority, and to have removed the national states from this area in a much greater degree. i know that this is an illusion at the the council. - mr president, in recent weeks we have witnessed a terrible natural disaster in central europe, which has caused damage of almost unimaginable proportions. both member states and candidate countries have been affected. it reminds us - and this is almost symbolic in this half-year, when we are facing enlargement - that the member states and the candidate countries share a common destiny, have common problems which we must be better able to solve by joint action. i would like to thank the european parliament for this opportunity to express on behalf of the council our deep sympathy with the victims of the disaster. many millions of people are affected. some have lost loved ones, many have lost their homes. the material destruction will mark everyday life for a long time to come. we all have to do our best to help. it is important, not least in view of the importance of enlargement for the european community, that the eu, which is also a community of values and solidarity, should contribute to the resolution of the widespread damage. this was also emphasised in the letter received on 21 august by the president of the european parliament and the heads of government of the member states from commission president prodi, chancellor schröder and chancellor schüssel. the presidency was closely involved in the deliberations leading to the dispatch of the letter. i would also like to thank the european parliament and the president of the european parliament on behalf of the council for the commitment and goodwill shown by parliament to ensure rapid and effective action by the community. the commission has likewise shown great and praiseworthy activeness in this difficult case. the commission deserves praise for the speed with which the eu has been able to initiate decisions which will benefit the regions concerned in germany and austria as well as in the candidate countries the czech republic and slovakia. some activities have already been launched, others may be launched in the near future. i believe that there is broad support in the council for the flexible use of existing instruments - things that go hand in hand: prevention and repair. you will allow me to say a word first of prevention. i know that prevention requires means, that it requires political courage. i am thinking, for example, of the desire to control urban planning, to avoid waterproofing too large areas, in short, to clean up rather than develop the territory. but i also know, ladies and gentlemen, that prevention always costs less than having to repair. at community level, it is clear that the structural funds and the cohesion fund are the financial lever for prevention. a simple example. several countries were affected by the floods of the rhine and meuse during the first half of the 1990s. we then mobilised more than 140 million euros under interreg, and this money has helped develop flood monitoring and warning systems, as well as identifying risk areas, developing retention basins, and facilitating the flow of water. for the current period, 2000-2006, a large number of programmes also contain risk prevention actions. this is the case, for example, of the objective 1 programme for brandenburg, which provides for the construction and development of flood protection installations. more than 40 projects will be implemented with a budget of eur 230 million. this is also the case in the austrian tyrol. following the galtur disaster in february 1999, which claimed 31 lives, nearly ten million euros will be allocated to a measure to prevent avalanches. i am convinced, ladies and gentlemen, that whatever efforts are being made today are not up to the risks we face. we have started to reflect with you on the future of regional policy after 2006. i will propose, in due course, that the prevention of natural, technological and environmental risks should become a strong, almost unavoidable priority in future regional policy programmes after 2006. we see that the frequency of these disasters is increasing, although not all of them are as severe. in addition, as we have seen in the case of germany, regions which, with the support of the structural funds, made considerable efforts to revitalise their economies after reunification, to rehabilitate towns and villages, are now seeing their efforts destroyed in a matter of hours. regional development cannot therefore be achieved without the prevention of natural, technological and environmental risks. the commission, on the initiative of our colleague margot wallström, will propose a european strategy for risk prevention before the end of this year. in conclusion, i would like to say that it is not unimportant that we are debating this subject today, at this very moment, when the heads of state and government are meeting in johannesburg. it is clear that our planet needs global thinking and collective courage, as the brundtland report called for in the late 1980s, before the rio summit. we also see that this global thinking, whether at the global or european level, must be implemented in concrete, local, on the ground. this is how the ecological challenge, the challenge of sustainable development, meets the regional policy which we have the responsibility to animate. i now come to the urgent need to rebuild, to quickly demonstrate our solidarity with the german and austrian länder, but also with the czech and slovak regions which have been devastated. first, we must mobilise all the instruments we already have to meet this challenge. this is the commitment made by the commission on 28 august, a commitment which was immediately translated into decisions in the first area, agriculture, at the instigation of our colleague mr franz fischler. the existing instruments include, of course, the structural funds for the member states concerned and the preaccession instruments for the applicant countries. for the eligible areas and regions, the structural funds will be able to be redeployed between the different priorities of the regional programmes, and we are prepared to increase the cofinancing rates to the highest possible level. meetings will be held in the coming days with the national and regional authorities to specify the amounts that can be reallocated according to requests from the member states. the flexibility provided for in the regulations will be fully exploited, particularly as regards state aid. i also confirm that the disaster areas will not be penalised by the application of the n + 2 rule if, because of the floods, the appropriations are not used up within the time limits laid down in the regulations. but again, ladies and gentlemen, there are limits to the instruments we have at our disposal. the structural funds cannot therefore intervene outside the eligible areas. in germany, most of the disaster areas receive support from these funds under objective 1, but not in austria. moreover, these instruments are governed by provisions which you are familiar with and which do not always allow the necessary aid to be released quickly. that is why, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is proposing to set up a fund for the regions and the member states to provide assistance in the event of a major natural disaster. a solidarity fund which, i stress, will make it possible to act for the benefit of both the present member states and the future member states. we thought it preferable to use a new flexibility instrument, which could be mobilised to the tune of at least eur 500 million in 2002 and in the future to the tune of eur 1 billion, which would be used to fund the fund in the event of a disaster. the purpose of this fund would be to help restore normal life to the community - i am thinking of repairing the energy, transport and telecommunications networks, rebuilding or constructing temporary accommodation - and to limit the damage by consolidating preventive infrastructure, such as dams and barrages. so this proposal is, as you can see, different. both in terms of the amounts involved and the nature of the interventions envisaged, it is different from the emergency aid system for victims which existed between 1977 and 1996. but i think that this proposal from the commission is in line with the wishes i have heard here in this house for the last three years, for example after the disasters in greece, the azores, the canary islands, france and england. we want to adopt a proposal for a regulation on 18 september, in a few days' time, specifying the conditions and procedures for implementing this assistance fund. this tight timetable shows the commission's determination to move quickly, very quickly, as you yourself, mr pat cox, have clearly expressed your wish. i would therefore like to thank the committee on budgets, its chairman, mr terry wynn, and your rapporteurs, mr colom i naval, mr guido podestà and mr göran färm, on behalf of the commission and my colleagues here, for the quality and speed of their cooperation. this support and understanding is essential as we aim to make this fund operational in the coming months. the foreign ministers, as you said, mr president, have welcomed this proposal to mr elseneur. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to reiterate that prevention is always more effective and less costly than repair. but sometimes, as is the case at the moment, the urgency is what counts and it is important that the european union can provide its help, its concrete solidarity with the people and regions of germany, austria, slovakia and the czech republic who have been affected. this is proof that european solidarity, which goes hand in hand with local, regional and national solidarity, is much more than a name or a phrase: it has been the foundation of cohesion policy for the last 15 years or so. it has a meaning. and today we are showing that this sense is being confirmed, is being continued and is even being strengthened. commission. – mr president, the extended feed ban remains in force as a transitional measure until 30 june 2003. by that time, the feed ban should be reviewed. the review will take into account the forthcoming animal by-products regulation, the correct practical implementation of measures to control the feed ban, evolving scientific evidence and the availability of control methods. the commission services are already carefully examining the potential impact of different options for revising the feed ban but it is too early to predict the outcome of that exercise. the implementation of the feed ban in the member states is being monitored systematically by regular inspections carried out by the food and veterinary office. the fvo reports highlight the considerable efforts made by member states to implement the rules. however, where any weaknesses are identified specific recommendations are made after each inspection to further improve the controls. the commission has on several occasions expressed its concerns about the safe transport, storage and destruction of meat-and-bone meal. for this reason the adoption of the animal by-products regulation will be much welcomed. it creates a legal framework for the safe disposal of meat-and-bone meal by incineration, burial or landfill. it also lays down the rules for the safe use of meat-and-bone meal as fertiliser, in biogas production and in animal feeding. at present, meat-and-bone meal can only be used in pet food or in feed for animals. the new control framework created by the animal by-products regulation opens up the possibility of revising the present prohibition on the use of meat-and-bone meal. the animal by-products regulation includes provisions on channelling and traceability which will ensure that the present stocks of meat-and-bone meal cannot fraudulently be reintroduced into the feed chain. specified risk materials must already be marked as soon as they are removed from the carcasses, stored separately and finally destroyed. the commission is co-financing a research programme with two main objectives: firstly, harmonisation of the feed ban controlled by classical microscopy as well as improving its efficiency and secondly the development and validation of new methods based on alternative techniques. the commission is following the results of this research programme as well as private initiatives in this field closely and will take the results into account when reviewing the feed ban. whatever the outcome of the revision of the feed ban may be, i can assure you that the commission will not reauthorise the use of meat-and-bone meal in animal feed unless every possible risk to consumers and animals can be excluded and the provisions can be controlled properly.
- mr president, i have to go. commissioner byrne, your main argument for relaxing the feeding ban is the cost of disposing of animal by-products. now, this is more of an economic argument than an environmental argument. i am very surprised to hear this argument from you as the commissioner for consumer protection. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture and rural development. if you could give me an answer to that, i would be very grateful. i still believe that we need an absolute ban on feeding animal meal, at least until it is possible to determine the infection rate of prions responsible for causing bse and until it is possible to determine the different types of bone meal depending on the animal species. only then can we be sure that the bone meal we find in, say, poultry feed is not from poultry. commission. - mr president, regulation no 539/2001, adopted by the council on 15 march 2001, lists the former yugoslav republic of macedonia among the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of a visa if they wish to cross the external borders of the member states. the introduction of visa-free travel for macedonians would require amendment of the regulation, which only the commission can propose, in accordance with article 67 (2) of the treaty on european union. the relevant criteria for the inclusion of a country in the list of third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas or in the list of those whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement are set out in the fifth recital in the preamble to regulation no 539/2001. these criteria relate to the extent of illegal immigration from these countries, reasons of public policy and security, external relations, regional coherence and the principle of reciprocity. these criteria are not immutable. the extent and persistence of certain developments in this or that country may lead the commission to propose amendments to the regulation. the commission is constantly trying to detect such developments and to assess exactly their relevance. to carry out this task, the commission draws on a wide range of information from a wide variety of sources, paying particular attention to data and statistics from the member states which it collects in the context of the work of certain specialised council working groups. in this context, it should be noted that the european council meeting in seville on 21 and 22 june called on the council and the commission to give absolute priority, within the framework of their respective powers, to certain measures relating to the fight against illegal immigration. these measures include the review, before the end of the year, of the list of third countries whose nationals are required to be in possession of a visa and of those which are exempt. in the context of this review exercise of the regulation, the commission will take into account all relevant information on the situation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia in the light of the criteria set out in recital 5 of that regulation.

, the council. - mr president, i should like to thank you for this opportunity to discuss this very topical subject. the debate comes at a time of growing international attention to iraq, and this is a situation which virtually all the media speculate on daily basis - including this morning, as we have all seen. it is important to emphasize that the eu and the european countries have nothing against the iraqi people. historically, iraq has contributed in many ways to the region, and the iraqi refugees living in europe today are, in most cases, making a positive contribution in the countries where they live. in 1990, however, the iraqi regime chose to invade a small and defenseless neighbor, kuwait. a broad coalition of countries from around the world came together to reject this aggression. after the international community, led by the united states, had liberated kuwait, iraq agreed to a ceasefire with a number of conditions to end the war in kuwait. the european union has also expressed its support for the efforts of the united nations to combat terrorism. as soon as the un can confirm that iraq has lived up to its obligations to destroy existing stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction and to abandon the development of new weapons of mass destruction, the sanctions can be lifted. unfortunately, over the past 12 years, the iraqi regime has chosen not to cooperate fully in the dismantling of its weapons of mass destruction and long-range missiles. in 1991 the un security council established the first commission of inquiry, unscom (united nations special commission). it was offered completely unacceptable working conditions by the iraqi regime. it culminated in 1998 when the regime refused to grant unscom further access to iraqi territory. in december 1999, the security council established a new monitoring committee, unmovic (united nations monitoring, verification and inspection committee), to replace unscom, by means of resolution 1284. but neither has unmovic been granted entry into iraq by the iraqi authorities on conditions that would enable unmovic to carry out its tasks. in recent years, the un secretary-general, kofi annan, has made a concerted effort to persuade the iraqi regime to let the weapons inspectors do their job, so that iraq can comply with the terms of the ceasefire, which has been in place for more than 10 years. so far, these efforts have been fruitless. iraq continues to make new demands and new conditions, it continues to resist giving unconditional and unhindered access to the weapons inspectors. the economic and social situation in iraq has been deteriorating ever since the gulf war. the infant mortality rate in central and southern iraq is now twice what it was before the gulf war. the nutritional status is generally worse. the school system suffers from a lack of materials, and the infrastructure and water and sewerage systems need to be renovated and expanded. iraq has gone from being a relatively rich country with economic growth to a country with a shrinking economy and a very critical humanitarian situation. the need is particularly acute for the most vulnerable groups - women, children and the poor, as well as those who do not support the regime of saddam hussein. the international community is therefore providing iraq with a very substantial amount of humanitarian aid. the eu's emergency aid programme, echo, is the largest single donor of humanitarian aid to iraq, but the un system, the international red cross and associated donors are also active in the humanitarian field. to counter the impact of sanctions on the civilian population, the oil-for-food programme has been established, allowing iraq to supplement its own food and medicine production with imports financed by the country's oil revenues. the oil-for-food programme was proposed by the security council in 1991, but due to iraqi reluctance and delay, the programme was not launched until december 1996. the un security council resolution 1409 of 14 may 2002 revised the oil-for-food programme, which was adopted by the general assembly on 1 january 2002. the proceeds of the oil-for-food programme shall be used for food, medicines and other health equipment, as well as materials and supplies for civilian purposes in iraq, including equipment for the maintenance of the oil sector. the revised oil-for-food programme allows most goods to be exported to iraq without further ado, while tightening controls on goods that could be used to manufacture weapons, including weapons of mass destruction. the international community's position on the iraq question is taken by the un security council. the un secretary-general has had several contacts with the iraqi foreign minister this year in an effort to resolve the current impasse. last contact was yesterday. however, these efforts have not yet produced any concrete results. the eu's position is clear. it was most recently expressed in a statement by the presidency on behalf of the eu on 20 may 2002. it states that 'the european union welcomes the meetings between the iraqi foreign minister and the un secretary-general with a view to finding a diplomatic solution to the issue of weapons of mass destruction in iraq based on full compliance by iraq with the security council resolutions and with its disarmament obligations. the european union reaffirms its position on the unconditional respect for un security council resolutions. it called on iraq to comply with the resolutions without delay, including in particular the return of weapons inspectors to iraq as provided for in resolution 1284. the european union fully supports all the efforts of the security council and the secretary-general of the united nations. the european union welcomes the adoption of security council resolution 1409 of 14 may 2002. it involves substantial relaxations of the un sanctions regime against iraq. the new oil-for-food programme allows iraq to import civilian goods more freely, while maintaining strict controls on dual-use products. such control is necessary in the light of the continuing concern of the international community regarding the use of such products in the wmd or conventional weapons programme. the european union calls on iraq to cooperate fully with this new framework, which should help to improve the humanitarian situation for the benefit of the iraqi people. " there has been a lot of speculation in the international press over the summer about a possible imminent american attack on iraq. the american president has said that the united states wants regime change in iraq. that is what is concrete. the president has also said that he will consult his european allies and partners. we are convinced that this will happen if necessary.

commission. – mr president, firstly i would like to thank mrs stenzel on behalf of the commission for her report on the european agency for reconstruction. it is a thorough and thought-provoking report which raises important questions. my colleague, mr patten, discussed it with some of you at the meeting in strasbourg on 2 july and circulated an information note in june which i hope covered many of the concerns of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. mr patten has promised to present a report outlining the future implementation of assistance before the end of 2003. this will form the basis of the recommendations which the commission is required to submit by 30 june 2004 under the european agency for reconstruction regulation. today i will outline some preliminary thoughts, but first allow me a few comments on some specific points in the report. i am pleased that the report so clearly acknowledges the efficiency and high delivery capacity of the european agency for reconstruction. the agency is indeed a success story. it is doing an extraordinary job in channelling community assistance to the former republic of yugoslavia and former yugoslav republic of macedonia. in this context, i would also like to highlight the success of the deconcentration to commission delegations. this has, for example, been a major factor in the successful implementation of the european community assistance in bosnia and herzegovina. the commission endorses many of the observations in the report. we strongly agree, for example, with parliament's suggestion that we need to focus increasingly on institution and capacity building. that is certainly our approach. a large percentage of the overall assistance is allocated to institution building and it is increasing all the time. the country strategy papers and the multiannual indicative programmes allow for some flexibility and do not need to be revised for these transitions. mr swoboda mentioned the issue of illegal immigration and the balkan routes and we have made it very clear that we need a regional approach to fight illegal immigration and organised crime in south-east europe. under the swedish presidency we organised the first meeting of the five countries in the region, because without regional cooperation we will not succeed. some member states have developed a liaison officers' network and we have been cooperating with border guards and police forces in the region and that has definitely improved the situation although it is still far from resolved. the shift i have mentioned above applies to the countries with deconcentrated delegations, as well as those where the agency is operating. there is no reason to think that the agency will handle institution-building programmes any less successfully than it has physical reconstruction. the legal base for the agency is perfectly adequate and does not need to be amended. nor do we want to change its successful brand name, even if the focus is no longer principally reconstruction. the report suggests that if the territorial competence of the agency were to be extended its regulations should be modified. the decision to extend the agency's mandate to the whole of the former republic of yugoslavia and to the former yugoslav republic of macedonia was taken because of exceptional circumstances. we do not see a need to extend the agency's territorial competence further. in the report you emphasise the need for coordination. we share this view. it is an absolute necessity to ensure that our assistance brings the highest added value possible. we are therefore pleased to note the systematic and extensive coordination already taking place between commission services and between actors on the ground. from previous debates, i know that you want to discuss the broader issue of the future of assistance to the western balkans and its organisational aspects, including the competences of the european community delegations and the agency. our preliminary thoughts are as follows. there is no reason to assume that the coexistence of the agency and the commission delegation in the same country leads to an overlap. the political role and the status of all delegations in the region are identical, beyond assistance implementation. they are focused on developing the political and institutional relationship with the european union. as each country moves further into the stabilisation and association process, we will have to evaluate whether support for the process of bringing the countries up to european standards needs to be completely integrated with the political work of the delegations. this question will be at the heart of the decision on the future of the agency. but we cannot give a clear answer at this point. above all, we do not believe it will be to the region's benefit to dismantle recently established arrangements which are working well. administrative and institutional tidiness must not impede our primary objective of achieving real change on the ground. however, we clearly need to keep our options open and be ready to change how we deliver aid, when there are clear benefits in doing so. the commission will ensure that these decisions are taken on the basis of what is most effective in achieving the four objectives: more focus on quality, speedier implementation according to the highest standards of management, visibility, and above all the impact of our programmes on the ground. parliament's views will be invaluable in developing the arrangements that best suit the needs of the region and the strategic ambition for its closer integration into the european union.

the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. members of the european parliament! first of all, i would like to thank jonas sjöstedt, the rapporteur on this matter, who has made a substantial contribution to this complex area. this area is important not only for us here in europe but also for the rest of the world, in particular for our partners in the developing countries. as you are probably aware, the protocol we are going to discuss today is linked to the recent ratification by the european community of the cartagena protocol on biosafety. the overall objective of this un agreement is to establish common rules for the transboundary movement of genetically modified organisms with the aim of achieving global protection of biodiversity and human health. the european union must fulfil its international obligations. we must therefore incorporate the provisions of the biosafety protocol into our legislation. this proposal complements the existing community framework, in particular as regards the export of genetically modified organisms, in order to bring it more into line with the provisions of the biosafety protocol. the proposal consists of the following main elements. firstly, the obligation to notify exports of genetically modified organisms intended for deliberate release into the environment. secondly, the obligation to inform our international partners about community practices, legislation and decisions on genetically modified organisms and the unintentional release of such organisms. thirdly, a set of rules to be used to identify genetically modified organisms for export. these rules are in line with the latest developments in community legislation on genetically modified organisms, in particular with the provisions of the draft regulation on traceability and labelling. the current proposal does not contain any new specific community provisions on the import or movement of genetically modified organisms between member states, which will continue to be covered by existing community legislation. i would like to emphasize the importance of moving quickly on this proposal. the eu has played a key role in international negotiations since their inception. we must show that there is no doubt that we will meet our commitments and that we will be able to fully implement the protocol once it enters into force.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on agriculture and rural development. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the european union signed the cartagena protocol on biosafety in 2000. this international convention must now be transposed into community law as soon as possible. the protocol aims to avoid adverse effects on biodiversity and human health through international regulation of trade in live gmos. it regulates the safe transfer, handling and use of genetically modified organisms, with a focus on transboundary movements. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the matter. for gmos intended for direct use as food and feed or used for processing, notifications to the commission or to the biosafety clearing-house shall be provided. the regulation will apply only to exports to third countries outside the european union. trade between member states of the european union and imports into the european union are already subject to community law. the future eu regulation should follow the protocol's requirements as closely as possible in order to create legal certainty through uniform international standards and avoid unnecessary red tape. at the same time, it is necessary to ensure that european exporters do not face any additional formalities, but only those which must already be fulfilled when exporting to third countries. the report by mr sjöstedt has, however, largely lost sight of this objective of preserving biodiversity. it contains many requirements which go far beyond the cartagena protocol and which seek to artificially impede trade in living gmos. i do not think it is appropriate to include requirements on probative and liability in the regulation, because these issues are currently being discussed in a separate legislative procedure and therefore have no place in this regulation. the protocol assumes that gmos exported for use in closed systems are exempted from the complicated and time-consuming notification procedure. the commission's proposal is not a good one. i therefore re-submit amendment no 50 from the committee on agriculture and rural development together with mrs sommer and mr purvis and ask for support for it. i am convinced that gmos used in laboratories and not released into the environment do not pose a threat to biodiversity or human health. they should therefore be excluded from the notification procedure. in amendment no 51 we ask for further derogations from the notification procedure in order not to make trade in gmos more difficult by unnecessary bureaucratic obstacles. the regulation also needs to be aligned as closely as possible with the cartagena protocol in order to achieve greater legal certainty for international trade. it is therefore necessary that gmos for which the relevant importing country has already granted an authorisation to an exporter once and gmos for which the relevant importing country has already granted an authorisation for field trials can be exported without the need for complex authorisation procedures. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted. we need sensible and workable regulations to take advantage of the opportunities offered by biotechnology in third countries, while preserving biodiversity. commission. – mr president, let me give a single set of figures to illustrate this in responding to mr van dam, who mentioned correctly the low level of implementation of tacis and other programmes. when we took office at the end of 1999 the overall time it would take to work our way through the existing commitments at the level and the pace of spending at that time was 4.5 years. the following decisions on commitment and the actual implementation in terms of spending per year. we are moving in the right direction but i have not been silent in trying to clarify to this parliament what kind mr president, thank you for changing the list of speakers so that i can speak. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market is very concerned that the work of the european court of justice is still lagging behind in terms of translation. what is the practical effect of this? let us assume that a trial has been concluded and a judgment has been rendered. since the court of justice, unlike other community institutions, does not publish its decisions until they are available in all the community languages, the result of the congestion of translations is that the judgments are kept in the files of the court of justice for one or two years before they can be published. i think that is an intolerable situation. this is also becoming increasingly problematic for the courts of the member states, because in preliminary ruling proceedings the procedure before the european court of justice is only an interim procedure within the member state's court of first instance. in other words, these two years do not then conclude the whole procedure, but are added to the duration of the procedure in the member state. we therefore call for the appropriate means to be made available to put an end to this intolerable situation. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market is also responsible for internal market and eastern enlargement issues. we have always taken account of the particular challenges that enlargement to the east poses to the internal market, particularly to the border regions. we strongly support the amendments which seek to set the pilot programme for smes at eur 15 million, as promised last year.
