aspects. i would like to make it clear to members of this parliament that the commission has acted fully in accordance with the commitments i made on 2 october last year. i should like to add that in july this year, my services sent out questionnaires to over sixty companies and organisations representing many small and medium-sized enterprises, including both parallel traders and trademark holders, who might be at most risk from abusive restrictions on the sale in the community of trademarked goods. the results of this investigation, combined with our ongoing consultations with other commission services – in particular our colleagues in the directorate-general for competition – should allow us to build a clear picture of whether trademark rights are indeed being abused by right holders to stifle legitimate trade. that report, as promised at our previous meeting, will be transmitted to parliament by the end of this year. that is my answer to the question. i shall be most interested to hear what members have to say about it.
- mr president, mr commissioner, i would like to thank you for your reply. first of all, i'd like to apologize for being a little late. the car that was supposed to pick me up arrived half an hour later than we agreed. that is why i have only heard part of the speech. but i got their point. the commissioner, the committee and parliament have not taken these decisions out of a sense of humour or for fun, but because we believe that the nera study you are referring to does not meet the requirements we are trying to attach to such decisions. this means that we have assumed in particular that these things, which are everyday things that every woman and every man, especially those from the poorer classes, buy, for example, jeans, shirts, polo shirts, sneakers and the like, are proven, without my needing a nera study, to be offered outside the eu by the same branded manufacturers with the same quality at half price or even cheaper. that's one of the reasons. the second reason is that we do not think that trademark law has the purpose of foreclosing the market, of allowing different pricing systems inside and outside the eu, in particular having the higher price inside the eu and the lower price outside the eu; rather, we think that this is a matter of competition and not trademark law. the function of trade mark law is to designate, identify, uniquely identify the manufacturer, the trade mark, the product and to confer certain rights on the proprietor of the trade mark. they must be, and we will defend them to the last. but a very different and distinct question is the question of exhaustion. in germany, we have had international exhaustion for about 100 years since the stamps were introduced. with this international exhaustion, we have achieved the economic miracle in germany, all the growth and everything. in the last five years since the european trademark law has been in place, we have seen the two-price system, we have seen that trademark law has come first for companies because trademark law is much easier to prosecute than the other rights that are actually product-related, namely the rights of design, patent, copyright and the like; this is a more difficult case. that alone is the reason, and trademark law cannot be stronger than competition law. that's why we asked these questions. that is why we have asked you as the commission not to refer to a nera study but to investigate and answer these specific questions. finally, the question that has arisen since the debate on trademark law at the time is: what about internet commerce? the internet is supposed to be here. we're funding it. if someone buys outside the eu and the trader sends the goods to the eu, then under the current legal situation, this is against trademark law. that can't be the point of trademark law. so once again we warmly ask the commission to do its own research on these few points and to report to parliament and not to refer to a nera study which in our view does not address these problems.

commission. - mr president, the honourable member's question concerns the interoperability of interactive television services and the role of the mhp standard. the question has five points, which i shall answer separately. firstly, on the first point, i can say that the adoption of the framework directive in the field of communications is a strong signal both for operators in the digital television market and for consumers. the guidelines will help to achieve three important objectives. first, give broadcasters access to networks and related facilities such as guides and electronic programmes. secondly, to avoid excessive regulation through the application of proportional access solutions and, finally, to provide benefits to consumers by contributing to the provision of a wide range of services. in view of the legal position established by article 18 of the framework directive on electronic communications networks and services, member states should encourage openness in the provision of an api application programming interface. no specific api technology or single api will be imposed. the mhp standard is a standard that meets the needs for interoperability and openness in this field. this is why we encourage the voluntary implementation of this standard by the industry. the second point concerns the date of publication of the applicable standards for hcm. my answer is that the list of standards will be published after the meeting of the committee on communications on 2 october. third, the use of non-standardised api technology can give a company market power. the directive provides for specific solutions which can be used by national regulatory authorities to control the market power of certain undertakings. because it guarantees interoperability and offers greater freedom of choice to users, standardization will certainly help to prevent monopolies from arising. however, competition in itself is not a guarantee of fair competition. dominant actors may emerge even in the presence of open standards. fourthly, as i said in my answer to the first question, the objectives of regulation are openness and interoperability. the mhp standard meets the needs for interoperability and openness in this field. that is why we are giving political support to the voluntary implementation of this standard by the industry. however, the sector also wants to continue the dialogue on interoperability, in particular on migration. we have therefore launched a debate and a sectoral inquiry on interoperability. fifth, in its plenary statement of 12 december 2001, the commission undertook to publish the relevant mhp standards in the list of standards to be published in the official journal, in accordance with article 17 of the framework directive. under this directive, member states are required to encourage the implementation of the standards contained in the list. secondly, the commission undertook to examine, one year after the entry into force of the directive, whether interoperability and freedom of choice for users had reached a satisfactory level in the member states. if this is not the case, the commission may propose to impose the use of these standards. in accordance with our commitments, we will provide the list of standards after the relevant committee meeting on 2 october, as i have just said. they are expected to be examined by july 2004. article 18 of the framework directive requires member states to encourage the use of an open api. the commission will therefore engage in a dialogue with the member states and the national regulatory authorities, through the committee. the mhp will of course be one of the subjects discussed in this dialogue. at present, widespread adoption of the mhp seems to be the most obvious way to achieve interoperability. businesses must take the initiative in developing migration strategies because migration itself poses many technical and business problems. we welcome the industry's sustained efforts to address these problems and to reach agreements at national or european level for the transition to mhp.

president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is with deep emotion that i take the floor in this chamber today. at the beginning of my mandate, i made a commitment to you that enlargement would be the top priority of my commission, that my commission would be the commission of enlargement, because enlarging the union means consolidating an area of peace, security and democracy at continental level. today, three years later, i stand before you again to say that that commitment has been kept: the commission has done its job; the commission has kept its promise. after a thorough examination of the progress made by the candidates, i can announce the names of the countries for which we recommend that the council conclude the negotiations by 2002. let me read the highlight of the recommendations we adopted today: cyprus, the czech republic, estonia, hungary, latvia, lithuania, malta, poland, the slovak republic and slovenia fulfil the political criteria. taking into account the progress made by these countries, their track record in implementing the commitments made, and taking into account the ongoing preparatory work, the commission considers that these countries will have fulfilled the economic and acquis criteria and will be ready for accession by the beginning of 2004. the commission therefore recommends that the accession negotiations with these countries be concluded by the end of the year, with the aim of signing the accession treaty in spring 2003. in view of the progress made in the last year by bulgaria and romania, the commission takes note of the date - 2007 - indicated by these countries for their accession. the commission will do everything necessary to ensure that this objective is actually achieved. turkey has made great progress towards the copenhagen criteria through constitutional reform and a number of legislative packages. however, additional effort is needed. the commission therefore recommends that the european union increase resources and support for turkey's pre-accession preparations. to this end, we will propose a revised accession partnership and strengthen the evaluation of legislation. turkey is encouraged to continue on the path of reforms to advance its candidacy process. ladies and gentlemen, just 13 years ago berlin was still divided by the wall of shame. the wall fell, germany was reunited. thanks to the freedom we have regained, we have found the historical unity of all the peoples of europe. our common destiny is once again to build the future together, a future based on the shared fundamental values of peace, democracy, the rule of law, respect for human rights and the protection of minorities. in 1993, the copenhagen european council offered the countries of central and eastern europe the prospect of joining the union. since then, these countries have come a long way, peacefully moving from dictatorship to a stable and participatory democracy. this is an extraordinary budget: in the course of a decade, dozens of national, regional and local elections have been held in a transparent and democratic manner; thousands of laws and regulations were passed to give birth to new democracies and to transpose the community acquis into national legislation; training of tens of thousands of officials and judges is under way to enable them to apply the new legislation; hundreds of thousands of elected officials, experts and trade union leaders have become familiar with our policies through the training and cooperation projects we have funded; all 12 countries meet the political criteria set out in copenhagen and democratic institutions have been strengthened everywhere; finally, the economies of the ten countries as a whole are progressively improving their performance: growth rates are higher than ours; inflation and the deficit are managed and controlled; foreign direct investment is flowing in at high rates: this shows that the markets are confident. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report we have adopted today also highlights the shortcomings that still remain in certain areas, for certain countries. these gaps must be filled before accession and the commission will, together with the authorities of these countries, ensure that the difficulties are resolved in good time. we are particularly concerned about the level of administrative capacity and the functioning of the judicial system, which are hampered by a lack of financial resources and, even more importantly, of human resources. we have tried to respond to these problems by using a support programme with a budget of eur 250 million. this program is beginning to bear fruit. we also noted the insufficient preparation for the implementation of the acquis in some key areas: the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in bananas is based on the principle of the common organization of the market in bananas. two very serious problems must be added: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of corruption, which, with a few exceptions, affects many countries, and the shameful phenomenon of human trafficking. i do not mean by that that nothing has been done in these fields. in fact, much has already been done and for some countries the work is almost complete. our report, however, insists on the scrupulous monitoring that the commission has undertaken to carry out from now onwards. in this respect, we will publish a final evaluation document six months before the date of accession. to cope with the complex steps that accompany enlargement, the commission will take all the necessary measures to reorganise its services: on the one hand, we will strengthen our monitoring and support work after the accession of the new member states and, on the other hand, we will have to support the accession process of the countries that will follow those included in the recommendation adopted today. mr president, our aim remains the signing of the accession treaty in the spring of 2003. we are therefore entering the final stages of the process. the commission hopes that the european council in brussels on 24 and 25 october will take the necessary decisions on the following outstanding issues: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. that will allow these chapters to be negotiated and closed before copenhagen. the commission will put forward a strengthened preaccession strategy for bulgaria and romania in time for the copenhagen council to adopt it. for turkey, which does not yet meet the accession criteria, the commission will propose a strategy with additional financial resources at the beginning of next year. the treaty of nice remains for us an essential step which cannot be ignored. i therefore express my confidence in the irish electorate, which will be called upon to speak again in a few days' time. i hope that the historic goal of unifying our continent will not be called into question by this vote. i would like to mention, finally, the cyprus question. we hope for concrete progress towards the reunification of the island, although the conclusions of the helsinki european council do not make it a precondition for accession. the commission hopes that cyprus can join the union as a reunified state and considers this the best solution for all. the commission, in recommending that the council conclude the negotiations with cyprus swiftly, again calls on the parties concerned to promote the reunification of the island and invites all to join the efforts currently being made by the un secretary-general to reach a solution within the year. the seville european council has already stated that the union would 'consider the terms of such a comprehensive solution in the accession treaty, in accordance with the principles underlying the european union'. ladies and gentlemen, all too often i hear about the risks and costs of enlargement. i believe that we can and must speak about this in a very clear and unambiguous way, because the costs have been analysed in all their details and are compatible with the resources available. but we must also and above all communicate to the public the benefits of enlargement, namely stability in europe, the unification of a continent artificially divided by history, the creation of the largest single market in the world. with enlargement we will be linking up with economies that have a lower income level than the current member states, but that also have a higher growth potential. this was precisely the situation in 1985, when spain and portugal concluded their accession negotiations. no one can now doubt the farsightedness and correctness of that decision, which was also very controversial at the time. enlargement is the new frontier of the european project. it will boost trade, investment, education and research, and economic growth. as for the budgetary burden, we know that it is sustainable until 2006 because it is included in berlin's financial perspective. i do not want to hide the fact that the accession of the ten countries will involve, within the limits i have described, a considerable cost, which will, however, be largely compensated in the future by the benefits which will result from the consolidation process of enlargement. however, enlargement has not only economic value: its importance is above all ethical and political. enlargement is the completion of the european construction: the process that has given us half a century of peace and prosperity must be extended to the whole continent. let's think for a moment about the recent history of the balkans: thousands of people have died, entire populations have been displaced, cities have been completely destroyed. enlargement is our political masterpiece because it prevents all this. in this more complete and correct view, the minds and hearts of our citizens. enlargement is achieved through strong determination, political courage and a far-sighted view of history. it also requires us to be consistent, because accession commission. - madam president, i would first of all like to say, at the start of this debate, my sincere thanks to your assembly, and in particular to your rapporteur, mr berend, and to mr walter, and to presidents caveri and wynn for the very good cooperation of our two institutions and the speed with which you have been so kind as to examine this proposal for a regulation. we must now move as quickly as possible and also in terms of budgetary mechanisms so that the first aid can be provided before winter. i wish i could be a first-aid worker in november. given the progress of the discussions in the council this afternoon, i think it can be said that an agreement on this proposal for a regulation is now within reach, and i am happy to say that this is possible thanks to a very broad agreement between parliament and the commission, of which mr berend was one of the architects. in this final phase of the discussions, we have three points to decide. the first is to define precisely which disasters can be compensated for. the concern of your assembly is not to confine the system to a too rigid definition. the council, for its part, wanted priority to be given to natural disasters. the commission, as i said the other day before the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, has studied very carefully the recent history of disasters in europe. eighty percent of these disasters that have happened in recent years have been natural disasters, storms, earthquakes, or floods. i do not therefore think that there is any inconsistency in accepting the priority requested by the council, since the possibility for the commission to intervene in other scenarios - ecological, environmental or technological disasters - would be preserved, in some very limited cases. the second point is the threshold or thresholds for triggering the intervention of the fund. like the commission, your assembly is particularly concerned that we should have two criteria, one or the other, rather than just one, in order to assess fairly the impact of a disaster on the economy of a state, whether that state is a large state, a large country like germany, or a smaller state. and we know, unfortunately, that smaller states in our union are prone to real and serious natural disasters. even if the council is keen to substantially reassess the criterion expressed in absolute terms - we proposed eur 1 billion in damages, the council is stopping at eur 3 billion - the principle of having two alternative criteria is not called into question. finally, the third point: the maintenance of a qualitative criterion allowing exceptional intervention in a single region affected by a disaster. this is a top priority for the commission, and this is the margin of appreciation we have been asking for throughout this discussion. the higher the quantitative thresholds, and i have just said that they have been raised in the council's proposal, the more discretion is needed, because the worst thing would of course be, ladies and gentlemen, for this fund to be so constrained, rigidised by very limited qualitative criteria and too high quantitative ones, that at the end of the road it would never be used. i have said, and i repeat it to you in this house, that in the last 14 years we have, thank god, only identified seven major disasters with damage of more than one billion euros. that is why i proposed in the commission's first version that the quantitative threshold of eur 1 billion be retained. so the worst thing would be that we are so rigid, locked into criteria of any kind, that this fund, once created, is never actually used even though populations are hit by disasters. the council takes a very cautious approach to this qualitative criterion. i am saying that neither the commission nor, i believe, parliament wants the operation of the regulation to be hijacked by systematic recourse to this qualitative criterion. the commission is and will be extremely rigorous in its use of this particular solution. what we want, and i say this very simply, is to ensure that an exceptionally serious disaster in one region can be eligible for the fund. there are indeed regions in europe which are more exposed than others: the islands, the isolated or remote regions, or regions which we must protect, as the treaty asks us to do through a specific article - mrs sudre, who is here, knows this well - article 299 on the outermost regions. i therefore think that we must have the means, and that is precisely the means that the commission has given, to give them priority aid below the quantitative criteria. in conclusion, madam president, with your help and on this basis with the help of your rapporteurs, i now hope that agreement can be reached very quickly on this proposal for a regulation and on the amendment to the interinstitutional agreement. because behind the problems, the regulations, the thresholds, the standards, there are, let's not forget, i met them and i was moved, people who are waiting after being wounded, and we know that beyond the wounds there are also dead people. these populations now expect europe to help them, alongside the national and regional authorities, to return to the most normal conditions for their daily lives in an emergency.
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the floods that struck central europe in august of this year were of horrifying proportions. numerous lives were lost, and there was immense material damage. whole areas of the countryside and cities were devastated, agricultural lands and cultural monuments were badly damaged. the scale of the destruction has caused great concern throughout europe, and the desire to help the affected countries to cope with the many problems at eu level has quickly become concrete. the commissioner, the local population remembers with gratitude that you and commission president prodi were there a few days after the disaster and that you gave them an idea of the extent of the damage. but not just grateful, but hopeful. they hoped that the eu would intervene in such a case. however, there is still a lack of appropriate instruments at community level, as we know that an existing eu support fund was not renewed in 1998. as rapporteur, i see the establishment of this new solidarity instrument as an important complement to the community funds. it provides the eu with a non-bureaucratic disaster response tool in the form of a flexibility instrument, which can provide rapid assistance on the ground. the aim of the fund is to enable the people, regions and countries concerned to return to normal living conditions as quickly as possible, with immediate financial support. it is therefore limited to the most pressing needs. the long-term reconstruction of infrastructure and the economy remains a matter for other instruments, and this eu emergency aid is not intended to replace but to complement the efforts of the countries concerned. the 1 billion euro which is supposed to be in the fund is fictitious, i.e. not set aside in a fixed budget line, but will only be activated in the event of a disaster. the commissioner rightly asked: what is the disaster that this fund can help with? the definition of major disaster on the basis of a threshold of eur 1 billion or a ratio of 0.5% to gdp actually ensures that the use of the fund is limited to exceptionally severe cases of damage. that is why we in the committee have agreed by a majority on a definition which says: major disasters. we have deliberately avoided natural disasters, environmental disasters, technological disasters. what do you want to say to the people affected when a disaster like the one that happened in new york on 11 september occurs here in the european union, on a scale where many of those affected will also suffer the same fate? we cannot say: 'the eu cannot help here, we are sorry, this is not a natural disaster!' we should stick to the concept of major disasters here, and the three-month deadline for requesting funds proposed in the report is in fact in keeping with the principle of urgency and immediate rapid relief which characterizes the fund. as regards the availability of the funds allocated, i am speaking as rapporteur of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism for the period of two years to ensure the reconstruction of destroyed infrastructure and equipment in the fields of energy, water, waste water, telecommunications, transport, health and education at short notice. the appropriations will also be used to provide emergency services and to provide immediate protection facilities and measures for the immediate protection of cultural heritage and for the clean-up of natural areas, buildings and the commission is not prepared to accept this. a policy to limit government borrowing is acceptable if it is translated into practice by measures to limit inflation while simultaneously increasing growth. this is the crux of the present situation. the best way to produce growth is to boost demand: demand through public investment, through business investment and through private consumption. if, despite the european single market, it is still the national premise to gain location advantages within the european union - and this is possible because there is no sufficiently coordinated economic, fiscal and social policy - then the basic conditions for sustainable european growth simply do not exist. the increase in domestic demand cannot be achieved by lowering wages, because this reduces purchasing power, it cannot be achieved by taxing the medium-sized enterprises, which create the most jobs and training, and it cannot be achieved by relieving large companies of their burden of paying taxes at all. a reduction in investment rates in a downturn, even in the absence of significant inflation, is pro-cyclical and lacks any economic policy rationale. the budgets of the member states vary widely. shadow households are common. so there is no comparable basis for budgetary management and accounts even in the european union. therefore, if the discussion is held on amending the stability pact, it must not be because of the current complicated economic situation - this would be political opportunism - but it must be held because the construct does not work in principle. reform of the stability pact must be accompanied by increased coordination of european economic, social, employment, tax and environmental policies in order to stimulate investment.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. with the present legislation we have to ask ourselves whether we need more europe in the authorization of new innovative medicines or whether the mutual recognition procedure is the optimal approach. in other words, do we want a more internal market for medicines on the basis that patients across europe will have access to new, safe and effective medicines more quickly, or is the extremely cumbersome authorisation procedure intended to keep patients away from new medicines for as long as possible in the future? i am in favour of extending the scope of authorization to medicinal products containing new active substances. this is not only beneficial for patients, it is also beneficial for companies, who can bring medicines to market faster than before and thus improve their competitiveness. the aid for smes compensates for the difficulties of central authorization which they are facing. i believe that the patient and his needs should be at the heart of legislation. this means that the safety and efficacy of a medicinal product must be a central issue in the marketing authorisation procedure. the procedure must be transparent. it is therefore essential that patients, doctors and businesses have access to all non-confidential information. a public database will provide comprehensive information on the status of the marketing authorisation procedure, on clinical trials carried out, on side effects and on the prices of medicinal products. in this context, i regret that the commission's information project on asthma, diabetes and aids did not find a majority in the committee. the commission proposal was certainly misunderstood and raised the concern that advertising for prescription medicines would be allowed. the committee's decision, however, provided an opportunity to improve patient information. i am sure that this mistake will have to be corrected in the next few years. pharmacovigilance, i.e. the monitoring and reporting of adverse reactions, is important for the safety of a medicine. the obligation to report adverse reactions and the obligation to report periodically to the marketing authorisation authority ensure a continuous comprehensive evaluation of a medicinal product. the safety net in the field of pharmacovigilance is tightly knit. this makes it easier to identify side effects and provides the opportunity for rapid action in the event of a crisis. for these reasons, a re-authorisation procedure may be waived after five years. another focus of the reform is to prepare the bodies of the european medicines agency for future tasks and eu enlargement. the structure of the eu food authority will also be introduced at the european medicines agency, with open procedures for candidates for the management board and the administrative director. high scientific competence and a disclosure of interests are the prerequisites for membership of a body of the agency. in addition to the existing scientific committees, there will be an equal committee on herbal medicines. the commission will therefore be able to grant voluntary central marketing authorizations for herbal medicines. this will give patients across europe access to proven herbal medicines. in addition to the important point of health protection for patients, there is also the question of the competitiveness and innovation capacity of the pharmaceutical industry in europe. the harmonization of the protection of the underlying material is certainly a step towards greater competitiveness. the current rules in europe set it at between six and ten years and there is an urgent need for harmonisation. the ten-year plan is a signal to the pharmaceutical companies to intensify research and bring real innovation to the market. it is also a signal to generic manufacturers to use the bolar system. the commission proposal is, in my view, a successful attempt to strike a balance between the legitimate concerns of pharmaceutical companies to protect records and the public health systems' desire to improve access to low-cost generic medicines. overall, this legislation is an important contribution to improving healthcare in europe, which will benefit patients in the long term. commission. – the intergovernmental negotiating body for the who framework convention on tobacco control is at the moment holding its fifth meeting in geneva. concerning the regulation of contents of tobacco products, the text released by the chair for further discussion does not set harmonised standards but provides for each party to adopt and implement standards as recommended by the conference of the parties, including standards and best practices for testing and measuring the content and emissions of such products. the final text of the convention is expected to be ready in march 2003. should this provision become a part of the final text of the framework convention, and considering the timetable foreseen for the establishment of the conference of the parties, it is indeed possible that such recommendations could be produced by 2007. the commission believes that the adoption of common standards for the regulation of the content of tobacco products and emissions and the adoption of common rules for measurement methods are essential measures to be taken by all parties to the convention. recommendations made by the conference of the parties can be a very important instrument for harmonising standards, and parties should therefore be called upon to duly consider them. however, as such harmonisation could lead to a lowering of the level of public health protection, the community's position is that such recommendations should not be binding. that is to say, their adoption should be left to the discretion of the parties. this would allow parties, such as the community, to keep their already existing strong legislation in this field. in this context, i would like to draw to mr wuermeling's attention the fact that, according to the negotiating directives provided by the council, the negotiations must aim to base the operative provisions of the framework convention on existing community legislation. finally, concerning the very last part of mr wuermeling's question, the commission firmly believes that the negotiations on the framework convention will be successful and is doing its utmost to ensure that an efficient instrument with the maximum impact on tobacco consumption will be agreed upon. however, in the extremely unlikely event that the negotiations should fail, the commission would not see this as a reason to propose modifying the provisions of directive 2001/37 on exports.

the commission. - mr president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. first of all, i would like to thank parliament again for the intensive and efficient cooperation it has given us in the reworking of the financial regulation for the european budget. it was only thanks to the cooperation of all the institutions that the new financial regulation was adopted unanimously by the council on 25 june 2002. the new financial regulation is a fundamental part of the commission's reform and i am proud that we achieved this feat in 2002. i would like to thank in particular - and i would like to emphasize this again - mr van hulten and mr dell'alba. the latter is not here now, but i would like to mention it again at this point. one of the main objectives of the revision of the financial regulation was to simplify the financial regulation by incorporating the very detailed provisions into the implementing provisions. the commission will be able to adopt these implementing rules before the end of the year, so that they can enter into force at the same time as the new financial regulation on 1 january 2003. mr van hulten has done a very thorough job with the committee on budgetary control, and i thank you very much for that. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. firstly, several amendments in the report seek to include all the reports and information to be sent to the budgetary authority in an annex to the annual activity reports of the authorising officers. the commission is in favour of such streamlining of procedures. as regards the summary of the annual activity reports of the authorising officers, the report proposes that the obligation to provide such a summary to the discharge authority should apply not only to the commission but also to the other institutions. i share the intention behind it. the wording of the financial regulation does not allow us to impose such an obligation on other institutions. we believe that the other institutions should agree to such an undertaking. secondly, the report proposes changes to the financial actors mentioned in the financial regulation with two objectives: (a) the budgetary authority shall be informed when the authorising officers at a1 level and the accounting officer are replaced. (b) the posts of accounting officer and internal auditor should be externally contracted. we can see that the budgetary authority is informed of new appointments. however, we cannot follow the report's proposal. direct external publication would also be contrary to the statute. the statute expressly provides that vacancies must first be advertised within the institutions before they can be advertised externally. this means that direct external tendering would not be compatible with the staff regulations. thirdly, on the amendments concerning the financial irregularities panel, we can agree to the proposal that the panel should include an independent expert. however, we believe that the compulsory detection of irregularities would go too far even in minor cases. fourthly, on the directive on late payment, i note that parliament has again pointed out that the deadline for transposition has expired and that the institutions must now comply with the provisions on interest and payment deadlines, or at least should comply with them. fifthly, i can also agree to a number of amendments on accounting. in particular, the commission agrees with the clarification concerning the introduction of an integrated data processing system. this is in full accordance with the commission's proposals to date. as regards the requirement that a list of all persons with access rights to the electronic accounting system be drawn up and that a verification path be set up so that the nature and authorship of all changes made to the system are clearly apparent, i can inform you that both are already in place in the commission. we welcome the inclusion of this provision in the implementing rules, although i cannot at the moment say whether the accounting systems of the other institutions, apart from the commission, already meet these conditions. sixthly, in amendment no 17, you ask that the budgetary authority be informed of any waiver of claims over eur 100 000. the commission will also take this up. i would like to conclude by making a clarification on the last amendment in the report. it reads: 'the accounts for the financial year 2002 shall be drawn up and presented in accordance with the financial regulation of 1977, except for the obligation to submit them to the financial controller.' i would point out that the new financial regulation clarifies that there will be a transitional period for the clearance of accounts until the financial year 2005, that is to say that the clearance of accounts until 2005 will be carried out in accordance with the procedure laid down in the current financial regulation. given that the only member state to have so far largely adopted accrual accounting this more anglo-american accounting , namely the united kingdom, has required a transition period of more than seven years, the timetable for the commission remains extremely ambitious. i repeat my offer to the committee on budgetary control to inform you as soon as possible of the proposals which the commission has made here.

president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, now that ireland has voted in favour of the treaty of nice, we have overcome the last political obstacles to ratification of the treaty and have paved the way for enlargement. i am glad that the irish voters have made the choice, and they have shown openness and a sense of responsibility. what is true of ireland is true of all of us. it is in the common interest to pursue the enlargement process without delay. the next european council in brussels is therefore of fundamental importance. the debate will focus on our recommendations to conclude negotiations with ten candidate countries by the end of the year. the date of accession of bulgaria and romania and the next stage of the application process for turkey will also be discussed. among other subjects, we shall deal with the kaliningrad question. we shall perhaps have the opportunity to review the international situation, especially how to continue the fight against terrorism in the light of the recent tragic events in bali and the philippines. we shall also hear the report of the president of the european convention and have the usual exchange of views with the president of parliament. the first item on the agenda will therefore be enlargement. i would like to reiterate the strong reasons which led us to recommend to the member states that they conclude the negotiations with ten countries positively. it is our historic and moral duty to share with our european neighbours the stability and prosperity we have achieved in half a century of integration. peace, stability, democracy and the rule of law are the essential ingredients for political stability. they have worked well in the past, and the recipe will work for future member states. enlargement will bring european governance and standards across the continent. we expect positive effects in a wide range of areas: the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the principle of subsidiarity to all their activities, including the development of the internal market, the establishment of more efficient public administrations, stronger judicial systems, better protection of minorities, effective prevention of crime, especially international crime, stricter controls on illegal immigration, closer monitoring of products in circulation, especially food safety, and finally stricter standards for the protection of the environment. on the international scene, the union's growing size will increase its political capital. our trade, financial, environmental policies will have more weight; europe will be better able to defend human rights and work to reduce the gap between the north and the south of the world. if we can unite loyally and speak with one voice, we can make a difference on issues such as climate change and managing the impact of globalisation. but beyond that, the first group of ten new member states will bring enormous economic benefits to the union as a whole, to the union of the old and the new member states. the increase in population will strengthen the single market: the population will increase by some 75-77 million citizens, bringing the union's total to 453 million. to understand the meaning of this figure, consider that the total population of the nafta area which includes the united states, mexico and canada is about 400 million. some argue that if the population of the 10 candidate countries increases by 20%, the eu's overall gdp will only grow by 4 to 5%. this is not a negative figure, it is a figure that highlights the fact that we alone are realizing, albeit at a regional level, a process of democratic globalization; this is not a bad thing, because it means that there is a high potential for growth, given the characteristics of these countries. it should not be forgotten that the ten applicant countries are already growing at a faster rate than the 15 existing member states. on an annual basis, their growth in 2001 was 2.4 per cent compared with our 1.5 per cent. in 2000, it was 4.1 percent, compared with 3.4 percent in 2000. above all, the ten candidates will bring highly qualified human resources to the union. the enlargement countries have, it is true, 20 per cent more population and only 5 per cent more income, but they have 25 per cent of the science and engineering degrees. this is a resource that will strongly support increased development. these countries are therefore, for all these reasons, if interpreted intelligently, our new frontier. european companies will have new opportunities for expansion and development because there will be a great need for new technologies and because the new member states will offer a market for our goods and services. if this is the advantage of enlargement, we can now see the problems that remain. before i go into them, however, i would like to make a small general observation: we must be very careful not to jeopardise the success of enlargement by arguing over details, as is often the case when political decisions are being taken. the unification of europe must always take precedence over narrow national and sectoral interests. we must always keep the big picture in front of us and never forget the potentials i mentioned earlier. in recent years these ten countries have made enormous progress. the periodic reports which the commission has recently presented have fully recognised this and - i want to stress this - these have not been indulgent or optimistic analyses. the commission's confidence in the enlargement countries is based on sound, serious and analytical grounds. the progress made in the past shows that all 10 countries will be ready for accession at the beginning of 2004, including in those areas where it is obvious that work must be completed. however, although we are fully confident, the commission has undertaken to monitor the countries' latest preparations and progress even after accession. to this end we have prepared safeguard clauses for the internal market and for the justice and home affairs sector, which are the sectors our people fear most, in which they have the greatest distrust. these safeguard clauses will come into force if the commitments given are not respected in practice: it is a remote possibility, but it is always possible, and we must take it into account. as is well known, the central points of discussion between the heads of state and government will be financing issues, the last remaining but certainly not of minor importance. the broadest consensus is on net transfers. it is clear that there is unanimous agreement on two principles: first, at the time of accession, the 10 countries must not be in a position of net contributors; secondly, all expenditure commitments must be kept within the strict limits of the berlin agenda. we have adhered to these two principles, and so i think it will not be difficult to reach agreement on the exact amount in copenhagen. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be given the right to vote in the council. frankly, we can't offer our fellow citizens any less. under this financial commitment, cohesion countries existing countries will receive funds of eur 231 per capita in 2006, while citizens of the new member states will be entitled to eur 137 per capita. i don't think we can get any stronger divisions than this. finally, the problem of agricultural financing, which is well known. i am aware that some of the present member states have expressed reservations about the budgetary sustainability of these proposals and have asked for additional guarantees. it is legitimate to ask the question of the future financial assets of the union; in fact, we have to. the commission maintains its position: the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to accept them. for all the financial issues still outstanding, i hope that the european council in brussels will give the danish presidency and the commission a mandate to conclude the negotiations with a view to the final decision in copenhagen. that's why i'm asking for your support. however - and this is a final reminder - an important step we must take in this last phase of the enlargement process is that of information. the latest eurobarometer survey, two days ago, shows that half of the union's current citizens are in favour of enlargement, while a third are against it. the others have no opinion. these figures are quite comforting on the one hand, but they are also worrying on the other: in other words, 65% of those interviewed think that enlargement will lead to an increase in drug trafficking, international organised crime and unemployment, which is the exact opposite of what i think, seriously and on the basis of analysis, will happen in the future. why, then, is enlargement associated with these fears? the answer is found in the latest eurobarometer survey: only 21 per cent of the population think they are well informed about the subject, while 79 per cent think they are not. it is clear, therefore, that we must act on objective, serious, in-depth information. the group which claims to be not well informed, as the statistics say, is not necessarily opposed to enlargement but, more often than not, has an indifferent position. however, this is, for me, the worst prospect. we must convince the citizens that enlargement will be a solution and not a problem. this is why the commission has launched an information campaign aimed at both the current member states and the candidate countries. the success of enlargement will therefore depend on our ability to inform public opinion correctly, and in this respect too we cannot disappoint the expectations of millions of europeans. the future of our union depends on the enthusiasm, strength and intelligence we will put into the final efforts to complete this process. president of the council. - mr president, when i was asked to make a statement on this subject, we did not know how sadly topical it would be. we are discussing this matter today in the shadow of the horrific terrorist attack in bali on 12 october, which claimed the lives of over 200 people. it was a complete and utter disaster. it also stressed that the threat of terrorism must continue to be taken very seriously. we must not be too hard on ourselves - the fight against terrorism will be a very long and tough one. the last time i had the honour of speaking to parliament on terrorism was on 11 september this year, when we commemorated together the anniversary of the terrorist attack on the united states. at the time, i emphasized that the united states had been the target of the bali has shown that no one is a peaceful saint. the terrorists have twisted the many benefits of globalization to their inhuman and reckless games. the fight against terrorism is a global struggle, in which close cooperation between the eu and the us is an indispensable prerequisite for success. we have seen that if the terrorists intended to divide the western democracies, they have achieved the opposite. it must be a clue for all of us in the future. this is why the eu's external role in the fight against terrorism is a very important element. what has the eu done since 11 september 2001 and has it been effective? the eu reacted politically very quickly and decisively after the disaster last year. first, a strong statement by eu heads of state or government making it clear that the eu would do everything to ensure that those responsible were held to account and punished. the eu also stressed that the us government and the american people could count on the eu's full solidarity and cooperation in the continuing fight against terrorism. we're gonna have to stick with that. the eu did not stop at words. on 21 september, the heads of state or government adopted the action plan which became the backbone of the eu's action. the list of results is quite impressive. a key item on this list was the strengthening of police and judicial cooperation. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european year of the environment, which aims to promote the use of renewable energy sources in the european union. these are areas where the eu has made a quantum leap forward by rapidly adopting the necessary legislation. a decision on the freezing of assets and evidence was also agreed. it will lay down rules on the recognition and enforcement in the member states of freezing orders issued by a judicial authority of another member state. this too will make it more difficult to be a terrorist in the member states. in addition, negotiations have been launched with the united states on a cooperation agreement on extradition and mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and an agreement between europol and the united states on the exchange of personal data is expected to be in place by the end of the year. in sum, the eu has delivered what could be expected - and more. another key point is the effective stopping of the financing of terrorism. the necessary legal acts to implement security council resolution 1373 were adopted in december 2001. this is an important stop to the financing of terrorist acts, which is the lifeline without which international terrorism cannot exist. in addition, a number of important measures have been taken in the field of aviation safety. on the whole, we have reason to be satisfied and proud of the way in which the fight against terrorism has been handled. it has become harder to be a terrorist and to carry out terrorist acts in the member states and it has become safer and more secure for our citizens. can we rule out the possibility of terrorist attacks in the future? no, we cannot, but for the same reason we must continue the struggle with renewed energy. this applies both to the continued hunt for terrorists wherever they are and to targeted assistance to eliminate the underlying causes that help to feed terrorism. have we jeopardized the legal security of the citizens? for us politicians, it's a fundamental political dilemma: is it acceptable to limit our freedom to protect ourselves from terrorism? are we creating a big brother society under the guise of protecting our freedom and security? where do we draw the line? i think the famous liberal philosopher, karl popper, has given us a guide when he says, "over intolerance, tolerance must exhibit intolerance, or tolerance will be destroyed by intolerance". this is also the line i feel is being taken in parliament's motion for a resolution, which stresses the need to be firm in preventing terrorists from profiting from their crimes. the presidency fully agrees with the emphasis on the principle of non-reward contained in the motion for a resolution. i think we've found the right balance. at the same time, the presidency also considers that there is no need for further substantial counter-terrorism measures within the eu at present. the danish presidency attaches the highest priority to the fight against terrorism. the fight against terrorism has been directed in particular at the external role of the eu. at the same time, we will of course continue to work on the implementation of internal measures. the danish presidency aims to make progress in mainstreaming the fight against terrorism in all aspects of eu foreign policy. in addition to strengthening the eu's international role through a greater emphasis on the fight against terrorism in the eu's foreign policy and systematic assessment of third countries' efforts to combat terrorism, the ambition is for the eu to be a flagbearer in the un and other international fora. the maintenance of the international anti-terrorist coalition and cooperation with the united states is a necessary aspect. other aspects include the conclusion of a general convention against terrorism and the universal implementation of the 12 existing international conventions on combating specific acts of terrorism. the council conclusions of 22 july 2002 on the external action of the union against terrorism opened a new chapter in the fight against terrorism. in future, the eu will take greater account of the efforts of third countries in their agreements with third countries to combat terrorism and will conduct a more targeted and, if necessary, more intensive political dialogue with third countries. it was also decided to identify specific measures to assist third countries in meeting their obligations under security council resolution 1373 and to concentrate on a small number of countries with a view to launching a pilot project in cooperation with the un counter-terrorism committee. it must be directed in particular at those countries which have the political will but not the ability to comply with un resolutions. in the latter areas in particular, it is hoped that concrete results will be achieved during the danish presidency by the launching of one or two pilot projects. however, a precise and comprehensive threat assessment is a prerequisite for reassessing the content of contractual relations with third countries, strengthening political dialogue if necessary and assessing possible assistance to third countries. it has therefore also been a major priority for the presidency to draw up the necessary analysis of individual countries and regions. that work is progressing well. we expect the necessary analytical basis to be provided shortly. we must send our counterparts in third countries the message that their handling of counterterrorism will have a significant impact on their relations with the eu. i am therefore also pleased that this idea is reflected in the motion for a resolution. the eu can certainly be known for its actions in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks of september 11. we have put our own house in order in accordance with the un resolutions and we have done so in a way that takes account of the legal certainty of the citizens. it is now time to look outwards and play the international role that is expected of us. we must stick to the anti-terrorist coalition and to close cooperation with our closest partners, not least the united states. then we can hope for success. i therefore hope that parliament will continue to support the line which is being taken here and i would like to thank the two commissioners for their cooperation in this field. commission. – mr president, i welcome the chance to contribute to this debate. as both the president-in-office and my friend and colleague, mr vitorino, have said, recent events in indonesia show clearly that the threat to the international community from terrorist attacks is still very real – despite the enormous amount of work we have undertaken in the last year in an effort to counter that threat. our sympathy and condolences go out to all those who suffered bereavement and horrendous injury in bali. we think in particular of our friends in australia and promise them that we will be exploring ways in which we can work closely with them to confront terrorism in all its manifestations. we will shortly be sending a high-level troika to indonesia to discuss the contribution we can make to this campaign. that troika will be going on to australia to ensure that we can involve ourselves as fully as possible, working in cooperation with the australians as well. we in the european union have been at the forefront of the international effort to combat terrorism. our actions in the immediate aftermath of 11 september demonstrate a point i have made in the context of the debate on the effectiveness of the european union's foreign and security policy: when the political will is there, we can take effective action regardless of the institutional architecture. within days of the attack on america, a series of concrete measures was tabled by the european commission. this led to a plan of action adopted, as has been said, by a special european council on 21 september. a week later the united nations security council adopted resolution 1373 – a truly landmark resolution setting out for the first time a clear set of actions which all member states must follow to combat terrorism. and i say 'must' advisedly. it is a resolution adopted under chapter vii of the un charter, which means that it is mandatory. it is a mark of the strength of international outrage following the 11 september attacks that such a resolution could be adopted with universal support. the european union's action plan is not cast in stone. we have adapted it to reflect new realities, including the adoption of resolution 1373. we have also prepared a 'road map' setting out the means of implementing the action plan. we have taken practical steps at union level to outlaw terrorist organisations and cut off their funding, as previous speakers have said. my colleague has just outlined the significant steps taken on police and judicial cooperation, border security and other internal questions. but all such measures to combat terrorism can only be truly effective if they are applied everywhere – if there are no hiding places left for terrorists and their sources of funding dry up. the new challenge now before us is, therefore, to help those countries which cannot – for reasons of institutional weakness, lack of expertise or lack of financial resources – fully implement resolution 1373 themselves. here the european union clearly has a crucial role to play. much of the work which needs to be done is in areas where the european union has built up an enormous amount of expertise through its programmes such as phare, tacis, meda and cards. i am thinking here of the work we are already doing, helping our partner countries establish effective law enforcement institutions, improve border management and fight money-laundering. in addition to the work under way, the european council conclusions of 22 july asked us to consider what more we could do. we have just agreed a strategy, endorsed by the council at coreper on 3 october, of identifying pilot countries where we judge there is a clear need for help and we feel the commission has a comparative advantage. we are looking at the possibilities for action in countries of high importance in the fight against terrorism: in central asia, south and south-east asia and the gulf. we hope to send missions to some of these countries very soon to work up concrete projects, notably in the area of terrorist financing. we have also incorporated the fight against terrorism into all aspects of our external relations. we are systematically evaluating our relationships with third countries in the light of the support those countries might give to terrorism. in this context, we are examining where counter-terrorism cooperation elements can be added to, or form part of new agreements, as has been the case in our association agreements with lebanon, algeria and chile. however, it is worth remembering that our external action goes wider than political dialogue. the european union is a massive provider of development assistance. we provide about 55% of total international assistance and as much as two thirds of all grant aid. this is an often forgotten contribution to international security in its widest sense. poverty and environmental degradation do not cause or justify terrorism. nor are the poor more wicked than anyone else. but just as poor people are the major victims of crime in rich societies, so political instability and violence are more prevalent in the poorest countries. nowhere is this clearer than in failed or failing states. if we are to deny al-qaeda and other terrorist networks the territory from which to plan future atrocities, we must do all we can to bolster weak or failing states. our action in afghanistan is a case in point. the european union is the main donor helping to rebuild this shattered country. the community alone has pledged over eur 1 billion from the budget over the next five years, involving a substantial contribution to the operating costs of the new government, including salaries for police, nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants. this is what we have done so far in the fight against terrorism. but i want to close with the thought that we can take a wide or a narrow view of counter-terrorist action. the narrow view focuses exclusively on terrorists and terrorist acts, on tracking down the former and preventing or punishing the latter. but there is a wider view too: our actions must be seen in the context of our unswerving support for democracy, human rights and the rule of law. we have a wide range of instruments at our disposal to tackle the root causes of terrorism, both in terms of poverty and economic development, and of institution building and the rule of law. it is here that our contribution to the fight against terrorism will have the most impact. the fight against terrorism is not like a conventional military campaign. it is unlikely to have a beginning, a middle and a glorious end, with surrender documents and peace treaties. it will go on and on, in many different shapes and forms, a few thousand terrorists against the whole of humanity. earlier the president-in-office quoted from karl popper's the open society and its enemies. i suspect that, for our generation, it was almost as important a document in shaping our attitudes as any by the great political philosophers. when karl popper wrote the words quoted, he was referring to the enemy of totalitarianism – a much clearer enemy. in response to that, drawing on other political philosophers like burke, he argued that, to some extent, liberty had to be limited in order to be maintained. we face a different problem today. the ability to deliver terrorist assaults on free societies is much easier in open societies. the only way to make terrorism absolutely impossible is by a sort of global orwellianism, which would itself provoke from liberals, like the president-in-office and myself, the sort of assault others might regard as terrorist. we have a real paradox here. that is why it is so important that open societies and liberal democracies, without losing their values, work together comprehensively, cooperatively and intelligently. to prosecute the campaign against terrorism will require international cooperation of unprecedented breadth and depth: political cooperation, economic cooperation and security cooperation. the european union must play its part in those efforts – vigorously, generously and creatively – a key partner, i hope, in a well-planned and resolutely pursued campaign of multilateral engagement. pressure of work is great and we do not want to add to that. the directive guarantees freedom of expression and the liberty of the media. that is clearly expressed in the recitals, and the text of the directive itself introduces several safeguards for journalists, including the possibility of self-regulation. however, recent scandals in several member states have shown how recommendations by journalists to buy or sell a specific share can influence its market price to their advantage. what we do not want is to exempt from transparency obligations the small category of highly specialised financial journalists who recommend investment strategies. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments 6 and 7. it would not seem justified to exempt this rather small category of persons from basic market integrity standards which apply to all the other market participants. in addition, completely or partially excluding journalists from the scope of the directive would mean harmonising the definition of ‘journalist’ at community level, not a very easy task and something we do not wish to do. therefore, amendment 5 is a compromise proposed by the committee on economic and monetary affairs for today’s plenary. it is fair both to journalists and to the public interest, and therefore acceptable. i strongly hope that members of this parliament share the view of mr goebbels and of the commission on this point. after all, financial journalists who specifically recommend a certain strategy to the investing public should declare any conflict of interests they may have. i do not see why that should not be a useful aspect of this directive. so the commission can agree with amendments 1 to 5, but we cannot agree, for the reasons which i have already explained, to amendments 6 and 7. should parliament adopt the common position together with amendments 1 to 5 and reject amendments 6 and 7, for which i am now making a plea, i hope the council will be able finally to accept this text in the next few weeks. adoption of the directive before the end of the year would be a major step towards the integration of european financial markets by 2005 that we all aspire to. i recommend adoption of this directive to parliament and i hope that all who take part in the debate will agree with mr goebbels and myself.

commission. – mr president, the questions are very important in the context of the current debate on gmos in europe. we still do not have a clear-cut reply to some of mr graefe zu baringdorf's questions. please accept that my answers are to some extent preliminary ones, which will require further scrutiny and reflection, both within the commission and in our ongoing discussions with the member states and the different stakeholders. i wish to begin with a short description of the problem we are faced with when dealing with the adventitious presence of gm seeds in conventional products. this is also important for everyone who has followed this debate. on a global scale, gmo cultivation has increased dramatically in recent years. in 2001, 5.5 million farmers in 13 countries grew an estimated 52.6 million acres with gm crops. between 2000 and 2001, the number of acres planted to gm crops increased by almost 20%. for some crops, the increase was particularly large. in the us, gm corn increased from 4.4% of all planted acres in 1996 to 32% in 2002. gm soya beans increased from 7.4% in 1996 to 74% in 2002. to date, the cultivation of gmos has been geographically concentrated, with 99% of all gm crops produced by four nations: the united states of america, argentina, canada and china. however, gm cultivation is likely to spread to other nations in the next few years. so far europe has played a very marginal role, with fewer than 20 000 acres of gm crops, mainly in spain and france. that is some 0.03% of the worldwide area. europe has large volumes of trade with major gm producers – although trade in gm products has mainly concerned products for animal feed. imports of gm products for human consumption, like maize, have largely ceased, because of the inability of exporters to ensure the identity of all individual gmos in shipments. the last few years have shown that the adventitious presence of traces of gmos in conventional products has become inevitable. cross-pollination between plants is a natural phenomenon – that also happens between other seeds. we simply cannot completely control its mechanisms, which include factors such as wind and insect movements. it is therefore largely unavoidable that small traces of gmos will be transferred to conventional crops and their harvested products. storage and transportation practices may also make it difficult or extremely costly to ensure total segregation. consequently, conventional seed lots will contain traces of gm seeds. setting tolerance thresholds for impurities for gm seeds in this particular case is the only way to address the problem. closing our market completely is not a viable option. against this background, the commission is currently preparing a proposal for a commission directive amending the annexes to the seed directives. this proposal includes additional conditions and requirements concerning the adventitious presence of gm seeds in lots of non-gm seeds. the committee on agriculture has been informed twice about the status of this proposal. commissioner byrne has written to inform mrs jackson that the text will be formally submitted to the european parliament, which will then have the opportunity to scrutinise it. article 21(2) of directive 18/2001/ec provides for the possibility of establishing thresholds below which traces of authorised gmos are exempted from labelling requirements. hence, conventional products containing adventitious traces of such gm seeds below this threshold would not have to be labelled. let me now answer some of the questions raised by mr graefe zu baringdorf. on the competent body to set thresholds, the regulatory committee, provided for in directive 18/2001/ec, is competent for decisions pertaining to thresholds under article 21(2) of the directive, with regard to exemption from labelling requirements. however, it is not competent for decisions made under the sector-specific seeds directives, where thresholds relate specifically to marketing criteria for seeds. the standing committee on seeds rightly has the necessary competence in this case. consistency between the different pieces of legislation has to be maintained. on the risks that a significant percentage of gm seeds may be released out of control into the environment, i would first say that it is paramount that any threshold should take account of the protection of human health and, importantly, in the case of seeds, the environment. you will be aware that this includes a comprehensive free-market assessment of the potential risks. secondly, thresholds must be workable and enforceable. the proposed thresholds arise directly from the opinion of the scientific committee on plants and are scientifically founded with reference to the characteristics of the crop species. thirdly, on the registration of gmo cultivation, under the provisions of article 31(3)(b), member states are required to establish registers for recording the location of gm fields grown for commercial purposes. as detailed in the article, the objective of this is to allow the possible effects of these gmos on the environment to be monitored. as for the scope of directive 18/2001/ec, this clearly relates to cultivation of a gm seed product itself and not a conventional seed product containing traces of gm seeds. the gm seed product itself has to be labelled as such and also traced, so that growers will know what they are sowing. it will therefore be possible for member states to record the locations of the resultant crops. however, the threshold values, which are based on robust scientific assessment, should aim at ensuring that the cultivation of conventional seeds basically maintains the characteristics of non-gm cultivation. coexistence is a key issue in the commission communication on life sciences and biotechnology – a strategy for the future. the commission has commissioned a number of studies on this issue. the main aim is to assess the consequences arising from an increase in the cultivation of gm crops in the european union in the context of coexistence. so far, we only have preliminary data based on hypothetical scenarios, and further experimental data is required to provide a more accurate picture. the commission is actively pursuing such work before considering possible options to ensure the viability of conventional and organic farming and their sustainable coexistence with gm crops. as a further step in this process, the commission has commenced discussions in partnership with member states, farmers and other private operators to find the most appropriate solutions. it is important to say that the issue of coexistence is not one of risk per se. it does, however, highlight a possible need to establish correct agricultural management systems and practices for the different crop types to ensure their coexistence and consumer choice. this is my initial reply to your questions and i will be happy to make further comments at the end of the debate.
