commission. – mr president, this is a recurring institutional debate. should the codecision procedure or comitology be used? the seeds directives provide for purity criteria in the annexes and they can be adapted to scientific and technical knowledge by the comitology procedure provided for under the seeds directive. it is thus possible to set thresholds for gm presence in non-gm varieties through a comitology procedure. the 1% food labelling threshold provided for in a council regulation has been set by the comitology procedure provided for under the foodstuff labelling legislation. article 21(2) of directive 2001/18/ec also states that labelling thresholds may be set in the comitology procedure provided for under the directive. timing and the possibility of making it a practical procedure are also factors.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i too have complained on several occasions in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection that the seed-trading regulation is being pushed so far in the comitology procedure. i have said that i think it would be more sensible for the commission to wait until the european parliament has completed the procedures currently under way before adopting the gmo seed scheme in this comitology procedure. we need to ensure that the new seed regimes are consistent with the regulations on gmos in food and feed and on traceability and labelling of gmos. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the decision was as close as possible in some respects, and particularly in relation to the thresholds. we are currently awaiting the decision of the council of ministers, which has been postponed again since last week to december. a final decision by the council and the european parliament is not likely to be expected before the middle of next year. i think it would be better if the commission kept its paper in the drawer for another year and then adjusted the thresholds to the regulations currently pending. so much for the procedure. i would like to make a few comments on the substance. the question of whether gmos are good or bad is not really part of today's debate. but since mr graefe zu baringdorf is referring to positions on gmos in his questions, i am quite prepared to do so. all the questions asked by the honourable member show that he has not understood something or does not want to accept it. there is a difference between the release of gmos under directive 2001/18 on the one hand and the setting of a technical limit value for the incidental presence of gmos in conventional seed in the context of an amendment to the annexes to the seed marketing directives on the other. these directives contain a wide range of technical regulations and rules on the quality and marketing of seeds in the eu. mr graefe zu baringdorf himself has said that, as is the custom, the directives were adopted after the european parliament had itself been consulted. it also provided that certain technical details would be settled under the regulatory committee procedure. the commission is not, of course, deciding on the release of gmos, but on the definition of another quality standard for conventional seeds, and this is in accordance with a competence under existing eu law. that is what the commissioner said. the scientific committee, like countless other scientific papers, confirms that statistically semi-reliable statements do not allow a limit of less than 0.1%. this is the limit of analysis. there is no zero percent, there is no such thing as gmo-free. the commission's draft proposes thresholds for gmos which do not pose risks to the environment and consumers and which can therefore be grown commercially in the eu. the registration requirements of directive 2001/18 have nothing to do with the marketing of conventional seed. far more problematic may be the secondary seed that farmers themselves produce. it is not subject to any quality control obligation and therefore does not undergo any tests for the presence of gmos. mr graefe zu baringdorf himself is in favour of liberalizing these subsidy schemes. the lower the threshold for the incidental presence of gmos, the more likely it will be that conventional and organic products will be required to be labelled. the commission, several member states and a large part of the european parliament are therefore advocating the realistic 1% limit in the forthcoming gmo regulations. in conclusion, i would like to say that a practical farmer should not lack a basic understanding of the simple biological facts of the unintended and technically unavoidable presence of seed of type a in type b. a practical farmer is our colleague graefe zu baringdorf. there are natural events. gmos are always around.

commission. – mr president, i should like to express my gratitude to honourable members for tabling this motion for a resolution. naturally, the commission continues to be concerned by the human rights situation in iran and, in particular, by the persistence of repressive measures against democratic institutions, civil society and the media. the prevalence of arbitrary arrests, torture, discrimination against minorities and evident lack of the rule of law are all deeply disturbing. the all-too-plentiful evidence of the use of cruel, inhuman and degrading punishments, including the appalling stoning of children, of women and of men, continue to demonstrate the scarcity of civilised standards. the most effective way to raise these concerns is through the half-yearly comprehensive dialogue meetings, bilateral talks at ministerial level and similar sustained activities. in addition, avenues for more direct and specific dialogue have been explored recently by the troika, as several members said. on 21 october the gaerc endorsed the strategy for starting a human rights dialogue with iran on the basis of the recommendations of the exploratory troika mission that visited teheran from 30 september to 1 october last. during these explanatory talks, the iranian government voiced a political will to enter into a human rights dialogue and to do so largely on the eu's terms. no restrictions were requested in relation to the list of human rights issues to be discussed and the dialogue will be regularly assessed with the help of specific and realistic benchmarks, such as reports from the visits of the united nations thematics rapporteurs. the dialogue would initially take the form of an experimental round table in teheran in december of this year. its format will be assessed immediately after the first session and could be revised, as necessary, in the spring of 2003. the opening of negotiations with iran on a trade and cooperation agreement, indissolubly linked to instruments on political dialogue and counter-terrorism, gives the european union substantial leverage, since the progress in the negotiations will be directly related to parallel progress in, among other things, human rights. this connection is at the heart of the political package defined at the june council and formally adopted on 12 july. the establishment of a structured eu-iran dialogue on human rights is obviously not a complete antidote to the variety of deep and serious concerns. at this juncture, however, it seems to constitute the most effective available means of promoting our attempts to bring about tangible improvements in the grievous human rights situation in iran. i emphasise that, in all of this, our concerns relate to the basic rights and well-being of human beings, regardless of their faith, regardless of their customs. that is the fundamental value that guides us and provides the motivation of the european union. we will continue to act upon those fundamentals.

the financial perspective for the period 2004-06, as well as on the preparatory work within the commission and the other institutions. in particular, we will have to ensure that the acquis communautaire is fully and effectively applied throughout the union's legal area from the first day of accession. more generally, it is essential to reflect on the new dimension, quantitative but above all qualitative, in which we will be operating after enlargement. we are entering a reality of 25 countries and we are pursuing a new project of society for the european continent, a project which requires a strong popular support. the process of western european integration, the small european identity, is finally becoming a project of continental unification. enlarging the union means proposing a new philosophy of international relations. the eu's external relations are also affected by the political situation in the candidate countries. unity and multiplicity, community of values and differences will be even more the constitutive features of our union. europe itself, with its recent history, is the recognition of identities and differences; the enlarged europe will be the first attempt to build a new kind of citizenship on a continental scale and will be the strongest multiplier of citizens' rights. however, at the very moment when we are completing this great common undertaking, when we are achieving the unification of the european continent by consensus, we must also send a clear message to those states which are not part of this process but which look to europe with immense expectations: i am referring to the balkan region. we must tell them that the doors to europe are open and that we hope to have them on our side as soon as possible. we must be clear and unambiguous on this point, on the prospect of accession. we must also make it clear that the timeframe for achieving this objective depends on their determination to complete the reform agenda necessary to become full members of the union. our task will be to support this effort by defining a common agenda that provides them with tools and resources and by making full use of the potential of the association and stabilisation processes. enlargement also means laying the foundations for a more definitive arrangement of the relations of the new, greater europe with its immediate neighbours. the enlargement strategy and the neighbourhood policy are in fact closely linked, and we must be able to show that enlargement does not mean excluding those who are not included in enlargement; enlargement is not about building walls or barriers. we must therefore begin to define more specifically what we mean by a special relationship with the regions neighbouring the enlarged union, from russia to the mediterranean. the solution for kaliningrad, for example, is an important element in a relationship to be developed and consolidated with the russian federation. enlargement is also a great opportunity to reinterpret our role in the world and to invent a new kind of political regionalism, reorganizing the spaces of our continent. in this new perspective, however, it is all the more urgent to tackle with determination and courage the fundamental questions which the european convention is debating in these months. the consensus reached on financial matters does not make it any less necessary to reflect on the community budget, its transparency, its comprehensibility and its suitability to meet the new challenges we are facing. we must therefore define and specify the nature of the union's resources better and strengthen the role of this house. the difficulties associated with the ratification of the treaty of nice, which fortunately are now behind us, must not make us forget the imperative of democratic participation, simplification and greater legitimacy which we must pursue through institutional reforms. the work done so far by the convention and, in particular, the recent document presented by its president, represent an important contribution and a reference for future proposals. i shall be able to speak on these matters to this house shortly. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. economic and social cohesion is at the heart of the european union. it offers the possibility of a sustainable, harmonious and at the same time policy-oriented development of the union as a whole. the debate is now about the european union of the future, a union of 25 or even 27 member states. the idea of integration of this union will only be credible if there is also a willingness to share responsibility for the european social model in solidarity. we must assume that the idea of europe is valid for its citizens, regardless of their regional or social status, and is tackled as a common political task for all member states, that all citizens are given equal opportunities and at the same time are not living at the expense of the next generation. it is an illusion, however, to think that we have a lot more money available for this task than we do now. it is therefore our task to develop a concept which works according to the basic principles mentioned and at the same time manages to get by with relatively equal financial shares. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. one group says we have to argue now that everyone is fine, and then everything will be fine. the others think everything is fine as long as my constituency does not lose its privileges. they are calling for solidarity for their constituency, but they are not prepared for solidarity between us. there are others who are not happy with the european social model anyway, and for them this debate is just the right thing to do. and then there are those who don't dare to tell the truth and face the consequences. the truth is that we have to start with the concept now if we want to give the regions the first payments on 1 january 2007. then no one can talk their way out of it, we know two years is not long enough. the central question is, as everyone knows, how do we define the poorest areas of the european union? the main idea of economic and social cohesion is that where there is the greatest need for catch-up, there is the greatest flow of support. i think that the idea of common solidarity is being undermined by the constant invention of new criteria to ensure that the constituency in question receives the support that is actually intended for the poorest regions. besides, such thinking is short-term. the opening up of the previously valid and recognised criterion of 75% of the average gdp of the union, if lower than this, to the poorest regions - has the consequence that everyone gets less money, that the phasing-out is flat, that special regional support for the unemployed or rural areas would then just not be possible. it would also mean that areas which are really disadvantaged, such as those in the east, would simply be left to hang on to the drip for longer. and it can happen that constituencies that you have to work for today suddenly become net payers. the diw study says that would happen in three years. the worst consequence of this concept and this short-term thinking would be that solidarity would be cancelled. we have nothing, we have no concept, and economic and social cohesion is a mere speck. i come from an objective 1 region which, if the 75% criterion is strictly maintained, will lose its statistical status, and yet i am convinced that a generous phasing-out will enable it to solve its development problems. if we in parliament, with our structural funds concept, set a cornerstone here, with clear boundaries for the objective 1 area for the future union, we are on the one hand obliging the commission to follow us and on the other hand challenging the council to do so. i would like to have a roll-call vote on this tomorrow. there are two things we can agree on. the only principle we could agree on was a programme and a fund. this is an effective approach to simplifying the management of the structural funds. we also agreed to support the commission's proposal for a tripartite agreement with the member states and the regions on the use of the structural funds, so as to allow local actors to participate. i hope that this will help to promote an efficient and successful approach and not jeopardize solidarity in europe. (applause from the centre)

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. although it is only an interim report to be drawn up every three years, it should not only take stock of the situation but also give a view of the next planning period. it is right that we should not go into details and give figures, but we should identify the main points and clarify the key issues in good time. one such key issue is the 0.45% of eu gdp for cohesion policy, which must not be exceeded even in the context of eu enlargement. one such central issue is the regions as a reference for cohesion policy tasks and not national criteria. if you want something different, you're going about it on the wrong foot. one such key issue is the focus of support on the less-favoured regions in an enlarged eu with clear, transparent, accountable criteria for the concept of 'poor' regions. this can depend solely on the 75% criterion. all the other factors used as a basis for assessment are not clearly calculable and open the door to arbitrariness. this is the case even for a criterion such as unemployment, which is not uniformly defined across the eu and therefore has to lead to miscalculations. the priority for supporting less favoured regions must be to those regions which generate less than 75% of eu gdp. but even for those areas which are only raised above the 75% threshold by statistics as a result of enlargement, i.e. only counted as such, a more generous phasing-out must be introduced. we want regions to be given more support the closer they are to the 75% threshold. i agree with the rapporteur who has tabled an amendment to this effect.

president of the council. - mr president, i am very pleased that so many good and interesting points have been made in the debate today. as i mentioned in my opening remarks, we are taking decisions jointly on many proposals which have an impact on the functioning of the internal market and on the competitiveness of the union. it is therefore also important that we continue to debate the general issues of the internal market, not least to focus on the areas where the internal market does not work, often to the detriment of the eu's competitiveness. i have noted the views expressed today. many have given examples of areas where the single market is still lagging behind. i can agree with these views on several points and i would like to add the following comments to them: first of all, i agree with commissioner bolkestein and mr karas that the timely implementation of directives is crucial for the functioning of the internal market - for the benefit of both citizens and businesses. i support the commission's efforts to monitor this area. the implementation of directives is a top priority in the council, especially in the competitiveness council, which is responsible for legislation on the internal market. we must meet the targets set by the heads of state or government at the stockholm european council and then in barcelona, namely to have implemented 98.5% of the directives by the spring summit in 2003. i can only share the widespread concern, particularly with regard to the community patent, which many people have mentioned today. this is a very, very important matter. the failure to make progress in the negotiations at the council meeting on 21 may made it necessary to reconsider the strategy for the community patent. it was concluded that the judiciary should be the focus of attention during the danish presidency, and we have therefore carried out discussions on the judiciary on the basis of a report from the commission which we received in september. the question of jurisdiction, together with other key parts of the proposal for a community patent, constitutes a so-called package solution, so that nothing is finally adopted until everything has been adopted. in this context, i have of course noted parliament's position on the judiciary. we have included parliament's proposals in the consideration of possible solutions. the community patent is a high priority for the danish presidency, but despite great efforts it has not been possible to create the necessary basis for a comprehensive compromise proposal. the countries are still far too far apart and i would like to say to the members here that i too am very impatient on this matter. the council meeting on competitiveness on 14 november will therefore be about taking stock of the negotiations and clarifying how we can move forward on this very important matter. the council has now also succeeded in reaching political agreement on both procurement directives. the proposals are currently undergoing technical examination so that they can be sent to parliament as a whole. a number of parliament's proposals have been incorporated into the text, including the possibility of taking environmental and social considerations into account when awarding public contracts. i hope that parliament will look favourably on the proposals so that we can get the new, improved procurement rules in the eu as soon as possible. with regard to the internal market in services in particular, i would point out that the council is expected to adopt conclusions on the barriers report at the council meeting on competitiveness on 14 and 15 november 2002. the council gave political support to the commission's follow-up to the conclusions and a work programme was drawn up committing the member states and the commission to a number of deliveries in 2003. the commission will, inter alia, launch a legislative initiative on a system for removing barriers. member states undertake to actively comply with and implement the judgments of the court. i would like to thank you in conclusion for the inspiring debate. the danish presidency attaches the highest priority to the completion of the internal market. this is the basis for living up to our lisbon vision. we look forward to continued good cooperation with the european parliament in order to complete the internal market - not least because of enlargement.
commission. – mr president, thank you for giving me the opportunity to reply to all the members that have spoken this morning. may i begin by agreeing with mr harbour when he said that lord cockfield played an important role in constructing the internal market. this is perfectly true. he added that this happened with the support of the british government, and may i say that it is all the more regrettable that lord cockfield did not return to brussels as a commissioner for a second period. mr harbour commented on services. indeed, since our economies are roughly 70% service-based, he is quite right to raise the point. this point has also been mentioned by others. in reply, it cannot be right that companies are subjected to a number of requirements which they have already fulfilled in their home country. to do so would add considerable cost to doing business in the european union and would not be compatible with calls for less red tape. it is vital for member states to press ahead with action to modernise and simplify their legal framework. in many cases, the removal of barriers requires much improved administrative cooperation between member states or, where necessary, harmonisation. that action will necessitate involvement of member states, and in the light of the report on services, the commission intends to propose both a legislative initiative to remove unnecessary legal barriers, and also non-legislative actions to address non-regulatory barriers. the commission will certainly keep this uppermost in its mind and intends to return to parliament as the occasion requires. i also agree with mr harbour that the transposition deficit, which is now creeping upwards again, is a most serious matter. may i appeal to all members of parliament to use such influence as they have with their home governments to stress the absolute need for a transposition deficit that is as close as possible, if not identical to, the 1.5% which was set as an aim by the european council. mrs berger mentioned the need to look after and improve the mobility of employees. i agree with her and that is one of the reasons why the commission is at pains to see to it that in the area of pension funds, when employees contribute to a certain pension fund in their own country, they can then go and work in another country and contribute to the same pension fund, retaining their rights to tax deductibility on their contributions. recently, there was a case involving a citizen of finland who contributed to a pension fund which was not finnish. the tax deductibility of the contributions was not allowed by the finnish authorities. after recourse to the european court of justice in luxembourg, this error was redressed and we now have the possibility of retaining such fiscal advantages. that is a good thing in defence of the mobility of employees. mrs berger also drew attention, as did mrs wallis, to article 95, which is one of the bases, if not the basis, of the internal market. there have been noises in and around the european convention that article 95 should be amended. the latest comments that have reached me on that point assure me that this is not the intention and that the convention does not want to change article 95, which would be a very bad thing. mr maccormick drew my attention to services of general interest. it is obviously a general term but what is meant are public services which not only at national, but often also at regional or local level, have until now been shielded from competition. the commission is favour of liberalisation. i would like to make the distinction between liberalisation and privatisation. privatisation is not the concern of the commission. in fact, article 295 of the treaty says that nothing in the treaty should have any impact on the ownership of whatever it may be. member states' governments are free, according to the treaty, to nationalise, de-nationalise, privatise, expropriate or whatever. privatisation is not the concern of the european union and is not the concern of the commission. however, liberalisation is indeed our concern. liberalisation means opening up to competition and it is my view that if such services of national interest, otherwise known as network services, are open to competition, the ordinary citizen stands to gain from that. mr rovsing spoke on the community patent and suggested that such patents should be expressed in one language only. he may be right but i know at least one member state which would be strongly opposed to such a proposal. i wish mr rovsing the best of luck in trying to persuade that member state that all patents should be expressed in english. mr karas said mehr tempo statt verzögerung – more speed rather than delay – and i cannot agree more with him. he also said that the stronger our internal market is, the stronger europe's position in the world will be and, of course, he is right. economic clout is necessary for political clout. that is one of the reasons we should all support the internal market. he also agrees with the schutzklausel, the guarantee clause in the accession treaties about the internal market in its widest sense, encompassing energy, transport and so on, not just the areas under my portfolio. an important part of the accession treaties, the guarantee clause works for two years as from entry, but under the guarantee clause, measures may be proposed which go beyond this two-year period. we have the possibility, should the need arise, to impress upon accession countries the need for a period longer than two years. they should do whatever needs to be done to bring them into line with the internal market thus defined. to mr de clercq, who also spoke, perhaps i may answer in the language which we have in common.

commission. – mr president, i do not know whether europe can always assist but at least it tries. i would first like to thank the rapporteur and the members of the committee on petitions and the members of the employment and social affairs committee for their excellent work and analysis. as reported by the earl of stockton, reverend owen alleges that his fundamental rights have not been respected and that european directives have either been breached or incorrectly applied by the united kingdom authorities. in his petition, he refers in particular to the fact that he has been discriminated against, contrary to article 13 of the treaty of amsterdam, and contrary to articles 48(2) and 112 of the treaty of rome. he furthermore claims that council directive 91/533/eec concerning information on individual employment conditions has not been properly incorporated into uk law. it is true that we have been dealing with this issue for more than one and a half years and a lot of legal and other work has been done. as mentioned in the commission communication of 13 december 2001 on the case, and in my letter of 11 january 2002 to honourable members ford, cashman and hughes, the commission could not identify any breach of european law, nor any failure by the british government to transpose properly the relevant european legislation into uk law. i do not believe i need to add anything to what i have already communicated in my letter, but i will attempt to explain and analyse some of the aspects of the directives and the articles of the treaties. council directive 91/533/eec applies to every paid employee having a contract or employment relationship defined by the law in force in a member state. it does not, however, provide an eu definition of an employee, which is left to national employment legislation. the united kingdom confirmed that members of the clergy, in respect of their core duties as clergymen, are officeholders and not employees under uk employment law. as clergy are not employees for the purpose of the scope of this directive, it was not necessary to specifically cover or specifically exclude them. as regards the issue of discrimination, article 13 of the ec treaty allows the community to take action but has no direct effect. it does not, therefore, grant individuals any rights which can be enforced by national courts or the european court of justice. directive 2000/78/ec of 27 november 2000 establishes a general principle of prohibition of any direct or indirect discrimination. however, the directive does not need to be transposed by member states until 2 december 2003 so we cannot apply it to this case at present. article 48(2) of the treaty of rome (now article 39(2)) refers to the treatment of workers of different nationalities within a member state, and not to differences in labour law and employment rights between countries. it is therefore not obvious that article 39 is relevant in this case. article 118 of the treaty of rome (now art. 137), which i suppose the reverend had in mind as regards the harmonisation of working conditions, gives the community a number of competences in the social field, including the issue of working conditions. on the basis of these considerations i cannot identify any breach of european law nor any failure by the british government to transpose the relevant european legislation. i hope that this clarifies the issue.

commission. – mr president, in addition to the answers already given by president prodi, i would like to call the attention of the house to the fact that as far as return policy is concerned, very intensive work is under way on the programme for return to afghanistan, thanks to the commitment of the danish presidency. in 2003 the commission will present a directive on minimum rules on return policy, above all in order to guarantee the mutual recognition of return decisions taken by a member state. such decisions should be automatically recognised and executed by the other member states. the commission has recently presented a proposal for a european return programme. that is already under discussion in the council's specialised working groups. when it comes to integration policy, we have put forward a proposal to create some pilot projects between 2003 and 2005 in order to promote the exchange of best practices as far as integration policy is concerned. however, it has to be recognised that there is no explicit legal basis in the treaty for dealing with integration policy at european level. therefore we need to discuss the added value of addressing integration policy in european-wide terms. thirdly, as far as immigration and asylum is concerned, i can reiterate that the commission has put forward all the proposals asked of it by the tampere european council and the laeken council. the time has now come for the council to decide. the only two new elements of asylum policy that we are taking into consideration are two proposals that are included in our programme for 2003. the first one concerns resettlement policy and the second protection in the region – the possibility of asking for asylum outside the territory of the european union. these two proposals will follow very closely the consultations launched by the united nations high commissioner for refugees. thirdly, concerning the seville conclusions, i would draw your attention to the fact that the commission has already presented to the council the proposal on mandates for new readmission agreements with the people's republic of china, albania, algeria and turkey. in june 2003 we are supposed to present, as set out in our programme, the report on burden sharing on external border control. we are now preparing a report on the financial allocations for partnerships with third countries aimed at tackling illegal immigration. the report aims to identify effective allocations of financial tools, possible shortcomings and the vulnerabilities that must be overcome in the future. when it comes to external borders, i can confirm that the commission intends to present a reform of the common manual on external borders in march 2003. all the other actions asked of us in seville, such as joint training and joint operation in the control of external borders, are already being developed by the appropriate council working group and will be financed by the commission's argo programme. finally, we recognise the fight against terrorism as a priority for 2003. as far as legislative action is concerned, priority should be given to the fight against sources of financing for terrorism, and several of the proposals included in our programme address this challenge. as mrs terrón i cusí said, we intend to bring forward proposals concerning common procedural guarantees in criminal procedures. we have launched a consultation and intend to build upon the results of that consultation in a green paper. we shall therefore be bringing forward a proposal on common minimum rules on criminal procedure guarantees in the 15 member states by the end of next year. commission. – mr president, i should like to respond to the more specific questions raised by mrs frassoni and mr van den burg. to mrs frassoni, who talked about the outcome of the johannesburg summit, i will start by saying that the commission in many ways shares the worries about the softness of some of the decisions taken there but this has been duly commented on. as regards the question of the relationship between international agreements on the environment and the wto framework, in johannesburg it was a non-event and nothing new happened: nothing was added to wto, nothing was unhappiness. the second question from mrs frassoni concerned the category ii initiatives which are too weak and unclear. i agree that the risk is that these weak initiatives do not add up to anything substantial. the hard core of follow-up actions for the european union to johannesburg will be our water and energy initiatives. these are not going to be weak or unclear. they are already on the agenda for the spring european council and we are already engaged with the member states in clarifying these initiatives, which we see as big and important. i agree with mr van den burg that we need more rapid disbursement, especially regarding activities covered by the edf. things are moving forward and are somewhat better than they used to be, but we still have unsolved problems concerning van den burg when he returns to the netherlands to make sure that the last remaining country in the convoy takes the necessary action, so that we are ready to access 9th edf money. as regards the agricultural profile of europe in these global negotiations, this is back on track. we managed in johannesburg and we are still managing to keep alive the formulations embedded in the doha language on this front. we still see the external actions there as part of the necessary process of adaptation, which we in europe have to take seriously. this language is continually being confirmed at all the meetings. yesterday in the general affairs and external relations council this was again the case. we are on track.

president of the council. - mr president, the 10th eu-russia summit was held in brussels on 11 november with a satisfactory outcome. the meeting reflected the intensity and depth of eu-russia cooperation. the meeting showed that cooperation is now entering a new phase; the framework for the strategic partnership has been set and now it must be completed by concrete actions. as you know, there was a major problem, which this parliament has discussed many times, namely kaliningrad. a joint declaration was agreed on transit traffic between kaliningrad and the rest of russia. the agreement strikes a balance between the interests of the candidate countries, russia and the eu. the fact that the problem could be solved confirms the strength of cooperation between the eu and russia, while at the same time the eu has stated that we attach the utmost importance to the sovereignty of the candidate countries and to effective border control at the eu's external borders. we insisted that lithuania is a sovereign country and that lithuania has the same right to join schengen as all other applicant countries. that is something that was respected, even by president putin. an agreement was reached and i may add that president adamkus of lithuania has also accepted the agreement that was reached. the council also adopted a joint declaration on the fight against terrorism. this was crucial for both parties. the summit condemned terrorism in all its forms. the declaration and the accompanying cooperation plan show that cooperation between the eu and russia on this point is moving from the exchange of information to concrete cooperation. the european council also welcomed the progress made in the implementation of the eu-russia association agreement. there was a frank discussion of the situation in chechnya. it was agreed that the conflict could not be seen and treated as a problem of terrorism alone and that a political solution was the only way to lasting peace, stability and development in the region. i know that commissioner chris patten has on a previous occasion informed us of the extremely frank discussion that took place. the eu will follow developments closely. both sides must respect human rights and the union must demand that those who do not do so be prosecuted. the union will also demand that the international community be allowed to provide much-needed humanitarian aid to chechnya. regional conflicts, including in particular moldova, were also discussed. it is important to maintain that the political dialogue between the eu and russia is not geographically limited. the eu stressed the need for progress in economic and legal reforms in russia in order to secure russian membership of the wto. the need for russia to ratify the kyoto protocol and the energy charter was also stressed. in conclusion, i can say that this was a successful summit with a constructive dialogue in all fields. the eu-russia cooperation has entered a new phase in which everything can be discussed, and this will be to the benefit of both parties.
commission. – mr president, the european union/russian federation summit that took place on 11 november in brussels succeeded in producing an understanding, as you already know, on the issue of transit between kaliningrad and the rest of russia. as you are also aware, as a result of the discussions held at the may summit in moscow, the eu had agreed to carry out a review of the matter, taking further into account russia's concerns about unimpeded travel of russian citizens throughout the whole territory of the russian federation, including kaliningrad. in the relatively short time between the two summits, the union completed a comprehensive review of the situation. following a communication from the commission in september, this review formulated a new position on kaliningrad transit issues, which was adopted in october by the european council meeting in brussels. in parallel discussions with both russia and lithuania, the presidency and the commission managed to develop ways and means to ensure that the vital interests of all parties concerned would be respected. in addition to russia's legitimate interests, the eu was very much aware that any arrangements requiring further definition could not undermine the sovereignty of lithuania – a future member of the union – or carry negative implications for lithuania's future accession in full to the schengen regime. last but not least, the european union must adequately protect its borders at all times, a task for which it was essential to respect the schengen acquis. the european commission is confident that the understanding reached at the brussels summit strikes the right balance between these parameters, making it possible to resolve the issue of kaliningrad transit in a manner which is acceptable to all parties concerned. the commission has already started work to prepare for the implementation of the understanding reached at the summit. time is short and we are fully aware of the need to launch preparations without delay in order to meet the deadline of 1 july 2003, when lithuania will introduce the new regime for russian rail travellers crossing its territory. we are confident that by then the conditions will be in place to allow the introduction of simplified travel documents. i would like to add that resolving the issue of kaliningrad will allow us to substantially deepen and accelerate our cooperation with the russian federation in a number of important areas. among these, the european commission regards justice and home affairs as particularly important. indeed cooperation with russia on issues such as the fight against organised crime, illegal migration, drug trafficking, women trafficking and child pornography among others, is crucial. on this matter, russia confirmed at the summit that the agreement between europol and russia will be rapidly concluded. in addition, russia and the european union will immediately launch negotiations with a view to concluding a readmission agreement as soon as possible. in this context, the summit also produced a joint statement defining areas for further cooperation in the fight against terrorism, which is a clear priority for both sides. we intend to increase the exchange of information in a number of relevant areas, as well as to deepen cooperation against terrorism in multilateral arenas and in regard to the provision of assistance in this field to third countries. other important issues were discussed at the summit. the on-going conflict in chechnya featured prominently among these. in this regard, the european union raised its serious concerns over chechnya. i would like to assure you that the well-established position of the union on the matter was put forward to president putin in quite clear terms. while expressing its support for russia against terrorism in all its forms, the union explicitly stated that the fight against terrorism cannot be conducted at the expense of basic human rights. this is also valid for chechnya. the union raised again the problem of unimpeded and safe access for humanitarian workers on the ground in chechnya. in addition, the eu urged the russians to promote without delay a political solution that provides a framework for lasting peace, stability and reconstruction in chechnya. at the summit we also had a good discussion on a number of international issues, including the middle east, on which we agreed a joint statement. we reviewed the situation in afghanistan, as well as the need for iraq to comply fully with un security council resolution 1441. we also exchanged assessments regarding the threat of nuclear proliferation in the korean peninsula. finally, we reviewed the situation in moldova and belarus. russia has already agreed to the withdrawal and destruction of ammunition in the breakaway region of transnistria. the eu stated that it is essential that this takes place rapidly in order to promote a solution to the conflict which continues to impede the development on moldova, which is now the poorest country in europe. we also made it clear that we expect russia to use its influence on the government of belarus to adopt a more positive approach towards democratisation and respect of human rights. on the economic side, progress was less marked, except for the change in the eu anti-dumping regulations, which now accord russia market economy status. in addition, the summit endorsed progress reports on the energy discussions and on the concept of a common european economic space. the eu also raised a number of its commercial concerns, including the discriminatory charges levied by russia for european aircraft flying over siberia. the eu pressed russia to confirm expectations of early russian ratification - the next item is the report (a5-0373/2002) by mrs keppelhoff-wiechert, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on additives for use in animal nutrition (com (2002) 153 - c5-0143/2002 - 2002/0073 (cod)). transmission of the council's common positions: see minutes.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would like to begin by thanking the commission for this overall very positive proposal on additives in animal nutrition, which i welcome on the whole. i would also like to thank the danish presidency and my colleagues on the environment, public health and consumer affairs committees and the agriculture and rural development committees. the present proposal consolidates the existing provisions on additives in animal nutrition. the commission also intends to clarify the procedural aspects of the evaluation of a dossier and the corresponding authorisation procedures, and to make them more transparent for both the manufacturer and the consumer. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be given the opportunity to discuss the matter with the council. this ban is not arbitrary but is based on the opinions of the scientific committee for food. this ban also follows a public demand from medical professionals. since cross-resistance to human preparations can no longer be excluded, action is needed in the sense of preventive consumer protection. pressure must be exerted in the form of a temporary authorisation, pressure to develop other methods, such as suitable vaccines. i agree with the commission's proposal in principle. i also do not think it is appropriate, in view of the antibiotic problem, to issue a blank cheque for the unlimited use of coccidiostats in the future. it is not plausible that antibiotics should be banned for health reasons, but these health arguments do not apply in the case of the use of coccidiostats. the committee on agriculture and rural development, which is in charge of the programme, wants to allow coccidiostats and histomonostats until 2008. the commission should then present a report on the use of these substances before 1 january 2008, together with a proposal on their further use thereafter. what are the differences of opinion? amendment no 2 concerns the importation of additives from third countries for use in animal feed. in order to protect human and animal health, import regulations must be applied and controlled at least as strictly as those in the member states. with amendments nos 4, 7 and 9 i am very much in favour of guidelines for the authorization of feed additives. i call on the commission to draw up and present, in cooperation with the european food safety authority, guidelines for the authorization of feed additives. the committee on agriculture and rural development has clearly expressed its support for guidelines in its vote on simplifying the authorization of additives. after an additive has been authorised, it should be sufficient to update the dossier regularly rather than re-examining it completely every time. parliament calls for mixtures and premixes with flavourings and appetizers. they must be exempted from the labelling requirement. this explicitly excludes flavourings and appetising substances with a quantitative restriction for use in feed and drinking water. there are, of course, calls in this house to restrict the use of coccidiostats to veterinary prescriptions in future. i am of the opinion - and i say this from practical experience - that we must have preventive health protection for animals too. there is a kind of animal welfare, and it is clear that an animal that is already sick will need to be treated with much higher doses. i cannot understand this from practical experience. as regards the ban on the four antibiotics still authorised by 2006, i would like to say to you, commissioner byrne, that my amendment no 31 is a reasonable compromise proposal in this respect. finally, a heartfelt thank you to all those who have worked so hard on this subject!
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. the issue of animal nutrition is a constant topic here in the european parliament. we have been very successful in shaping eu feed law in recent years. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of animals used for human consumption. today we are going to take a new leap in the world of additives in animal feed. the socialist group supports many of the points raised by the rapporteur, such as the ban on antibiotics, etc. she has done a very this area. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the use of coccidiostats and histomonostats in animal feed is not restricted to additives, but that in the long term they are covered by veterinary legislation. we must be consistent here. if we ban antibiotics in animal feed in general, we cannot immediately make an exception for one category of product. the commission has not yet taken a decision on this. in the case of coccidiostats, controlled administration must be carried out on prescription by a veterinarian who is familiar with the situation on the holding concerned and able to react appropriately. otherwise, the general prophylactic use of these products, which are also antibiotics, may mask any hygiene problems that may exist in the establishments. i am firmly opposed to the idea that i want to open up a new source of income for veterinarians. we have tabled amendments on this subject, and i would ask you to support them. the second point concerns the duration of the authorization. we support an unlimited authorization, provided that the safety of the products is not affected. therefore, a re-evaluation of additives should be carried out every 10 years, taking into account current studies and research data. this means reliability for the applicants on the one hand and safety for the animals and consumers on the other.
commission. – mr president, i certainly have no intention of keeping you here until midnight. allow me to explain my position on the major points of this proposal and in particular the differences which in some cases still remain between our institutions. concerning the date for the phasing out of antibiotics, i am happy to note that the commission's approach has your broad support. but there are some slight differences concerning the date of withdrawal of authorisations. the scientific advice on which this risk management measure is taken mentions the need for a transitional period to allow for animal rearing practices to adapt and also for the development of alternative antibiotics. for these practical reasons, i cannot accept the amendment which envisages the phasing out of antibiotics from 1 january 2005, despite my recognition of parliament's desire to get rid of antibiotics in animal nutrition as soon as possible. i agree with that sentiment but would add that this should be in accordance with scientific opinion and should take account of possible effects on animal health and welfare. concerning the external dimension of the phasing out process, let me clarify my position. this has been raised by a number of people, including mr parish and mrs doyle. the prohibition of antibiotics will also apply to feed imports. with respect to the imports of food of animal origin, the residues testing system currently in place will be used to check for the use of banned substances. this testing system protects human health, since it is designed to reveal residues of medicines, additives and substances in food at levels that present an unacceptable risk to the consumer. it is not sufficient to verify whether forbidden substances were used in the feeding of animals in third countries, as the residues of such substances may not be present at the time of importation. i welcome any suggestion that may be made to increase the resources of the fvo and particularly welcome that observation from a member of the budgetary authority. i believe that the control of imported products and the condition of equivalency between eu rules and third country rules on the rearing of animals should be considered under horizontal legislation. the commission will propose a regulation on feed and food controls that will impose rules on this issue. that - the report (a5-0365/2002) by mr nistico, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending directive 2001/83/ec as regards traditional herbal medicinal products (com (2002) 1 - c5-0026/2002 - 2002/0008 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr nisticò, as well as the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, for the work and effort they have put into this report. mr nisticò is a well-known expert in the field, but it has been quite a challenge for me and my services. let me start with the objectives. what are the main objectives of this proposal? there are three. first and foremost, to guarantee a high level of health protection for european patients. they will have access to the medicines of their choice, as long as all necessary safeguards are met. secondly, to promote the single market for herbal medicines. laying down harmonised rules and procedures will facilitate the cross-border trade in herbal medicines, which currently is very limited. thirdly, to create a clear and favourable environment for the mainly small and medium-sized companies working in this sector. as far as specific proposals are concerned, i will concentrate on three key issues. first, the scope of the new simplified procedure. the use of herbal medicines is a long-standing tradition in europe. back in the middle ages they were already well known and widely used. for new medicines, providing fresh scientific data is indispensable if patients are to be treated with safe medicines. but if we already know enough about a medicine, new pre-clinical and clinical tests impose an unnecessary burden and unnecessary testing on humans and animals. to protect the patient’s health, the information on the product’s traditional use must be reliable enough to enable us to conclude that the product is safe. such information exists for many traditional herbal medicines. for that reason, the new procedure should initially be limited to herbal medicines. secondly, the minimum period of use. to ensure that the information is soundly based, we consider that 30 years should enable us to decide whether the product can be considered safe and effective. the assessment has to be for use in the eu. i stress this because the effects of a medicine depend on the setting in which the product is used as well as on the product itself. as a rule, therefore, the product should have been used for 30 years within the eu. at the same time, we recognise that there are important medicinal traditions outside the eu. for that reason, we propose that up to 15 years of the use can be outside the community. finally, the new scientific committee. herbal medicines are different from other categories of pharmaceuticals in various respects. for some years now, an informal working group has been working on herbal medicines at the european medicines evaluation agency. our proposal offers an opportunity to establish an explicit legal basis for this working group and to give it a clear mandate for herbal medicinal products. this will also allow us to rely on specific national expertise to ensure quality, safety and efficacy of herbal medicines on a european level. at the same time it helps to improve the free circulation of these medicines. i am looking forward to the debate in the house today and call on the european parliament to support this initiative.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would like to thank you for your reply. you're absolutely right. we have a great deal of experience in dealing with traditional medicines. this is a matter which is becoming increasingly important to consumers in the european union. i think it is time to create a harmonized legal framework for traditional herbal medicines. for too long, trade in traditional products in the community has been hampered by differences in national requirements. i believe that the directive as it stands will correct this misunderstanding, thanks also to the excellent work of the rapporteur, mr nisticò. let me address two points which are particularly important to me. firstly, the creation of a new committee on herbal medicines within the european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products. i think it is necessary. i also think it is good that the commission is taking this approach. one of the main tasks of the committee will be to draw up a list of plant-based substances. i also think that the mere division into different groups, as the committee is calling for, is particularly important. i would particularly like to see a further division of labour. the so-called 'well-established medical use' plant protection products should be included in the group of rational plant protection products. the significance of this distinction is briefly explained: in the case of well-established use phytopharmaceuticals, the evidence for an application may already be provided by monographs representing the generally available knowledge. this type of evidence does not collect extract-specific data. the situation is different in the case of the rational plant protection companies. they shall demonstrate this by providing specific extract-related data describing the exact effect of the individual extract. in order to avoid distortions of competition - and i attach particular importance to this - the manufacturer who has carried out costly research into the effects of rational plant protection products should be allowed to make his particular efforts in the context of authorization visible for the benefit of the consumer and his better information.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. herbal medicines have been used throughout the world for centuries. in europe too, consumer interest has long since outgrown the regional household resources. whether it's chinese ginseng root or indian tea tree oil, many citizens swear by natural products. however, there is still no uniform regulation of herbal medicines in the european union. in some member states they must be authorized, in others a simple demonstration of efficacy is sufficient. mr nisticò has presented a very good report which creates broadly uniform rules for the manufacture, marketing and labelling of herbal medicines and sets high standards of quality and safety. the following points are of particular importance. first of all, quality and safety. the manufacturers of herbal medicines must demonstrate their safety to the same extent as chemical medicines. in the simplified authorization procedure, the proof of the efficacy and safety of a product is sufficiently substantiated by a long - and traditional - period of use. we also need a new committee on herbal medicines at the emea. this committee is to be responsible for all tasks relating to herbal medicines. it will produce plant monographs for the purpose of accurate but rapid assessment of applications for authorization. with this proposal, we are not only ensuring broadly uniform conditions for authorisation in europe, we are also making it easier to market herbal medicines in all member states while respecting subsidiarity. european consumers can continue to choose from a wide range of products, from products duly submitted by the manufacturer and carefully examined and authorised by the authority. this ensures the quality of the products and the greatest possible protection of human health.

- the next item is the report (a5-0356/2002) by mrs van den burg, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the working conditions of temporary agency workers (com (2002) 149 - c5-0140/2002 - 2002/0072 (cod)).
the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities has adopted an opinion. - mr president, i have to go. in the fight against mass unemployment, more flexible working models must be found. the contribution of temporary work is increasing. successful placement of temporary work increases the chances of permanent employment. this applies to low-skilled, long-term unemployed people, but also to specialists. in my opinion for the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, we refer to the charter of fundamental rights. we have included in the draft directive the safeguarding of maternity protection and the need for parental leave. we are against any discrimination, whether in pay for equal work or work of equal value, or in the form of discrimination on grounds of sex, whether in the case of temporary workers compared with similar permanent workers. it was important to us that temporary workers were not used to break strikes or to contribute to the drastic reduction of full-time jobs or regular staff. more than three quarters of temporary workers are still men. the reason for women's absence is the difficulty of reconciling work and family life. in this context, temporary agency work in particular provides the desired individual adjustment and offers women good opportunities for entering or re-entering the workforce. however, there are problems in practice. in germany, personnel service agencies are now being set up at the employment offices, which are tax-subsidized public bodies and bear no risk. this is to the detriment of the selfemployed temporary agency. the federal government is not implementing the supposedly groundbreaking concepts one by one as promised, madam rapporteur, but is diluting them. the aim is to ensure that temporary workers earn the same as the employees of the company from the first day. however, equal pay from the outset and exclusively collective bargaining structures prevent temporary work. my proposal to introduce a six-month deadline at european level was unfortunately not supported by a majority. in the epp group we will then develop a compromise which takes due account of the different rules of the member states and respects subsidiarity.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. after many months of intensive work, we can now vote for the first time in plenary on the draft directive on temporary work. all those who have dealt with this issue have tried to find the best possible solution for temporary workers, temporary work companies and a favourable economic development in our eu member states. it's been a rough road to get to this point. i thank all those who have helped us to present a fairly good compromise today. in view of the fact that there are some 10 million unemployed in the european union and the economic situation is unstable, we must be careful not to close down an entire sector of the labour market with the good intention of guaranteeing temporary workers basic social security. it would be completely absurd to speak of temporary work as an atypical or even unworthy form of work. temporary work can help newcomers to orient themselves for the future, or prevent exit from working life or facilitate re-entry into work for workers who are difficult to find. my group attaches particular importance to flexibility in this area of work. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's social policy is not distorted. if we are guided in tomorrow's vote by the principle of subsidiarity and by the idea of active economic promotion, which creates the basis for more jobs, we will leave the member states of the european union more room for their flexible, individual labour market development, which is not incompatible with adequate labour protection. the measures in germany concerning temporary agency work lead to a dead end. i hope we can create a better framework here.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. most member states already have laws on temporary agency work or collective agreements, but they vary widely in quality. the german law in particular was not as simple as it is now claimed to be, and it was not accepted by the public, either by employers or by employees. i should like to mention some of the curious features of the german restrictions: the ban on synchronisation, the limitation to 12 months, the limitation period, the ban on the construction industry. i therefore consider it a very courageous and important step that the german government, the german parliament, has already included the european directive currently under discussion in the qualitative improvements for germany. it was not acceptable that the workers in germany were paid up to 40% less than the regular workforce. it is not surprising, then, that the whole industry has such a miserable image. that's what we're trying to change. but it is interesting that the highest levels of social acceptance and, incidentally, the highest growth in temporary agency work are found in those member states where the principle of equality prevails, namely france and the netherlands. of course, employers also want social acceptance. the main reason for using temporary workers, as our dublin foundation has found out, is not cost savings but flexibility in dealing with seasonal shortages, staff fluctuations and sometimes extended probationary periods. this is precisely what the european directive with its amendments by ike van den burg makes possible. the necessary flexibility is also ensured by collective bargaining. let us show, by adopting this legislation tomorrow, that social europe really exists!

the commission. i would like to begin, mr president, with three general comments. firstly, several of the honourable members referred to the issue of subsidiarity. the commission has already made a develop the sector, which in many countries is particularly badly burdened. this is a very clear reference to the netherlands and the dutch model, a model which has managed to combine flexibility with burden of the model. i'd say that's completely wrong. the legislation does not introduce any new procedure for the recruitment or transfer of workers. the existing system is maintained in each country. flexibility, as it has been interpreted in europe at least, means a set of policies and practices that help the enterprise, the worker, the public sector, the legislation, to adapt to the new needs of production. flexibility cannot be interpreted as fewer or no rights as a precondition for job creation. there have been specific reports in the uk that there will be job cuts, etc. the difference that will emerge in this country is that there will probably be a slight increase in labour costs in terms of the minimum social rights that, according to the british labour market situation, these workers should have. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. there are two kinds of amendments. the first category concerns the clarification of the think it is useful to mention that a company may receive reasonable compensation for the services it has provided to the user company, and that at the same time the workers are not burdened with agreements. i agree with the amendment which provides that member states must ensure that both workers and their representatives have adequate means of paying the obligations arising from this rejected. i welcome the amendment which extends the scope for suspending restrictions and prohibitions on temporary agency work. this field is very limited in the proposal for a directive, since it concerns only restrictions or prohibitions relating to certain categories of workers or certain sectors. and it is clearly the spirit of the amendment that is intended to ensure that company employees are not used to replace workers who are involved in collective action, strikes, etc. that is accepted. i also find the new wording of the anti-discrimination principle very interesting and i believe it is clearer and easier to focus on the working conditions that temporary workers would enjoy if they had been hired directly by the user company. i can accept that the exemption from indefinite contracts is limited to wages only, but i cannot accept that this derogation should be extended to cover fixed-term contracts. nor can we accept the abolition of the six-week period, which allows in restated. the other amendments are rejected. i would like to thank all of you for the effort you have made to draft a new text which will facilitate the final adoption of the directive, which is certainly a difficult directive, politically and technically. i would like to congratulate mrs van den burg again and encourage the danish presidency to take all the necessary steps to reach agreement in the council on 3 december.

realisation among europeans that this technology is important for our future competitiveness and welfare. a consensus is emerging on how we might strengthen its development in a manner consistent with our european values and ethical standards. we are faced with a policy choice: either stand aside and see these technologies developed elsewhere, or exploit them ourselves in a responsible manner and to the benefit of european citizens. as was made clear in the report that mr purvis submitted to parliament last spring, biotechnology is an enabling technology. it affects, or can even transform, broad areas such as healthcare, environmental protection, agriculture and food and industrial production processes. it can be a source of innovation for new and established companies alike, and it offers unique approaches to finally solving problems, for example in the fields of healthcare and novel pharmaceuticals. europe cannot afford to miss out on the benefits biotechnology will bring. members of the european commission under the leadership of president prodi have worked together to provide a strategy that encompasses all the various applications of biotechnology, but also tries to enable us to come up with coherent answers to the more difficult questions and choices we are faced with. the commission’s communication on 'life sciences and biotechnology: a strategy for europe' builds upon the common knowledge base in life sciences and will lead to skills-based jobs that sustain the economies of the future. we propose a number of actions for the promotion of biotechnology development in europe, and at the same time, further measures for responsible governance, to ensure that this development takes place in accordance with our societal values and needs. the sixth framework programme for research and technological development, under the leadership of commissioner busquin, will provide substantial support for the supply of skilled resources and for overcoming the fragmentation of research and lack of critical mass. we need to ensure that research results can be protected by means of harmonised intellectual property protection, and translated into commercial products and processes through effective innovation and technology transfer. the strategy also stresses the need to overcome the previous fragmentation in the commercial development of biotechnology in europe and several actions will contribute to linking up researchers, emerging companies, service providers and financial institutions. the present downturn in the capital markets and the lack of risk capital needs particular and urgent attention. the success of the biotechnology strategy will only be assured if the technology is built on a basis of societal trust. it is vital for developments, and in particular public policy-making, to take place with a maximum of transparency. we need to encourage public dialogue throughout europe to ensure that societal goals are met and public concerns are addressed. the strategy pursues the overarching goal of enhancing coherence between policies at the different levels. in this way, we can give proper, broad consideration to policy decisions that have an impact on our competitiveness and the future prosperity of our societies.the commission has started implementing measures in its own areas of responsibility. we will shortly publish the first regular report on the stage reached in this implementation work. however, this strategy will only work well if we all – european institutions, member states, regions, industry, academia and civil society alike – now make commitments according to our respective responsibilities and resources. the adoption of parliament's report and the forthcoming council conclusions will provide the essential political backing for the effective implementation of the strategy at european level.

possibly for a limited period - market distortions or whether the measures are likely to eliminate existing market distortions in the medium term. in this context, commissioner, i would like to recall two points on which i raised questions and demands during the same debate a year ago. it is true that the most competitive region we want to be must be characterised by competitive enterprises. this means that companies can do without aid wherever possible and that any aid must be aimed at increasing the competitiveness of these companies. but we must not only look at the individual company, but we must also look at the entire value chain in which that company is involved. the emphasis on one company is not enough if qualitative criteria are to be applied. the second point concerns a request i make in the field of regional policy. we are already discussing how regional policy should be carried out after 2006. a lot will change for the current eu of 15, for the old member countries. that is true, but in this context we really have to think about how we can bring about a new orientation of regional aid by the member states. we have to discuss it, we have to do it in time. we can conclude that everything remains the same, but we can also conclude that we need new arrangements. let us not wait until the end to discuss this, but let us start now.
- mr president, european competition policy is one of the central policy instruments of the european union and i would therefore very much welcome it if the commission were to stand by the european parliament and include this area in the area of co-decision. i really think it is important that we democratize competition policy and give it even more legitimacy than it has so far, because the european union's decision on the internal market, the market economy and competition is based on the fact that competition, through its distribution function, should contribute to a fair distribution of income, increase social welfare and exercise a control function through an efficient allocation of the factors of production. the aim is to improve supply for the benefit of producers and consumers and, finally, to help ensure that its incentive function promotes technical progress and maximises the social product. we all think that market power and concentration are harmful. these maxims should also play a role in the constitutional debate, in the revision of the treaties, and i very much hope that this will become even more visible in the application and reform of competition law. finally, this approach must also be brought into line with the lisbon process and its objectives. the annual report is therefore certainly a success story and it is also positive that the annual report addresses the issues of social protection for the first time. i expect the green paper -
