the commission - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i want to reply to mr miller, because i think the information he has is wrong. i have here at your disposal, supplied by the bahamian maritime authority, the exact movements of the prestige vessel in the years 1999, 2000, 2001 and 2002. in 1999, it calls at the port of rotterdam and is, for the last time, subject to a thorough inspection in accordance with the paris memorandum in a european port, until it calls again, before the summer, at the port of kalamata, in greece, port and authorities to whom i have turned to ask how the prestige was in greece and was not subject to an inspection in accordance with the paris memorandum. then it comes to the port of gibraltar and again i have approached the british authorities to ask them why they did not carry out the check. it is true, ladies and gentlemen, that i have not asked you only about the prestige. i have asked the greek and british authorities about the implementation of the current legislation, the directive requiring port authorities to carry out port controls, in accordance with commitments which correspond in practice to the paris memorandum. i have asked about the controls and the application in these ports - in kalamata and gibraltar - of the directive currently in force. i have to tell you, your honor, i have facts. i can tell you that in gibraltar in 1999 five ships were checked. in the year 2000, six. in 2001, two. in 2002, there were 12. that's the data. that is why i say that the legislation must be revised to ensure that such checks by port authorities take place in all ports in the european union. because the controls of the port authorities have a deterrent effect, a deterrent effect from these 'substandard' ships, which must be applied in all ports. because if we leave holes in our network, in our system, we automatically weaken the whole set. that's what i'm proposing. it's not like i'm going against this or that port. in this case, these two came out, kalamata and gibraltar, and i asked for the information. but the problem is not just this or that port. the problem, ladies and gentlemen, is that there has been an ecological disaster, a catastrophe which we should have avoided, which we should have avoided if the commission's proposals had come into force. and i want the thanks and recognition extended to all the members of the directorate-general for transport who worked - we say in spanish, excuse the expression - like mules, that is, extraordinarily, without counting the hours, so that when the erika disaster occurred, in a short three months, they could present a coherent and comprehensive package to this parliament and the council of ministers so that these problems would not happen again. that's what i'm talking about. and i'm talking, ladies and gentlemen, about the fact that it's only been 23 months. and precisely because only 23 months have passed and because there was no ambition - we all know that - the disaster has happened again. how many more? well, that's what i say. could it not be that in the time remaining until june 2003 or february 2004 a disaster could occur in the baltic, the mediterranean, the atlantic or on any coast of the european union because the measures already adopted have not been put into effect? ladies and gentlemen, what we must demand - and that is what i have done in a letter i have sent to the ministers - is that they be implemented now. what happens is that governments are a "band of incoherents". the heads of state and government said in nice that these measures should be put into effect sooner and then they are not applied... (applause) i have opened infringement proceedings against some of them for failure to apply, not the new rules, but the rules in force, which are much more lax and much easier to comply with. our proposal was that single-hull, category 1 tankers, i.e. the largest, should have a maximum life of 23 years. because there is clearly a structural problem associated with the fatigue of metals due to sea-strikes, which occurs from the twenties. and what i regret is that our proposal was not accepted and that it was raised from 23 to 27 years. and that's where the current problems arise. ladies and gentlemen, help them. that's what we're working on. there will be the aid put in by the spanish authorities. what's there is clearly fipol funds. and i would point out that there is an expert from the directorate-general for transport in spain who is working with the spanish authorities, as he once worked with the french authorities, to facilitate the payment of all this aid and the claiming of all this compensation for the various victims. we are also looking at the fisheries issues to see what possibilities of support there may be in terms of fifg funds. we are looking at - but i think it will not be possible, i say it very clearly - the possibility of implementing the solidarity fund. the entry thresholds for the solidarity fund are so high that i hope we do not reach those figures with the damage, because then it would be a brutal tragedy. we are talking about over 3 billion euros, ladies and gentlemen. let's hope we don't get there. we are therefore also looking at the support that can be provided if, despite everything, the 3 000 million euro is not reached but it affects the regional level of galicia in a decisive way, a reason and a situation in which support could also be launched through this solidarity fund. i hope that portugal can be spared this tragedy. i hope the winds will allow the black tide not to touch those shores. i would like to see the spanish coastlines also left untouched, but let us hope that at least the portuguese coastlines will be left clean. in any event, if the portuguese coast was also affected, the funds would also be available, in the same form and manner, to be made available to the spanish authorities and to the spanish affected parties. ladies and gentlemen, we must put this decision into practice. there is a whole series of measures which form a coherent overall package, with a maritime safety agency which ensures, together with the commission, that the rules are properly applied. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i'm sorry, i'm not going to wait for you to agree or disagree. it is hopefully before the end of the year. question number two. within the aspects which are the responsibility of the individual countries - strengthening port control, strengthening the requirements of the classification societies - we will of course do a thorough investigation of what has happened - as i said before - in the whole chain, and i will present the result of our investigations here: the whole chain of events which leads us to the final result, also with regard to the classification societies. we shall also be calling on the member states to designate ports, refuge areas, to deal with situations such as that of erika in her day, which was also a point of controversy, or the question of the prestige in this case. severity in the application. in the application and enforcement of the rules. we talked about going further. i have made it very clear: the international maritime organisation, corridors for dangerous goods, safety distances, special controls at the crossings and straits, increased capacities for coastal states. all this within the framework of the international maritime organisation, giving maritime law a genuine adaptation to the requirements and new circumstances of the 21st century. in the meantime, ladies and gentlemen, we must also look more closely at the question of liability, we must put the cope funds, which are complementary to the fipol fund, back on the council of ministers' table, we must put the question of criminal liability back on the council of ministers' table and we must demand of the ministers that in all the member states - and i believe that this is possible in all of them with an administrative rule - double helmets be required for the transport of the most dangerous and polluting products, such as heavy oil. mr savary spoke of an autonomous european maritime safety area. the truth is that this is a question which could of course even be raised in the context of the discussions within the convention and the next intergovernmental conference. you can imagine that i'm not the one who disagrees with these views. in conclusion, i would like to say to mrs grossetête that, in fact, all i have, with all that has been happening these days, is deep anger, deep anger at the knowledge that we could have avoided it and we did not. - doc. b5-0593/2002 by mr van den bos and mr sanders-ten holte, on behalf of the eldr group, on the human rights situation in sudan; - b5-0594/2002 by mr sjöstedt and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on sudan; - b5-0601/2002 by mrs maij-weggen and others, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on the situation in sudan; - b5-0604/2002 by mr belder, on behalf of the edd group, on the situation in sudan; - b5-0605/2002 by mrs carlotti and others, on behalf of the pse group, on human rights in sudan;
- mr president, mr commissioner, this afternoon we must also discuss the war in sudan, one of the largest and most populous countries in africa, in the context of this urgency. civil war has raged for 19 years. over two million people lost their lives in that war. the people of southern sudan, who are fighting for cultural, political and economic autonomy, have suffered immeasurable hardships. in the majority of sudan, which is under government control, there is no freedom of expression, no freedom of religion, no freedom of peaceful assembly. human rights are still being trampled underfoot. government bombing raids are ravaging the southern regions with heavy losses for the population. more than 200 death sentences were handed down without due process by emergency courts in dafour state. the oil discoveries in sudan have not yet led to a return to peace. on the contrary, they are used to replenish the war chest of the government in khartoum. there is a glimpse of the peace negotiations in machakos, kenya, which led to a ceasefire agreement which has been drawn up but not yet implemented. firstly, the unhindered access of aid to the starving population in southern sudan must be ensured. it must also lead to a permanent ceasefire on both sides, which is respected by all. as long as this crisis is still ongoing and the peace process is not yet sufficiently advanced, there is no possibility of holding the 6th session of the acp-eu parliamentary assembly in sudan in spring 2003. we shall not go there as long as the situation there is as it is now, but we hope that we can do so at a later date. i would like to emphasize that the sudanese ambassador is doing a great deal here through diplomatic channels to speed up the peace process. we therefore call on the african states to organise the next acp-eu summit in another, more peaceful country in africa. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. (applause from the centre)
- mr president, i have to go. we must look at the situation in sudan in a very different way. in the north we are dealing with a problematic regime, but one in which there are also reformist forces, supported by egypt. in the south, we have a brutal, bloody civil war, which would be simplified to the conflict between islam and christianity. there are also conflicts between muslims among themselves or even between christian tribes, although the main conflict is between christians and muslims. this shows that what is really going on is not a religious war, but tribal conflicts, ethnic conflicts, systematically - and this must be said - fomented by interested circles, including those in the oil companies. i am therefore very grateful that this resolution addresses it very clearly: the problematic role of certain commodity interests, which also exist in the caucasus and the congo, and the abuse of ethnic conflicts to increase brutally one's own profits. the european union is therefore not only called upon to intervene in a special way with the people of sudan, to work towards a peaceful solution and to put pressure on all parties to the conflict, but we are also obliged to deal seriously with our european oil companies operating there and to make them aware of their responsibility for this strategically important region of the world and for the people there. (applause from the centre)
the commission mr president, the promotion of a peaceful solution and respect for human rights and humanitarian law remain at the heart of relations between the commission and sudan. the current conflict and the persistent violations of human rights represent the main obstacle to the socioeconomic development of the country, as several interventions have appropriately highlighted. the commission is firmly convinced that respect for human rights would make it possible to bring peace to sudan. in line with the conclusions adopted by the council in june 2002, the union intends to proceed in a phased manner. until a peace agreement is concluded, the union will pursue the political dialogue on the basis of the commitments made by the government of sudan for 2002 on human rights, democracy and the rule of law, with particular attention to the signing of a peace agreement. if such an agreement is concluded, the union will begin to normalise its relations with sudan, in the context of the cotonou agreement, on the basis of respect for human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law; at the same time, the peace process and conflict resolution will be promoted. it is envisaged that a national strategy paper and a national indicative programme will be signed after the conclusion of the peace agreement or when the commission considers it politically appropriate, after consulting the member states. i can add, also in relation to specific points that have been raised, that the commission will be participating in the visit of the european union troika to sudan scheduled for december, during which the 2002 eu-sudan political dialogue will be evaluated. i would like to stress, however, that the implementation of the measures envisaged in the national strategy document is conditional on progress in the political dialogue.

- doc. b5-0591/2002 by mr van hecke and mr van den bos, on behalf of the eldr group, on torture and murder by the military regime and the human rights situation in bangladesh; - b5-0596/2002 by mr vinci, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on bangladesh; - b5-0602/2002 by mr thomas mann and mr martens, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on human rights in bangladesh; - b5-0606/2002 by mrs carrilho and others, on behalf of the pse group, on the human rights situation in bangladesh; - b5-0609/2002 by mrs lambert and others, on behalf of the green group in the european parliament, on bangladesh.
- mr president, i have to go. the escalation of violence in bangladesh in recent weeks has reached a new dimension. in october alone, some 40,000 soldiers were mobilized in the military operation clean heart, under the pretext of combating rising crime and private gun ownership. several thousand people were arrested. we know from independent, reliable sources that this military operation by the islamist government in bangladesh was primarily aimed at its critics. among those arrested are members of parliament from the opposition parties, including former minister chowdhury. this includes the heads of unpopular ngos. they were abducted by the army units without any legal authority. most of the suspects are relatives or sympathizers of the hindus. but these have been living peacefully with the muslim majority for decades as a minority. the increasing, radical islamization of society and of political rulers is creating ever greater problems in everyday life. the prisoners are isolated from the outside world. many are being tortured. hundreds of injured had to be treated in hospitals. last month alone, there were 25 deaths. the army's claim that they all died of heart attacks is cynical. it is inhumane and in violation of the united nations charter of human rights. the position of the epp-ed group is clear: we call on the government of bangladesh to return to the rule of law, pluralism and parliamentary democracy. the imprisoned parliamentarians and other innocent people must be released. i agree with mr van den bos that we need an independent body to be set up to investigate arrests, ill-treatment and killings. only then will bangladesh be able to return to the necessary domestic political stability. the european union, commissioner monti, must also make its contribution. in our resolution we called on the commission, on a bipartisan basis, to send observers to bangladesh before there is further discrimination and persecution. the agreement between the european union and bangladesh is based on the consistent respect for human rights and democratic principles. if these rights are to continue to be violated, we must apply political pressure and then we must also succeed in suspending such cooperation. such important signals are known throughout asia and other countries as well. we in the saarc delegation can confirm this again and again. we hope that the responsible people in bangladesh will understand this, also because of the great pressure that can be exerted within saarc. only then can the serious interlocutors in bangladesh be taken seriously at the international level. (applause from the centre)
commission. – mr president, while politically motivated violence and confrontation, as well as the prevailing law and order situation, have been a major concern for the bangladeshi population for years, the european union and the international donor community in general are fully aware that the law and order situation has worsened during the last year. the eu has underlined its concern at the deterioration of law and order and the increase in violence against minorities in its 'human rights in the world' speech at the 58th session of the un commission on human rights. the european union is very concerned about the general human rights situation and the continued reports of torture and deaths in custody, following the launch of operation clean heart, aimed at halting the decline in law and order in bangladesh, to which several members referred to a few minutes ago. we are also very concerned about the possible bias in the implementation of this operation and about the delays in implementing or failure to implement reforms such as the separation of the judiciary from the executive, the ombudsman and the creation of an independent human rights commission. the eu consequently welcomes the european parliament's resolution on operation clean heart and the general human rights situation in bangladesh. however, there are a couple of points in the resolution which we believe no longer reflect the current situation or are not substantiated by evidence on the ground. if one compares the situation of politically-motivated violence against the hindu community before and after the national elections, we can see that reported violence and intimidation of minorities has significantly decreased. we should send a clear message calling on the government to ensure that the rights and security of all minority communities are fully respected. as regards operation clean heart, it must be noted that donor communities, as well as civil society, have frequently voiced their concern over the deteriorating law and order situation during this government's first year in office. the government launched the operation as a result of this pressure and the failure to deal with the situation by introducing new laws and tightening up on the existing ones. while we acknowledge the need to improve the law and order situation – and we are ready to support the government of bangladesh in its attempt to restore law and order – we firmly believe that this must be done under the rule of law and with full respect for human rights. under no circumstances can exceptions to these principles be allowed. that is why the european commission, through its delegation in dhaka, will continue to monitor the situation and the political developments very closely.

- mr president, i have to go. we have been discussing the human rights situation in this parliament for less than a month, on 23 october. we have all condemned the death sentences and the stoning and, in general, the inhuman treatment of its citizens by the iranian system. we also regretted - at least my group - that the council had decided not to bring forward a human rights resolution on iran at the next meeting of the un commission on human rights. now, shortly after, someone is sentenced to death who has done nothing but demand: think about everything! do not let your opinions be taken for granted, and do not follow a priori a religious dogmatism! in this situation, the european union is continuing to negotiate cooperation agreements, economic cooperation. i do not think the wording of the resolution is sufficient. it is of course good that in future cooperation agreements reference is made to human rights. i think it is better - and i say this on behalf of my group - that there are no cooperation agreements and that they will not be concluded at all unless human rights are respected. it is schizophrenia. we also have very few opportunities to exert real pressure. the possibility of putting economic pressure on iran should not be taken for granted. of course it's positive that the students are going out into the streets. it is of course positive that president chatami has said that this judgment is unacceptable. of course, it is positive that the speaker of the iranian parliament is in the same boat. but that has not changed the structure of iranian society as it is today. i think it is also no coincidence that legitimate opposition in iran is being eliminated by the iranian religious leaders and by the iranian government, by trying to label them as terrorist organizations and put them on the appropriate lists, so that they get rid of this opposition once and for all. i also believe that we have a great responsibility. we need to pay more attention to who gets on these lists and what reasons someone gets on the lists. we must ask ourselves and as the european union we must not always be a subsidiary of the executive. we therefore call on the commission to make it clear and unequivocal in the next negotiations that there will be no economic cooperation with iran and no cooperation as long as this inhuman system continues to violate human rights as it does at present.
- mr president, the case of dr. aghajari has rightly attracted great attention and concern in iran and abroad. i share the view of the president, the iranian president majlis karubi, who has described the death penalty as a disgrace to the country's judiciary. however, i am not so convinced that the country's religious leader, ayatollah khamenei, has instructed the country's judiciary to review the verdict out of conviction. rather, chameney's past behavior suggests that he is trying to buy time. the student demonstrations are expected to slowly wane, as is the attention of the national and international public. however, the demonstrations have made it clear that the protesters are not just about dr. aghajari, but about the desire for more democracy in general. this judgment, like many others, is not really religious but politically motivated. we know this from europe, when the separation of church and state was not yet established. christianity too was used by the rulers to the point of obscurity to assert their own claims to power. but iranian society is a long way ahead of the conservative judiciary and clergy. this is reflected, among other things, in the recent reform proposals of the iranian parliament, which seeks to limit the absolute power of the guardian council. i call on the council and the commission to continue the human rights dialogue in all contacts and to be clear that there will be no trade and cooperation agreement without the european parliament. the opposition in the iranian parliament, both at home and abroad, also has high hopes that our contacts with this country are not motivated solely by economic interests. i think that we will also be making these statements and this basic attitude when we, as the european parliament, receive our colleagues from the iranian parliament on their return visit. we will always be clear that we are on the side of greater democracy and not on the side of those who want to turn the wheel of centuries back.

the commission mr president, we are very concerned about the new round of arrests and sentences against reformists and those exercising their fundamental right of expression in iran. after his speech system by refusing to appeal. tehran has been the scene of several days of violent student protests and, fortunately, president khatami has spoken out against the sentence, which was ordered to be reviewed on november 17 by supreme leader khamenei. in the past, we have repeatedly called on iran to impose the death penalty only on those responsible for the most serious crimes, in accordance with its obligations under the international covenant on civil and political rights. in its conclusions of 21 october, the council agreed to open a human rights dialogue with iran, reiterating its concern on this matter, including violations of civil and political rights, in particular freedom of expression. it also recalled its longstanding and stubborn opposition to the death penalty. on 18 and 19 developments with the greatest attention, keeping in touch with parliament and the member states. i would add that the commission believes that the opening of negotiations, which will also include a political dialogue, is in the interests of both iran and the european union - see the conclusions of 17 june - not to mention that the trade and cooperation agreement will contain a human rights clause. the negotiating process also allows pressure to be exerted while supporting president khatami and the reformists.

court of auditors. (es) mr president, mr secretary-general, honourable members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to present to you today the annual report of the european court of auditors for the financial year 2001. i have organized my speech around four main points: first, the analysis of budgetary management; second, the follow-up to the court's previous observations; third, the statement on the reliability of the accounts (sad); and fourth, the reform of the commission. let us begin with the analysis of the implementation of the budget. for the second year in a row, there was a large budget surplus of over eur 15 billion (16% of the final budget). the surplus is due to the cancellation of appropriations mainly due to the delay in implementing structural measures. the budget should have been amended to balance the revenue and expenditure forecasts. another determining feature of budgetary management has been the low use of payment appropriations in some areas. in the case of the structural funds, the rate of utilisation was below 70%, the lowest level since 1999. the implementation of pre-accession aid, especially the sapard programme, has also been slow, with only 9.2% of appropriations paid. in addition, the final beneficiaries of this programme have received only eur 1 million and, if implementation is not accelerated, appropriations will have to be cancelled in 2003. the commission should continue its efforts to clean up the accounts by cancelling those commitments which are no longer operational. outstanding commitments to be settled total more than eur 12 billion in external aid and almost eur 3 billion in new pre-accession instruments. the implementation of the european development funds is also slow. after four years of operation, only 30% of the 8th edf has been disbursed. in conclusion, the estimates of implementation and payment of the programmes should be more realistic and adjusted to the absorption capacity of each country. the result would be a more rigorous and balanced budget. the court has examined the follow-up to its previous observations. in general, the commission has taken appropriate measures to correct the shortcomings identified, for example by simplifying the customs outward processing arrangements, improving the system for promoting joint ventures in the fisheries sector and revising the tendering procedures for the tacis programme. other sectors have not developed so well, such as the durum wheat aid scheme, where the shortcomings identified by the court in 1998 remain and where eur 450 million is unnecessarily spent each year. this is also the case in the common organisation of the market in sugar, where, despite the 2001 reform, problems of overproduction and high prices persist. i hope that the setting up of the audit monitoring committee will enable the commission to pay greater attention to the follow-up of the court's reports. let us now look at the declaration of reliability. the court considers that the accounts for the 2001 financial year reflect accurately the revenue and expenditure and the financial situation of the communities. however, the report contains some reservations and observations, which are largely due to shortcomings in the accounting system, as already pointed out by the court. in its response to our report, the commission acknowledges the shortcomings and undertakes to present a plan to modernise the accounting system by the end of 2002. the court will monitor the design and implementation of this plan and will, of course, inform parliament of its progress. as in previous years, the court considers that the transactions relating to revenue, commitments and administrative expenditure are legal and regular. however, due to the errors detected, we cannot yet offer that guarantee for the other payments. the majority of errors are in payments relating to agricultural policy and structural operations, i.e. in the areas of shared management between the commission and the member states, which account for 80% of the budget. reducing the incidence of errors requires a significant improvement in the administration and control systems, both in the commission and in the member states. thus, in relation to the common agricultural policy, the declarations submitted by the beneficiaries of the subsidies have not improved compared to previous years. the implementation of the integrated administration and control system has not been completed and in almost half of the member states the system for identifying bovine animals, which has been compulsory since 2000, has not been introduced. other errors relate to deficiencies in member states' controls, for example in the case of olive oil and cotton. the court's recommendations obviously involve the full application of the control mechanisms provided for in the regulations. in the case of structural operations, irregular payments were again detected due to weaknesses in the control systems and declarations of expenditure of the member states. the court is concerned about the delay in the implementation of the management and control arrangements for the new programming period by the national administrations. inspection units are not functioning and there is no independent control of operations. it is recommended that the commission intensify its checks and systematically exploit the results obtained. in the area of internal policies, managed directly by the commission, the analysis of the fifth framework programme for research has revealed incorrect payments due to non-compliance with contracts by beneficiaries. the court recommended simplifying the systems for reimbursing expenditure and introducing more effective penalties. national authorities in beneficiary countries and non-governmental organisations play a key role in the management system of external aid programmes. the analysis of the supporting documentation, which is available at central level in brussels, shows that the commission has made the commitments and payments legally and regularly. however, the court is not sure that these operations have been properly implemented in the beneficiary countries. control systems are inadequate and frequent errors have been detected on the ground. the commission should deepen the transformation of external aid, which has already made positive progress. to conclude this point, i would like to open a small parenthesis. in recent months we have witnessed a heated debate on the commission's accounting system. this is good and i hope that the interest generated will serve to promote the reforms long advocated by the court. however, in some respects the debate has lacked rigor and serenity. it is time to put some order and establish an objective map of the situation. in this connection, it should be stressed that, despite certain reservations, the commission's accounts are reliable; thus, with the exception of perhaps a few specific aspects, the figures supplied by the budgetary accounts correspond to the actual implementation of the appropriations. this opinion is backed up by rigorous and professional audit work, in which the court invests considerable resources. but as a result of this work, the court has criticised the accounting system. the shortcomings identified make it difficult to obtain better quality information, which is necessary to improve management. i am referring, for example, to the shortcomings of the balance sheet in presenting the commission's assets and liabilities. the court has been insisting on these shortcomings for years, and it seems that its observations are finally getting some support. we are now demanding decisively that the commission take corrective action; next year, in this same forum and with the same determination, we will demand results and i hope they will be positive. in the meantime, let us please let the commission concentrate on the task, which is not a simple one. let us now turn to what i consider to be the crucial theme of the report: the reform of the commission. 2001 was a transitional year in which significant progress was made, especially in financial management and internal control. the court's main observations on this point are as follows: first of all, some measures are not being introduced within the time limits. this delay is mainly due to an initial timetable which was too ambitious, as the court has already pointed out. secondly, the council has adopted a new financial regulation which the court considers to be adequate overall. although there are still some unsatisfactory elements, it is a good instrument which will improve the administration of community funds. the directors-general have drawn up a report on their activities and made a statement on the quality of information and internal control. this accountability of the manager is one of the keys to the success of the reform. this is a real revolution in the commission's management culture. we recommend improving the methodology for drawing up reports and declarations: the date for submission should be brought forward; more precise guidelines should be established to avoid ambiguity, to specify possible observations and reservations and to define more rigorously the action plans. the commission has summarized the reports and statements of the directors-general in a document sent to parliament and the council. this document includes an action plan to correct the problems identified. the plan should address more in-depth issues such as monitoring of internal control rules or reform of sincom. finally, one aspect of the reform requires more attention. this is the management of programmes by the member states, known as 'shared management'. the commission is having difficulty integrating into its strategy concrete actions to verify and improve the functioning of these management systems, which cover more than 80% of the budget. the commission is unable to do this on its own and will therefore need the active cooperation of the national authorities. i believe this message serves as a conclusion to my presentation. the reform is progressing positively. the commission has fulfilled its commitment to work vigorously on improving its administrative and control practices. however, it will take some time to achieve the excellent and exemplary administration we all want. this is a laborious process to which all the institutions must contribute their expertise. the court shall each year review progress made, report on shortcomings and recommend any measures it deems necessary. i am very grateful for your attention. (applause) i would like to thank
the commission. mr president, mr president of the european court of auditors, members of the european parliament and the court of auditors! i would like to thank the president of the court of auditors very warmly for his speech and for his strong support for the reform of the commission. i would like to thank all the members of the court of auditors and the auditors for the good cooperation they have shown throughout the year and for the recommendations made by the court of auditors, which are essential for the proper use and administration of the european budget. i would also like to thank you for the methodological openness, particularly with regard to the declaration of assurance. i too can concentrate on three points, as the president of the court of auditors did, namely the 2001 surplus, the accounts and the reform of the commission. the annual surplus of 15 billion is criticized by the court because it does not come from savings, which would be a positive thing, but because the budgetary estimates adopted by parliament were not used up, because programmes, especially in the structural policy, simply started more slowly than planned. the surplus is the difference between the estimates and the actual figures as recorded in the cameralist accounting, which is the accounting of the parliament. why was the discrepancy so great in structural spending? the commission always relies on proposals and forecasts from the member states, and it is simply working on unrealistic assumptions. i reiterated yesterday in ecofin that there is still no systematic procedure in the member states to make a sound forecast of the actual amount of appropriations that can be called up in a financial year. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the surplus of a financial year shall be credited to the member states as revenue for the following year in accordance with the financial regulation. we have done this mainly through two supplementary budgets, which have also played a role as instruments in the debate on the budgetary regulation. as regards the accounts, the court has again, as in previous years, found that the annual accounts for the financial year 2001 give a true and fair view of the community's revenue and expenditure and of its financial position at the end of the year. the court examines in detail the accounting system, including, of course, the cash management system. the commission has not yet taken any action to ensure that the budget is properly used. the court shall carry out detailed audits of the accounts and the presentation of the accounts. the court has again made restrictive remarks on the accounting of assets and he here calls for the system to be further developed. as you know, the new financial regulation will make it compulsory for all the institutions to have an integrated periodic statement of assets from 2005. this is also true of the european parliament. i would like to make a fundamental point, as the president of the court of auditors has done, to clarify the situation, because i have the impression that there is confusion here. traditionally, the accounting of the public sector is the cash accounting, i.e. the accounting of revenue and expenditure in relation to what has been established as budgetary estimates by the budgetary legislator. the system thus reflects the responsibility of the budgetary authority. in some member states, accounting is still based on this principle and it is wrong to say that this cash accounting is per se susceptible to fraud. but for an efficient administration, this information is not enough, and that is the concern of the court of auditors, which it has been stressing for years, and that is also the concern of the commission. the adoption of commercial standards in the public sector is strongly linked to the overall reform of the administration in the commission, but also in some member states in particular. these are the points which are so important for the budget and especially for the balance sheet. however, intermediate bodies must be able to obtain more information from the accounts. we are committed to further development, and the court urges us to do so, including improving the underlying computer system. we have a high-performance computerized accounting system. the medium-sized enterprises in all the directorates-general and in the representations are grouped together in a system which some member states can only dream of. here too, there have been various false claims that 4,000 officials could make direct transactions, almost arbitrarily. that's wrong too! they have the duty to put everything together in a system and the actual transactions are then carried out by the directorate-general for budgets. there have been various measures to improve this. the improvements in the area of security, i.e. access for system managers, which the court of auditors had warned about on several occasions, were also a concern this year. the committee on budgetary control of the parliament has the important task of examining the financial statement year by year, and if you need help with that, my services are of course always at your disposal. if you, mr elles, have decided that your group will use external aid, that is of course a matter for your group. as regards the hearings of a suspended official, the conference of presidents had dealt with them and the official was informed of them and of the proceedings in progress at your request, but that is all. in conclusion, i would like to thank mr fabra vallés again for the fact that the court of auditors, on the basis of a rigorous and professional audit, has confirmed the reliability of the commission's accounts. the commission is currently finalising a precise approach to further modernising the accounting system, which takes account of the court of auditors' suggestions and criticisms. i shall be able to present it to parliament in january. the third point concerns the area of reform. the commission has taken a number of measures which are far-reaching. in the budgetary field, as you know, activity-based budgeting is changing the way the budget is drawn up. the commission's annual policy strategy for strategic planning in the college is also a major change. the internal audit service and the central financial service were also established. the most important thing is the decentralization of responsibility for accountability, which is reflected in the report by the directors-general. it shall state whether the objectives set out in the annual plan have been achieved and whether a statement can be made to the financial management that all control measures have been put in place and are functioning. these are also new structures, such as this annual reporting, which we did for the first time in 2001, and the court of auditors rightly notes that the declarations of the directors-general are still too different to be used as a basis for a kind of single audit concept. the commission agrees with this statement and we will shortly adopt appropriate improvements to be passed on to the directorates-general. i would like to take up one suggestion made in the court's report, which will also be relevant to the work of the committee on budgetary control, namely that the annual reports of the directors-general should also specifically state which recommendations of the court have already been implemented and which steps have been taken to reduce any criticism. that is a very substantial and very good proposal. we'll take him in. this will make the work of the budget commissioner easier, and it will also make the work of the committee on budgetary control easier. i would also like to congratulate the court of auditors on its 25th anniversary and to thank it once again, on behalf of the commission, for the work it has done. i should also like to address a word to the main rapporteur, mr casaca. the work on the discharge procedure has already begun. they submitted a very extensive questionnaire. the commission will do its utmost to provide you with satisfactory answers within a reasonable time, i.e. by 18 december. the questionnaire also showed: it will be a very intensive cooperation, mr rapporteur, and i can say this for the committee, but at the same time, in my opinion, a very good one. the commission mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, in 1993 the european council in copenhagen launched the current enlargement process, which is the largest in the union's history. after almost ten years, we're about to arrive at the port. at the end of next week the heads of state and government will meet again in the danish capital to take the final decisions. what will be discussed in copenhagen? basically, three arguments: first, to conclude the negotiations with the 10 applicant countries mentioned in the commission's report last october; secondly, to strengthen the pre-accession strategy through which we intend to help romania and bulgaria to accelerate their preparations for accession to the union; thirdly, to decide on the next steps in the application process for turkey. i will illustrate these three points in my speech today. before that, however, let me mention the decisions we must make to manage the three big transitions of 2004: the accession of the new member states, the appointment of the new commission and the elections to the european parliament. we can build the busy calendar of political and institutional appointments for 2004 on the basis of the reflections currently taking place in parliament on how to harmonise the different deadlines for the arrival of new member states and the european elections. to this end, i believe that the indications coming from the council can, if necessary, be subject to verification and supplementation in order to accommodate parliament's specific interests as best as possible. i suggest that we should give the most practical sequence of events and, in the absence of any indication from the treaty, follow common sense. it is a very important political signal that the european elections are the focal point of the institutional action for enlargement. the new parliament will immediately be hosting the elected members of the new member states in their full capacity, and in this way it will be able to approve with full legitimacy the new college which will take office as soon as possible. how does the copenhagen summit look in terms of its main theme, enlargement? the brussels european council reached agreement within the union on the major supply balances to be submitted to the ten applicant countries, especially on agricultural and budgetary matters. the european council conclusions were immediately presented to the heads of state or government of the candidate countries and were generally welcomed. however, there are still many issues to be resolved before an agreement can be reached that is acceptable to all parties. the presidency of the council and the commission have worked and will work tirelessly to achieve this agreement. without going into the details of the discussions under way, i would like to mention a few of the main points: firstly, we must find a way to respect a principle we all share, namely that the candidate countries cannot be in a position to receive net inflows from the european union in 2004, 2005, 2006 that are less than those in the year 2003. secondly, the candidate countries must be helped to prepare themselves better to take over the control of the union's external borders, which means enabling them to carry out their schengen tasks fully. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. firstly, on all these issues the commission fully supports the danish presidency and the efforts it has made and is making to reach the necessary compromise. some member states have expressed reservations about the content of the offer to the candidate countries, reservations which we do not share, and i share the view of mr rasmussen, president of the council, that a reasonable offer should be made. this will enable the representatives of the applicant countries to defend the results achieved in copenhagen before their public. we must remain within the general framework defined by the brussels european council, but we must also be open, flexible and generous. secondly, last week i publicly called on the political leaders of the applicant countries to show realism in this final phase of the negotiations. i should like to point out that there are still many open questions, and we have only a few days left. we can't take a risky situation without taking a step forward. there are historical circumstances in which small sectoral interests, even if legitimate, must bow before the general interest: that is the law of democracy, and we must apply it. i would like to emphasize once again that most of the points of the final compromise must be decided at the next general affairs council on 9 and 10 december. we cannot allow the european council to be faced with the need to decide on dozens and dozens of particular points. i therefore appeal to the political leaders of the candidate countries and the 15 member states to show their wisdom. the latest difficulties must be resolved swiftly in the spirit of partnership and friendship, as has already been the case in all accession negotiations. as regards the conclusion of the negotiations with cyprus, i should like to comment on the latest developments. as is well known, the european union has always supported the efforts of the un secretary-general, and in recent weeks kofi annan has taken the courageous initiative of proposing a comprehensive resolution plan, which deserves our full support. the parties' response was generally positive. they have accepted the proposals as an acceptable basis for the - the next item is the report (a5-0397/2002) by mrs sörensen, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the proposal for a council directive on the short-stay residence permit for victims of illegal immigration or trafficking in human beings who cooperate with the competent authorities (com (2002) 71 - c5-0085/2002 - 2002/0043 (cns)).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. international estimates suggest that traffickers abduct up to 700,000 people each year, mostly women and children. the european union is attracting 120 000 women and children from central and eastern european countries alone every year. these figures do not take into account illegal immigration or human smuggling. this highlights the urgency of tackling this form of organised crime through coordinated cooperation. the draft directive providing for short-term residence permits for victims who cooperate with the competent authorities is an important step. until now, there were no pan-european rules on the treatment of victims of illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings. but to combat this form of crime, we need europe-wide standards. the common practice of deporting illegally arrived persons is not called into question by the short-term residence permit proposed here. instead, authorities are given the opportunity to obtain information and evidence through cooperative victims for the purpose of apprehending and prosecuting traffickers and smugglers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat organised crime, including the introduction of a system of 'common minimum standards' for the protection of victims of crime. a short-term residence permit for cooperative victims, on the other hand, includes the ability to identify structures, disrupt criminal networks and prosecute perpetrators. that must be the target. i would like to take this opportunity to thank patsy sörensen, who has worked very hard on this report. i would like to thank the commission and the other groups for the good cooperation which, in my view, has led to a good outcome and conclusion in this report. president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission will be presenting its second contribution to the convention today, which will deal with the future institutional architecture of the union. i want to make it clear from the outset, in order to avoid any misunderstanding caused by press reports, that i am presenting today, as planned, the only text that the commission has adopted. as for the document on the constitution of the european union, which has been echoed in the press, it is nothing more than a technical exercise, a feasibility study which commissioners barnier and vitorino and i have commissioned from a group of legal experts from the commission in order to get a first idea of how a treaty could be organised. this document is essentially based on the structure of the preliminary draft submitted by the praesidium to the convention. as i have said, this is a technical working document and has not been discussed or approved by the college, which is therefore not politically responsible for its content. although it was mainly designed for internal use, i felt it was my duty to inform president giscard of this and, in the interests of transparency, we decided to make it available on the internet by this evening, in order to offer - as others have already done - a working tool to the convention and to anyone who might find it useful. to set the tone for my presentation and the debate that will follow, i would like to recall a key figure in the first major foundation of the european project. explaining his famous method, jean monnet said: i never thought we could change human nature, but we can change the context in which people operate. by giving the same rules and the same democratic institutions, we can get men to behave differently among themselves. in the community, europeans thus learn to live together as one people. we are not bringing states together, we are bringing people together. if we are to look forward today, far ahead, we must stand on the shoulders of the great statesmen who have gone before us. it is a gesture of seriousness and humility, and it is with humility that i propose to take up monnet's intuition in view of the great challenges of the future. to unite all the citizens of europe we must create complete harmony between the states and the peoples. the debate over the last few months, since the convention took office, has already cleared up many doubts and answered many questions. firstly, this debate has made it clear that the citizens do not want the union to withdraw from the fields in which it is present. in fact, people are calling for more europe in foreign policy, in the field of justice and security and in social matters. in addition, there is a broad consensus on the community method, which is at the root of so many of our successes. relations between the main institutions certainly need to be clarified and streamlined, but even the most sceptical have understood that without a strong community element europe would become less efficient but also less democratic. our contribution to the convention is to make these demands our own. in summary, it has three objectives: the union must become more democratic, more effective and clearer. the road to achieving them is not yet mapped out in detail, but we already know the starting and finishing points. the re-founding of europe must start from the dual nature of the union, which is a union of peoples and states, to which is added a third source of legitimacy for the union, namely the defence of the common interest. our path must lead us to build the world's first true supranational democracy. to give our structure a more democratic dimension, the role and responsibilities of the main institutions must be better defined. we therefore propose two innovations. the first concerns the procedure for appointing the commission. the president of the commission must be elected by the european parliament by at least two thirds of the votes cast and by secret ballot. the council then, after confirming the appointment of the president, appoints the other members of the commission in agreement with him or her. the european parliament finally approves the newly constituted full college. the second innovation concerns the commission's dual responsibility to the european parliament and the council. we propose that both institutions should have the right to censure the commission. this will bring greater balance to the institutional triangle and strengthen the commission's position as a guardian of the general interest. it is clear that this is a particularly delicate and courageous proposal, but in my view the system proposed distributes decisionmaking power more equitably between the representatives of the governments of the member states and the representatives of the peoples, that is to say between the council and parliament. for the same reason, we believe that we should generalise the codecision method. all european laws, always proposed by the commission, must be adopted by a majority in the council and also decided by the european parliament. finally, as i have often said in this house, the time has come to bring this house up to the level of any other democratically elected parliament by reforming the union's financing, which is the hallmark of this kind of responsibility of all the world's parliaments. we want to give the european parliament more power in deciding on resources. the union's budget must therefore be adopted by the european parliament and the council, following a procedure based on codecision, as we have just said. as the draft treaty submitted by the praesidium also recognises, the resources of the union should have their own character; the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure is thus made. ladies and gentlemen, the highlights of the communication are all part of one system. the democratic legitimacy of our institutions, for example, is closely linked to their functioning. our main proposals in this respect are summed up in three points: the first is the abolition of the unanimity rule, and that is because the darkest moments in the recent history of the union are linked to this rule. if the right of veto has sometimes led to paralysis of decision-making with 15 members, imagine what can happen with 25 or more. that is why i think that the majority rule should be general. however, the current weighting system is very complex and is not accessible to citizens, and not only to citizens: it's impossible for even the experts to understand. we therefore propose that the council should take almost all decisions by a simple double majority, that is to say, by a vote representing both the majority of the member states and the majority of the citizens of the union. for the most delicate decisions we obviously envisage the use of a strengthened majority. the second point concerns the presidency of the council, an issue which has caused rivers of ink to flow. in my view, the proposal put forward by several parties to create a president of the union creates more problems than it solves. (applause) i would like to thank if, on the one hand, it contributes to the continuity and visibility of the union, on the other hand, it denies the member states and deprives us all of participation at european level. there are two other problems. who would elect the president of the union? who should he answer to? and, above all, as prime minister verhofstadt said, what would you do for 360 days a year when the council is not in session and george bush does not call him? it is clear that this charge would open a breach in our institutional structure. we therefore recommend that the rotation system for the presidency of the european council, the general affairs council and the permanent representatives committee be maintained. for all other formations, we propose a new formula: the members of the council formations shall elect a president from among themselves, who shall hold office for one year. this formula gives greater continuity to the work and entrusts the presidencies to personalities who enjoy the full confidence of their peers. the third point concerns external representation. the union must act as a single actor on the international stage to defend its values and promote its model of society. in the field of trade, the union is already on an equal footing with other players on the international scene. so why can't we be just as credible politically? we must have imagination and courage here, because it is absolutely necessary to give the union a single voice in international politics. our solution is the union secretary for foreign affairs. this new figure is appointed by the european council together with the president of the commission and is also vice-president of the commission itself. similarly, it is clear that the secretary of the union must answer personally to both the european council and the president of the commission. however, as a member of the commission, he shares the responsibilities of the college towards the european parliament. as you can see, this is an important innovation, but, again, unavoidable. given the scale of the change - this is important - we have provided for a transitional period, at the end of which the secretary of the union would assume his full functions, which i want to indicate here briefly. the secretary of the union shall exercise the commission's right of initiative in foreign policy independently within the framework of the council's guidelines. the council, or a group of member states, may, however, request it to submit to the council appropriate proposals for the attainment of common objectives. the union secretary for foreign affairs is also responsible for implementing joint decisions and, more importantly, is the union's sole representative in foreign policy vis-à-vis third countries and other international bodies. several of the union's activities are linked to foreign policy, such as trade policy and development cooperation. the continuity of these actions will be ensured by the cooperation between the secretary of the union and the president of the commission, who in this case acts as coordinator. the question of the union's external representation also arises in the economic field. the question of the eurozone's representation in international fora must be resolved. the euro is a recognised economic force: it must also be a political force and must make its voice heard abroad. i now turn to the third and final point of our proposal: simplification and clarity. the current corpus of directives, decisions and regulations which together make up our legislative activity is perhaps the greatest barrier to citizens' understanding of the european institutions. the commission feels that it is time to put the instruments at our disposal in order. we therefore propose to classify the standards into only three categories: the council, acting by a qualified majority, shall adopt the laws referred to in article 1 (2) by a qualified majority of its component members. the constitutional treaty must draw a clear distinction between laws and implementing regulations. in addition, it is necessary to clearly define who implements european legislation. we propose that the commission alone should have the executive powers - i repeat, the executive powers - and that it should be accountable to parliament and to the council. the principle of transparency must also apply to the so-called comitology. we therefore think that it is appropriate to retain only the advisory committees. i repeat: when the legislator decides to implement a law at european level, the commission must have the executive responsibility. where, on the other hand, the commission is to exercise a delegated legislative function, it is appropriate that the two legislative branches - the council and the parliament - should be placed on an equal footing as regards the possibility of exercising control over the commission's activities, i.e. the so-called callback. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i said at the beginning, recalling the words of jean monnet, that we must look far ahead in this phase of the construction of a united europe. the debate, stimulated by the convention in recent months, has already greatly broadened our horizons. national parliaments and governments have believed in you from the start and have sent leading personalities to represent them. the convention's objective has become more ambitious. it is no longer simply a question of ensuring the functioning of the institutions after enlargement, but of defining the general shape of our union for the next generations. i'm happy about this development. the convention, which your parliament and i have strongly wanted, offers our citizens and the whole world a reflection on all aspects of our institutions. i'm also glad it's done in the sunlight. in the coming months a new united europe will be born, and we can be proud of having brought it into being in a transparent and democratic way. the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. first of all, i'd like to apologize for the hoarse voice. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease. in the late 1990s, after much debate, a directive was adopted allowing only dried, flavoured herbs and spices to be irradiated in the eu. the eu is now again faced with the decision whether to continue to allow only herbs and spices to be irradiated, whether to add to this list a few foods with problematic hygiene conditions such as frog legs and shrimp, or whether to allow the foods allowed in the transitional national rules such as potatoes, poultry, vegetables, shrimp, seafood, frog legs or egg whites. the commission - and the commissioner has just made this clear - has identified these three options in its communication, and in so doing it puts us, the ep, more or less in the position of having to decide whether to accept one of them. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has in fact taken a contradictory decision in its report. i think the commissioner responded shortly afterwards. on the one hand, paragraph 3 calls for us to take note of the commission's proposal that the current list could be considered complete, and it is argued that further herbs, spices and herbal condiments should only be authorised for irradiation in the eu if scientific evidence shows that this is safe and effective. at the same time, the environment committee proposes in paragraph 4 that the significant quantities of irradiated products in some member states should be included in the positive list if this technology can increase the safety of certain foods. this makes it clear that we do not have a clear position, because on the one hand we say in paragraph 3 that we want a very restrictive decision, but on the other hand we make it clear in paragraph 4 that we are in favour of a more far-reaching decision. however, the european parliament is quite clear about its position, as expressed in paragraph 5 of the report, that before amendments are submitted to include foodstuffs in the positive list, a thorough examination must be carried out for each foodstuff, demonstrating that all the conditions for authorizing food irradiation, as laid down in annex i to the 1999 directive, have been clearly fulfilled. the commission communication makes it quite clear, and the commissioner has just made it quite clear, that consumers do not want food irradiation, that even a large part of the food industry rejects food irradiation and declares it to be unnecessary. the eurotoc, an independent consumer initiative for healthy food - we all know the eurotoc chefs - also made it clear that irradiating food is not compatible with their self-image and within a few days they had also won a very large majority for their resolution against food irradiation. i think that this shows that the radiation directive is very critical and very contradictory. we must be clear about one thing: radiation is only useful if it is used to conceal, hide and perhaps to give consumers a false impression of a quality that does not exist. only then does irradiation make sense, because if we had good hygiene conditions, then the products would be perfect and would not need irradiation. secondly, it is essential to make them durable for long haul journeys. this is particularly evident in the shrimps that are brought from northern germany to morocco for shelling. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would therefore like to conclude by saying that the committee has taken very different positions on paragraphs 3 and 5 and tomorrow's vote will show whether we are acting in the interests of consumers and consumer protection or whether we are also making concessions to the industry, which has been lobbying heavily in recent weeks. i think we should all be aware that radiation is a very critical issue, that it can also involve certain risks, although we may not yet know all these risks, and that consumers reject them. i hope that tomorrow we will reach a decision in the interests of consumer protection so that the commission and the council can begin their work and that we will also make the report of the committee on the environment a little clearer in its contradictions and arrive at a clear position which will then also be a basis for the further work of the council and the commission.

commission. – madam president, in 1966 the community first established a comprehensive system to monitor and control the presence of residues in food of animal origin from the member states and from third countries. this system involves the setting up of a residue monitoring plan as well as a legal framework to allow for official controls and a practical infrastructure for laboratory testing. this legislation requires member states and third countries exporting to the eu to submit annually a monitoring plan for residues in products of animal origin. monitoring should be targeted at detecting illegal treatment of animals and at controlling compliance with the maximum residue limits for veterinary medicinal products, the maximum levels for pesticides and the maximum levels set in relevant legislation covering environmental contaminants. the residue plans are subject to an extensive evaluation procedure. only those third countries that have submitted satisfactory residue monitoring plans are allowed to export to the european union and be included in the appropriate list. this list is kept under constant review in order to take into account the results of the evaluation of the annual updates of residue monitoring plans. however, this approach must be complemented by measures on the ground. first, import controls must be carried out by the member states at the external borders of the union. secondly, the food and veterinary office verifies how the residue plans are implemented in the member states and third countries. over the last year, we have been particularly concerned about discoveries of banned veterinary medicinal products – namely chloramphenicol and nitrofurans – in food of animal origin. these substances are banned for use in food-producing animals in the european union because it has not been possible to set a safe level of residues due to their toxic effects on human beings. the commission has not hesitated to take measures whenever this problem has arisen. for example, imports from china of all products derived from farmed animals, including aquaculture, have been banned on the basis of the conclusions of an fvo mission, underpinned by discoveries of contaminated food. in other cases, it has not been necessary to ban imports, as the third countries concerned have initiated extensive action plans to resolve the problems – in particular the testing of all consignments exported to the european union and suspension of the offending establishments. these measures taken in third countries are complemented by strict, mandatory import controls to provide sufficient guarantees. this is the case for both thailand and brazil. the commission will ensure the maintenance of the necessary level of scrutiny on imported products to ensure a consistent approach to consumer safety. the rapid alert system for food and feed is the tool to disseminate all relevant information between member states and the commission, as well as to third countries. let me say that it is not just in relation to third country imports that the commission has identified problems of residues in food. indeed, residues monitoring plans carried out by member states also enabled the identification of contamination cases in food produced in the european union. some concerns have been raised – and the issue has been raised and the question sent to the commission by parliament – about the cancellation of fvo inspection missions to the third countries from which contaminated products have been identified. perhaps i should explain the background to this. indeed the commission has postponed a number of planned missions in respect of residues. these include missions to brazil and thailand. it is considered that such missions would be a waste of valuable resources at this moment as 100% testing is in place for poultrymeat from brazil and thailand and for shrimps from thailand. consignments which test positive are destroyed. these measures are necessary because there are serious failings in residue controls in the countries concerned. it is not necessary to send a mission team to establish what is already known. in the case of china there is already a comprehensive ban in place on exports to the european union on a range of products and increased testing is in place for other products. it is premature to carry out a mission now, as the commission is not convinced that the necessary preparatory measures have been put in place. instead it is considered best to await concrete evidence of progress in the form of regulatory controls, such as legislation and so on. however, in the coming months, fvo missions could be deemed necessary to assess the implementation of actions and the changes introduced by the third countries concerned in the area of residue monitoring. the fvo programme of inspection for 2003 mentions such missions. that is the position in regard to the issues that have been raised in the questions. i am happy to outline that for parliament.
